## Findings by confidence

### High-confidence MATERIAL roots

#### R45: Fail closed when a NIC identity read fails

Title: Fail closed when a NIC identity read fails
Severity: P1
Confidence: High
Gate verdict: MATERIAL
Evidence: `pkg/devicemap/devicemap.go:298-307` discards the per-interface netlink error and appends a successful-looking partial record:

```go
nic := PresentNIC{Name: name, PCIAddr: pci}
if link, err := netlink.LinkByName(name); err == nil {
    a := link.Attrs()
    nic.RunningMAC = a.HardwareAddr.String()
    if len(a.PermHWAddr) != 0 {
        nic.PermMAC = a.PermHWAddr.String()
    }
    nic.LinkUp = a.OperState == netlink.OperUp || a.Flags&1 != 0
}
nics = append(nics, nic)
```

`pkg/devicemap/devicemap.go:125-152` checks mismatch only when the observed permanent MAC is nonempty and otherwise returns `BindBoundPCIOnly`. `pkg/devicemap/devicemap_test.go:43-51` explicitly pins that empty observation as a successful PCI-only bind even when configuration includes a MAC.
Trace: Daemon startup calls `applyStartupNamingPolicy` -> `enumerateAndRenameMapped`; the swallowed per-NIC failure yields a Bound result and becomes a rename candidate. Commit preflight fails closed only when the whole enumeration returns an error, which this path suppresses. A replacement NIC occupying the configured PCI address can therefore pass without the configured permanent-MAC identity check and be durably renamed into a management or trust role.
Refutation attempt: A successful read can legitimately expose no permanent MAC for VFs or virtio, so unconditional rejection of empty `PermHWAddr` would be wrong. That does not refute the defect: the representation conflates successful absence with failed observation. Independent verifier tests confirmed matching PCI+MAC binds, mismatches refuse, and an empty observed MAC takes the PCI-only path; no startup, preflight, or show-layer guard recovers the discarded error.
HPC/invariant check: For configured dual identity, the PCI occupant must be MAC-checked or explicitly marked unreadable and refused. This is cold boot/commit work; retaining a validity/error state has no packet-path cost.
Why it matters: A transient identity-read failure on replacement hardware can bypass the topology-swap guard, rename the wrong management or zone NIC, and strand remote management or place traffic in the wrong trust domain.
Fix direction: Return typed per-NIC observation state distinguishing `read succeeded, no permanent MAC` from `identity read failed`. Abort mutation for mapped/protected dual-identity interfaces when observation is incomplete, expose uncertainty in diagnostics, and add injected `LinkByName` failure tests asserting zero rename side effects.
Labels: `critical`, `userspace-control`, `device-map`, `lifecycle`, `fail-closed`, `operator-truth`, `management-lockout`
Dedup note: #6546 covers duplicate logical entries, #6678 covers OriginalName fallback, #5842 covers later write/rename/reload failure, and #1958 is a broad architecture umbrella. None owns the lost per-NIC observation error.
Verified against origin/master: Still present at origin/master `ad959117748181dabe46b8ddc2827de670380cea` at `pkg/daemon/daemon_run_naming.go:90`. Independently retained in verify-R37-R48.md at the final target SHA.

#### R06: Binding-plan expansion registers new slots unarmed and disables the entire dataplane indefinitely

Title: Binding-plan expansion registers new slots unarmed and disables the entire dataplane indefinitely
Severity: High
Confidence: High
Gate verdict: MATERIAL
Evidence: the narrow live manager contract at `pkg/dataplane/userspace/manager_ha.go:601-607` suppresses the only global re-arm because it compares only the retained global bit: ```go func (m *Manager) syncDesiredForwardingStateLocked() error { if m.proc == nil || m.proc.Process == nil { return nil } desired := m.desiredForwardingArmedLocked() if m.lastStatus.ForwardingArmed == desired { return nil ```
Trace: Start with forwarding globally armed and every existing binding armed. Apply a valid snapshot that increases the binding plan, for example by adding a data interface or increasing the common RX-queue count. `snapshot.rs:344-350` replaces the old bindings with this replan. Existing numeric slots retain `armed=true`; each appended slot becomes `registered=true, armed=false`. Reconcile can bind its worker, but status computes `enabled=false` because the all-bindings predicate fails. The Go manager applies that disabled status, then its periodic desired-state loop sees `ForwardingArmed == desired == true` and sends no `set_forwarding_state`; therefore `set_bindings_forwarding_armed` never runs. The retained shim keeps transit fail closed until an operator explicitly toggles forwarding or another path happens to re-arm every binding.
Refutation attempt: I traced both snapshot branches, `replan_queues`, reconciliation, status refresh, BPF-manager status application, and the one-second desired-state loop. There is no post-replan propagation of global arm state. Existing planner tests cover only a same-identity/same-cardinality slot and manual unregistration, not plan expansion. The manager's skip predicate has no per-binding or `Enabled` condition. The candidate survives.
HPC/invariant check: Planning is cold-path, so the fix must not add packet work. Binding state must be preserved by stable `(interface/ifindex, queue_id)` identity, and every newly valid binding must initialize `armed` from the accepted global forwarding intent. A map built during replanning is acceptable; no atomics, locks, or per-packet allocation are needed.
Why it matters: A routine live config expansion or queue-count change causes a total, persistent transit outage on standalone and HA nodes. The posture is fail closed rather than fail open, but it can leave an HA standby permanently not takeover-ready and can drop traffic on the active node after commit.
Fix direction: Key preserved state by stable binding identity, not slot. Initialize a genuinely new valid binding as `registered=true` and `armed=guard.status.forwarding_armed`; clear all live socket fields when identity changes. Alternatively call a single arm-projection helper immediately after every replan. Add expansion, contraction, reorder, and armed-HA snapshot tests plus a Go test proving the periodic loop does not strand `Enabled=false` when global intent is true.
Labels: bug, userspace-dp, control-plane, binding-plan, HA, availability, fail-closed, vsrx-parity
Dedup note: Final 721-row searches used `replan_bindings`, `binding armed`, `forwarding_armed`, `slot binding`, `plan expansion`, and the consequence `enabled false`. GH#6702/C179-017 is the unbounded queue-count allocation boundary, not arm-state initialization. Historical #1921/#580 concern EBUSY/bind recovery, not a newly defaulted `armed=false` slot. No symbol+mechanism+consequence match exists.
Verified against origin/master: Still present at origin/master `ad959117748181dabe46b8ddc2827de670380cea` at `pkg/dataplane/userspace/manager_ha.go:601`. Independently retained in verify-R01-R12.md at the final target SHA.

#### R07: Failed forwarding/queue reconciliation retains requested state and suppresses automatic recovery

Title: Failed forwarding/queue reconciliation retains requested state and suppresses automatic recovery
Severity: High
Confidence: High
Gate verdict: MATERIAL
Evidence: `userspace-dp/src/server/helpers/status.rs:403-410` documents that a pre-teardown error leaves prior runtime state live, not that desired status was applied: ```rust // #3789: propagate the reconcile outcome. A pre-teardown abort // (integrity / mandatory-map failure) leaves the prior workers + // forwarding + generation live (#2440/#2484); the caller uses the // Err to fail closed instead of persisting a rejected snapshot. let result = state .afxdp .reconcile(snapshot.as_ref(), &mut bindings, ring_entries); state.status.bindings = bindings; ```
Trace: On a disarmed helper with an accepted snapshot, request `armed=true`. The handler sets the global and binding bits, then reconcile can fail during mandatory-map/integrity preflight or post-teardown worker bring-up. It returns `ok=false`, so Go discards the response status, but the Rust state retains the requested bits. The next status poll receives `ForwardingArmed=true`; `refresh_status` updates live fields but does not roll back desired `registered/armed`. Manager status application keeps binding rows non-READY/fail closed, records this status, and `syncDesiredForwardingStateLocked` returns early because global desired and reported arm bits now match. No automatic arm reconcile is retried. Queue registration failures similarly report requested bits rather than applied state.
Refutation attempt: I checked `requestDetailedLocked`: it discards an `OK:false` response, so the immediate caller cannot accidentally repair from its status. I then traced the periodic status poll, map application, busy-binding rebind watchdog, deferred-worker debt, and desired forwarding loop. None records debt for this handler error; the busy watchdog only handles its own error class, while desired forwarding compares only the retained global bit. The #6135 test asserts `ok=false` and error text but deliberately seeds/retains `forwarding_armed=true`; it has no rollback or retry assertion. The candidate survives.
HPC/invariant check: This is cold-path transactionality. The invariant is `reported applied state == successfully reconciled runtime state`; failed desired changes must either roll back or create explicit retry debt. Snapshotting a few booleans/BindingStatus entries is acceptable off path and adds no packet latency, lock, allocation, or cache-line traffic.
Why it matters: A transient pin, integrity, spawn, or bind fault can become a permanent total transit outage and an HA cold-boot/takeover-readiness failure even after the underlying fault clears. Status misleadingly says forwarding is armed, preventing the reconciler designed to heal desired-state drift from running.
Fix direction: Stage requested control state separately and commit it only after successful reconcile, or restore the previous global/per-binding values on every `Err`. Prefer explicit desired-vs-applied fields plus retry debt if asynchronous convergence is intended. Apply the same transaction helper to forwarding and queue/binding state handlers. Add fail-on-revert tests that inspect retained state and exercise the next manager poll/retry.
Labels: bug, userspace-dp, reconcile, control-plane, HA, cold-boot, availability, fail-closed, vsrx-parity

#### R08: Interface SNAT admits indistinguishable no-PAT return tuples and sends replies to the first session

Title: Interface SNAT admits indistinguishable no-PAT return tuples and sends replies to the first session
Severity: High
Confidence: High
Gate verdict: MATERIAL
Evidence: the narrow live consumer at `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/session_glue/mod.rs:1294-1301` installs reverse state from that selected match: ```rust let forward_match = lookup_forward_nat_across_scopes(sessions, shared_nat_sessions, &flow.forward_key)?; let (resolved, reverse_installed) = install_reverse_session_from_forward_match( sessions, session_map_fd, shared_sessions, shared_nat_sessions, shared_forward_wire_sessions, ```
Trace: Internal hosts A and B use the same source port and protocol to the same external server. Interface-mode SNAT rewrites only both source IPs to the same interface address, preserving the port; their external 5-tuples and return `SessionKey` are identical. Both handles occupy the same bucket, and `reply_matches_forward_session` recomputes the same identical key for both, so the first-installed session wins. The live reverse path synthesizes and installs its reverse decision from that match. A reply belonging to B is therefore rewritten/delivered to A (especially direct for UDP; TCP may subsequently reject on sequence state, but only after cross-host misdelivery/disruption).
Refutation attempt: I read all forward/reverse/canonical key transforms, the local and shared lookup order, and the reverse-install consumer. No ingress field, NAT binding ID, TCP sequence state, or other discriminator survives on the wire or enters `SessionKey`. Pool SNAT is safe because it allocates a unique translated port; interface SNAT does not. Scanning more candidates cannot recover information absent from the packet. The source test itself proves both candidates validate. The candidate survives.
HPC/invariant check: NAT admission must preserve a bijection for every simultaneously live translated tuple. Do not add an unbounded per-packet candidate scan; on collision at session-install time, allocate PAT for the later interface-SNAT flow or fail its install closed. The common noncollision hot lookup should remain one inline SmallVec element with no allocation or shared lock.
Why it matters: Concurrent ordinary client flows can suffer cross-host reply delivery, session hijacking, or deterministic denial. The bug is reachable without malformed packets and violates vSRX stateful NAT isolation.
Fix direction: Detect translated-tuple collision before publishing a no-PAT interface-SNAT session. Allocate a unique translated source port/ICMP identifier for the later flow, using the existing pool allocator discipline, or reject the flow if interface mode is contractually forbidden to PAT. Replace the current test's first-installed expectation with two uniquely reversible sessions and add UDP/TCP live-path tests across local/shared scopes and HA import.
Labels: bug, userspace-dp, NAT, interface-snat, session-integrity, security, HA, vsrx-parity
Dedup note: Final searches used `interface-mode SNAT`, `no-PAT`, `genuinely ambiguous`, `first-installed`, `nat_reverse_index`, `reverse tuple`, and `non-bijective`. Closed #1760/#4399/#4438 fixed single-value index displacement/deletion by introducing multimaps and validate-on-lookup. This is the residual admission bug: current code preserves both handles, but both validate because the tuples are information-theoretically identical. The mechanism and required fix differ, and no current 721-row item covers it.

#### R14: Kea LFC finish file is ignored as a zero-content marker, allowing a trusted-empty destructive lease view

Title: Kea LFC finish file is ignored as a zero-content marker, allowing a trusted-empty destructive lease view
Severity: High
Confidence: High
Gate verdict: MATERIAL
Evidence: `pkg/dhcpserver/lease_lfc.go:24` (9 lines) and `pkg/dhcpserver/ddns_leases.go:178` (8 lines) ```go //	<f>.2          PREVIOUS -- the COMPACTED result of the last COMPLETED cleanup //	                          (one row per active lease). Present once any LFC //	                          has run. //	<f>.output     kea-lfc's temporary compaction output. //	<f>.completed  kea-lfc's finish marker. //	<f>.pid        kea-lfc's pid file. // // The .output/.completed/.pid files hold no lease union we must read and are // ignored. ``` ```go func parseActiveLeases(path string, family int, now time.Time) ([]ddnsLease, error) { acc := newDDNSLeaseAccum() for _, f := range keaLFCLeaseFilePaths(path) { if err := parseActiveLeasesFileInto(f, family, now, acc); err != nil { return nil, err } } out := make([]ddnsLease, 0, len(acc.order)) ```
Trace: High MATERIAL: Kea moves the current memfile to input and starts a fresh current append log. LFC writes the compacted generation to output, moves it to the finish file, deletes previous and input, then moves finish to previous. During the post-delete/pre-final-rename interval, and after a crash there, `.completed` is the complete baseline while the assigned reader opens only `.2`, `.1`, and current (`lease_lfc.go:69-80`). A header-only current then validates and returns trusted-empty (`ddns_leases.go:193-198`); `keaLeaseParser` feeds that set directly to DDNS, whose pass 1 deletes every owned record absent from desired state (`manager.go:1290-1304`).
Refutation attempt: This was checked against the project-targeted Kea 3.0.x schema and the official [Kea 3.0 LFC documentation](https://kea.readthedocs.io/en/kea-3.0.0/arm/lfc.html). Kea documents `finish` as containing the completed output and retaining it until the other generation files are deleted. The live socket does not mitigate DDNS: display and HA sync can prefer `lease_cmds`, but `keaLeaseParser` calls the memfile parser directly (`ddns.go:45-58`). `lease_source_5938_test.go:172-207` creates an empty `.completed` fixture and therefore pins the incorrect assumption rather than the real state.
HPC/invariant check: LFC files form a generation protocol. Last-row-wins replay is valid only after selecting a complete generation; treating suffixes as an unordered union omits the sole committed baseline during a legal transition.
Why it matters: A routine cleanup or crash can make active leases disappear from the authoritative DDNS input and trigger bulk A/AAAA/PTR withdrawal. Display and memfile fallback can also under-report leases during the same phase.
Fix direction: Implement generation-aware LFC snapshot selection that recognizes `.completed` as the finished compacted generation and retries around unstable rotations. Prefer the live Kea socket for destructive DDNS when available; if generation completeness cannot be proven, return an untrusted error rather than trusted-empty. Add fixtures with populated `.completed`, absent `.1/.2`, and header-only current, including crash points before the final rename.
Labels: `dhcpserver`, `kea`, `lfc`, `ddns`, `data-loss`, `fail-open`
Dedup note: No `.completed`/finish-file ownership defect was found in `dedup-index.tsv` or `docs/issues/issue-history.md`. This is a residual of `#5796/#5938`, whose local invariant describes the finish file incorrectly.

#### R15: BootNext can remain armed while all durable software gates classify the node as unarmed

Title: BootNext can remain armed while all durable software gates classify the node as unarmed
Severity: High
Confidence: High
Gate verdict: MATERIAL
Evidence: pkg/upgrade/kernel_run.go:374 (8 lines) ```go 374 // Positively confirm the firmware accepted the one-shot BEFORE recording the 375 // verified-ARMED journal. If the readback disagrees (firmware silently 376 // dropped / partial-wrote the variable), do NOT advance to ARMED - stay 377 // ARMING and surface the error so no false-ARMED journal is persisted. 378 got, err = sys.GetBootNext() 379 if err != nil { 380     return fmt.Errorf("kernel-upgrade arm: read back BootNext (staying ARMING): %w", err) 381 } ```
Trace: `Arm` durably writes ARMING, `SetBootNext` succeeds, then readback, arm-record creation, or the final ARMED journal write fails. The firmware one-shot may still name the candidate, but `IsArmed` returns false for ARMING (`kernel_run.go:696-701`), `Promote` skips states below ARMED (`kernel_run.go:421-430`), and `xpf-kernel-promote` tests for exact `"state":"ARMED"`. On a later reboot the candidate can therefore boot as an ordinary image, with no promotion gate and no unconditional HA election hold. The shipped fake makes the mismatch concrete: `SetBootNext` stores `f.bootNext` at `kernel_test.go:123-126`; the injected `GetBootNext` error returns without clearing it at `:132-140`; `kernel_arm_two_phase_5847_test.go:48-54` then requires ARMING and `IsArmed == false`.
Refutation attempt: A readback mismatch can mean firmware dropped the write, but a readback error cannot prove that, and failures after a successful readback (`recordPromoteBinary` or `ktransition(ARMED)`) definitely occur after BootNext is set. There is no compensating BootNext clear/readback on any post-write error. Treating ARMING as armed everywhere would recreate the earlier false-armed availability failure when `SetBootNext` really did fail, so the current two-state model cannot represent "possibly armed" safely. Candidate survives.
HPC/invariant check: This is a crash-consistency/publish-order violation: external NVRAM state becomes effective before durable software state can authorize and contain it. It is cold-path work; the fix needs no dataplane allocation or hot-path branch.
Why it matters: A transient efivarfs read or journal/record write failure can turn a deliberately gated kernel trial into an ungated HA-eligible boot. A defective candidate may preempt or forward before verification, defeating the A/B rollback contract.
Fix direction: Persist a distinct fail-closed `ARMED_UNKNOWN`/possibly-armed intent with complete candidate and verifier identity before touching NVRAM. On every post-`SetBootNext` failure, clear BootNext and positively confirm the clear; if that cannot be proved, retain the fail-closed state and election hold. At boot, resolve the state from BootCurrent: gate/promote when the candidate actually booted, or clear it only after known-good is proved. Add crash/error tests after SetBootNext, readback, arm-record write, and ARMED journal fsync.
Labels: upgrade, kernel, UEFI, crash-consistency, HA, fail-open, vSRX-completeness

This is the inverse residual of the source's #5847 false-ARMED fix, not that defect repeated.

#### R16: Image-roll recreation erases the drain before the new node's authenticated identity is validated

Title: Image-roll recreation erases the drain before the new node's authenticated identity is validated
Severity: High
Confidence: High
Gate verdict: MATERIAL
Evidence: scripts/deploy/xpf-deploy.py:2327 (9 lines) ```python 2327 # it. The recreate wipes /var/lib on the node, so the node's own 2328 # lease is gone afterwards; from here the still-up PEER's lease is 2329 # the sole reservation (renewed every poll tick below), which is 2330 # what actually blocks a successor from acquiring both leases. 2331 _fence_before_mutate(runner, backend, [(node, nid), (peer, nid)], 2332                      holder, lease_ttl, f"image-recreate {node}") 2333 _recreate_node_from_image(runner, backend, node, args) 2334 2335 # 3. poll until the node is back AS THE EXPECTED NODE ON THE NEW ```
Trace: The old daemon's `ForceSecondary` drain is in-memory (`pkg/cluster/failover.go:140-167`). Recreation destroys that process and `/var/lib`; the fresh image has neither the manual-failover state nor the old kernel-upgrade journal that drives `kernelUpgradeHold`. The hook launches and applies day-0, allowing xpfd to join heartbeat/election before the driver first polls `xpf-version` and `/etc/xpf/node-id` at `xpf-deploy.py:2335-2384`. A stale but cluster-authentic image with the expected node ID can complete startup sync and, in supported `preempt` configurations, take primary immediately (`pkg/cluster/election.go:172-182`). The driver notices only afterward and can leave it participating for the entire boot deadline.
Refutation attempt: Non-preempt configurations usually preserve the incumbent, but preempt is a supported contract and can be immediate. Startup sync hold delays preemption until sync readiness; it does not bind the boot to the signed manifest version or orchestrator token. The kernel candidate hold is irrelevant on a fresh image, and the peer-side lease prevents a second orchestrator but does not suppress the new node's local election. Existing identity tests prove eventual rejection, not absence of forwarding before rejection. Candidate survives.
HPC/invariant check: Identity/configuration must be validated before publishing forwarding ownership. This is a cold control-plane sequencing defect; no dataplane cost is needed beyond a generalized startup election hold.
Why it matters: A stale alias, wrong build, or partially restored image can become primary and carry traffic before the orchestrator authenticates what came back, exposing incompatible protocol/dataplane behavior and undermining never-both-down/session-preservation guarantees.
Fix direction: Carry an authenticated image-roll quarantine token in the fresh day-0/config-drive state and set a generalized upgrade election hold before the first election. Release it only through an owner-bound API after exact signed image version, node ID, config generation, and session-sync readiness are confirmed. Add a preempt-enabled end-to-end test proving zero primary/forwarding eligibility before release.
Labels: deploy, image-roll, HA, election, preempt, identity, fail-open, vSRX-completeness

#### R17: An indeterminate qcow2 backing-file probe is treated as proof that no dependent overlay exists

Title: An indeterminate qcow2 backing-file probe is treated as proof that no dependent overlay exists
Severity: High
Confidence: High
Gate verdict: MATERIAL
Evidence: scripts/deploy/xpf-deploy.py:734 (9 lines) ```python 734 except FileNotFoundError: 735     return None 736 if r.returncode != 0: 737     return None 738 try: 739     info = json.loads(r.stdout) 740 except (ValueError, TypeError): 741     return None 742 bf = info.get("full-backing-filename") or info.get("backing-filename") ```

If qemu-img is removed, temporarily broken, denied one sibling, or emits malformed output after overlays were created earlier, every dependency becomes invisible. A nonzero probe can likewise be image-specific corruption/permission failure, not "no backing". Existing tests inject only known backing or explicit `None`; none exercise unknown/error. Candidate survives.

Why it matters: Replacing bytes beneath one or both HA qcow2 overlays can silently corrupt guest filesystems and both nodes' identity/configuration state in one operation.
Fix direction: Return a tri-state result (`NO_BACKING`, resolved path, `UNKNOWN/error`). Abort replacement on any unknown sibling or unreadable image directory, with the exact qemu-img error. #### R18: Golden replacement is an unlocked check-then-in-place-copy and races overlay creation or interruption

Title: Golden replacement is an unlocked check-then-in-place-copy and races overlay creation or interruption
Severity: High
Confidence: High
Gate verdict: MATERIAL
Evidence: scripts/deploy/xpf-deploy.py:790 and scripts/deploy/xpf-deploy.py:805 (8 source lines) ```python 790 golden = libvirt_golden_path(image) 791 if os.path.isfile(golden): 792     deps = _dependent_overlays(golden) 793     if deps: 805 print(f"==> installing verified qcow2 -> {golden} (libvirt golden)") 806 try: 807     os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(golden), exist_ok=True) 808     shutil.copyfile(srcq, golden) ```
Trace: No common lock spans `_install_libvirt_golden` and `libvirt_disk`'s `qemu-img create -b <golden>` at `xpf-deploy.py:835-847`. A deploy can create a new dependent after the installer's scan and before `copyfile`; the installer then truncates and rewrites the backing in place. Independently, process death, ENOSPC, or a failed copy leaves the existing golden partially overwritten. A synchronized focused reproduction created an overlay after the scan barrier and observed `race_overlay_created=True`, `race_golden_bytes=NEW-GOLDEN`, with no error.
Refutation attempt: Domain-name preflight does not serialize a concurrent `fetch --install-libvirt`, another VM name, or another tool. Atomic artifact verification protects source bytes but not destination publication. The lease flocks are remote HA-roll locks and do not guard `/var/lib/libvirt/images`. Existing disk tests are serial and assert only the preexisting-dependent case. Candidate survives.
HPC/invariant check: Dependency discovery and backing publication form one ownership transaction. The current check/use split violates that invariant; a host-local lock and atomic rename are cold-path operations.
Why it matters: A normal concurrent deploy/fetch or interrupted copy can corrupt every VM backed by the golden, commonly both HA nodes, or leave future launches on a truncated image.
Fix direction: Use a host-wide/per-golden flock shared by install, overlay create, and relevant destroy operations. Stage verified bytes to a same-filesystem private temporary file, fsync it, acquire the lock, rescan all siblings fail-closed, then atomically rename and fsync the directory. Never copy over the live golden inode in place.
Labels: deploy, libvirt, qcow2, TOCTOU, concurrency, atomicity, data-corruption

#### R19: Lease renewal stops during the arbitrary destructive hook and other unbounded remote mutations

Title: Lease renewal stops during the arbitrary destructive hook and other unbounded remote mutations
Severity: High
Confidence: High
Gate verdict: MATERIAL
Evidence: scripts/deploy/xpf-deploy.py:2436 (10 lines) ```python 2436 hook = args.recreate_hook 2437 if not hook: 2438     die(f"image-roll needs --recreate-hook <script> to recreate {node} from " 2439         f"the new image (the backend-specific destroy+launch+day-0 step). " 2440         f"This keeps the never-both-down sequencing here while the recreate " 2441         f"mechanics stay environment-specific.") 2442 env = dict(os.environ, XPF_ROLL_NODE=node, XPF_ROLL_BACKEND=backend) 2443 print(f"   recreating {node} via {hook}...") 2444 r = subprocess.run([hook, node], env=env) 2445 if r.returncode != 0: ```
Trace: The driver renews both leases once immediately before calling the hook (`:2323-2333`), then performs no keepalive until the hook returns. `subprocess.run` has no timeout; the same unbounded wrapper is used for remote drain/arm commands (`:1421-1433`). If the operation exceeds TTL, successor B can reclaim both serialized lease files while predecessor A's hook/remote command is still mutating. A later fence can stop A's next step, but cannot undo the concurrent destructive work already underway. `_renew_lease` also checks holder identity but not whether its own deadline already elapsed, so absent a successor it silently revives an expired lease after the call.
Refutation attempt: `docs/in-place-upgrade.md:1319-1324` documents sizing TTL above one uninterruptible hook and the default 1800 seconds is generous for ordinary VM launch. That is not a fencing guarantee for an arbitrary bare-metal hook, hung hypervisor, package install, or caller-selected positive TTL, and it contradicts the preceding claim that renewal never elapses while the driver is live. Existing tests advance time only in poll loops or inject loss at phase boundaries; none block inside the mutation while a successor reclaims. Candidate survives.
HPC/invariant check: Ownership must remain continuously valid for the complete side effect, not merely at call entry and exit. A background lease heartbeat is cold-path; a server-checked fencing token is needed to contain orphaned remote work.
Why it matters: Two live orchestrators can destroy/relaunch or drain/reboot the same HA pair concurrently, causing no-primary outages, unintended dual mutation, or irrecoverable half-roll state despite the advertised cross-orchestrator mutex.
Fix direction: Maintain an independent heartbeat for the load-bearing peer lease for the entire critical subprocess lifetime, bound local/SSH/incus execution, and pass a monotonically fenced roll token into hooks and remote mutations so the target verifies ownership immediately before each destructive step. On heartbeat uncertainty, terminate/cancel and refuse subsequent mutation. Test a blocked hook past TTL with a real successor acquisition.
Labels: deploy, HA, lease, fencing, concurrency, timeout, availability

#### R22: Changed SNAT/NAT64 pools reissue live translated tuples on retained addresses

Title: Changed SNAT/NAT64 pools reissue live translated tuples on retained addresses
Severity: High
Confidence: High
Gate verdict: MATERIAL
Evidence: the purported add/remove/reorder regression at `userspace-dp/src/nat64_tests.rs:4161` allocates from the old pool but only changes to a disjoint address: ```rust // A pool CHANGE (addresses added/removed/reordered) must NOT reuse the old // allocator — the round-robin counters are pool-position indexed, so stale // reservations against a different pool must not be replayed. The new flow // therefore starts fresh at the low port on the new pool address. #[test] fn nat64_4518_pool_change_resets_allocator() { let state1 = Nat64State::from_snapshots(&[single_addr_prefix()]); let dst_v4 = Ipv4Addr::new(8, 8, 8, 8); let c1: Ipv6Addr = "2001:db8::1".parse().unwrap(); ```
Trace: 1. Under pool `[A]`, flow F1 to remote tuple `(R, rport)` is the first allocation. `AddressOccupancy::claim` starts at cursor zero, so F1 receives `(A, port_low)` (`nat/allocator.rs:589-617`). Its forward session remains installed. 2. An in-process config refresh adds/reorders an address, renames the pool, or changes an overlapping port range. The refresh passes `Some(&self.forwarding)` into the builder (`afxdp/coordinator/snapshot_refresh.rs:273-288`), but source NAT reuses state only for the exact allocator key and NAT64 only for a byte-identical ordered pool. A changed pool containing A therefore starts a new zeroed allocator. 3. The refresh purges remapped tunnel sessions and swaps forwarding state (`snapshot_refresh.rs:371-380`); it does not purge sessions using the replaced NAT allocator. F1 continues forwarding with its stored `NatDecision`. 4. The first suitable post-refresh flow F2 to the same `(R, rport)` selects retained address A and `port_low`, because the new allocator has no occupancy record for F1. F1 and F2 now have an identical translated source tuple and identical remote tuple. 5. Both forward handles enter the 1:N NAT reverse bucket. `reply_matches_forward_session` compares only the complete derived wire key (`session/key.rs:19-26`); both candidates match the same reply. `find_forward_nat_match` returns the first match (`session/lookup.rs:222-249`), so replies can be delivered to the wrong internal flow or the other flow can blackhole. 6. Teardown is not a repair: source release scans allocators in the current rule set (`source.rs:781-826`), so an old-generation allocation cannot be found after replacement.
Refutation attempt: - I checked the #4518 compatible-reload fix. It correctly preserves the `Arc<PortAllocator>` for a byte-identical pool, but deliberately creates a fresh allocator on add/remove/reorder; it does not cover an address retained across the two generations. - I checked the changed-pool test. It changes `198.51.100.1` to disjoint `203.0.113.9`, where tuple collision is impossible, and then explicitly expects reuse of the old low port. It does not exercise `[A] -> [A,B]`, `[A,B] -> [A]`, reordering, pool rename, or overlapping range change. - I checked snapshot strict-overlap validation. It can reject duplicate ownership domains inside one incoming snapshot, but it has no inventory of sessions and allocations owned by the previous live generation. - I checked #4399/#4438's multimap indexes. They retain both handles, but validation cannot disambiguate two forward sessions whose complete translated and remote tuples are identical; both pass the same equality predicate. - I checked the refresh commit path for a NAT-session purge or migration. The only pre-swap session purge there is tunnel-remap-specific. HA reservation fixes operate on peer imports, not same-process local refresh.
HPC/invariant check: The broken invariant is one live owner per `(protocol, translated source address, translated source port/identifier, remote address, remote port)` across all active config generations. Current reset is cheap but discards that ownership. The fix belongs on the cold snapshot path and must not add a per-packet lock. Migrate/reserve old live tuples by actual address and port into the new allocator, remapping positional address indexes, or synchronously purge every session tied to the replaced allocation domain before publishing the new state. Migration should remain O(live allocations in changed pools), bounded outside packet processing.
Why it matters: A routine pool add/remove/reorder, pool rename, or port-range change can immediately duplicate a still-live public 5-tuple. Replies can cross internal sessions, reset an established connection, or expose one client's reply traffic to another client able to target the same remote endpoint. This violates the core NAT BIB/tuple-uniqueness contract and persists until the old session ages or is removed.
Fix direction: Add generation-aware allocator migration keyed by actual `(pool address, port)` rather than old vector index. Carry `live_by_flow`, address-only owners, persistent leases/expiry indexes, deterministic ownership, cursors, and HA reservations for retained addresses and overlapping ports. For removed domains, either retain a draining allocator referenced by old sessions or purge those sessions before the swap and propagate closes. Add source-NAT and NAT64 integration tests for `[A] -> [A,B]`, removal retaining A, reorder, rename, and overlapping range changes, with two internal flows to one remote endpoint and reverse lookup assertions. Also assert old-session teardown releases the correct generation.
Labels: `userspace-dp`, `nat`, `nat64`, `allocation-lifecycle`, `tuple-uniqueness`, `session-integrity`, `config-reload`, `vsrx-parity`
Dedup note: Fresh searches found no changed-snapshot/retained-address allocator-generation entry. GH#6600 and the historical #4512/#4388 class concern peer-import reservation ordering; GH#6522 concerns sibling-holder release; GH#6528 concerns wrong-mode teardown; #4518 preserves only byte-identical reloads. The mechanism and trigger here are distinct: local in-process state replacement loses old occupancy while sessions survive.

#### R23: Conflicting `icmp-type` and `icmp-code` leaves inside inline application terms bypass the duplicate-scalar gate

Title: Conflicting `icmp-type` and `icmp-code` leaves inside inline application terms bypass the duplicate-scalar gate
Severity: High
Confidence: High
Gate verdict: MATERIAL
Evidence: The strict gate at `pkg/config/compiler_validate_strict_application.go:588` enumerates only port, timeout, and ALG leaves, so no later validation recovers the missing ICMP duplicate: ```go 588             if len(app.DuplicateTermLeaves) > 0 { 589                 return fmt.Errorf( 590                     "application %q: conflicting duplicate %q inside `term`; a single-valued "+ 591                         "term leaf (destination-port / source-port / inactivity-timeout / "+ 592                         "timeout / alg) may carry only one value — a repeat with a different "+ 593                         "value is last-writer-wins and silently overrides the earlier one by "+ 594                         "token order (use repeated `protocol` only for an intentional "+ 595                         "multi-protocol term)", 596                     name, app.DuplicateTermLeaves[0]) ```
Trace: (1) A hierarchical application term, or a packed flat term, reaches `applicationTermKeys`, which deliberately reassembles both AST shapes. (2) `parseApplicationTerms` parses two valid `icmp-type` or `icmp-code` tokens and overwrites `icmpType`/`icmpCode` with the last value. (3) Because no duplicate marker is recorded and `schema_security.go:1282` declares `term` opaque (`children:nil`), strict `CompileConfig` returns success. (4) The generated `Application` carries only the final pointer. (5) `pkg/dataplane/userspace/capabilities.go:323-333` copies that pointer into the live policy snapshot; `userspace-dp/src/policy.rs:953-971` installs only that final ICMP constraint. A deny application authored with types 8 then 3 therefore denies only type 3; echo traffic can fall through to a later permit or explicit default permit.
Refutation attempt: I checked the typed schema, direct-application duplicate tracking, strict application semantic validators, application collision pass, snapshot builder, Rust matcher, and relevant tests. The direct-body path explicitly tracks ICMP duplicates, proving repeats are not intended as a list; the inline-term duplicate table omits them. The schema cannot help because term contents are opaque. Downstream code does not retain a union. The #3366 regression table tests destination/source port, timeout, and ALG only. The candidate survived each attempted guard.
HPC/invariant check: No concurrency, cache-line, atomic, or byte-order issue is involved. The violated compiler invariant is: every conflicting repeat of a single-valued term leaf must either be rejected or represented without loss. Values themselves are safely bounded to `uint8`; the defect occurs before wire encoding.
Why it matters: This is a strict-commit policy widening. A configuration that Junos-style scalar semantics should reject is accepted while an earlier deny constraint is discarded, allowing traffic outside the last ICMP type/code to reach a permit/default-permit path.
Fix direction: Add `icmpTypeSet`/`icmpCodeSet` plus first parsed values in `parseApplicationTerms`; append `icmp-type`/`icmp-code` to `DuplicateTermLeaves` on a conflicting repeat while allowing identical repeats. Update the strict error text and add hierarchical, packed flat-term, apply-groups, idempotent-repeat, and deny-policy regression cases for both fields.
Labels: security, config-compiler, application-matching, policy-widening, ast-dual-shape, vsrx-parity
Dedup note: The refreshed 721-row index contains `codex-review-180` for conflicting direct application scalars and GH#6564 for compact-leaf operand loss; neither covers valid repeated ICMP scalars inside an inline term. Closed history #3366 is the incomplete predecessor: it names only destination-port, source-port, ALG, and timeout at `issue-history.md:54223-54227`. Closed #2545 concerns multi-valued firewall-filter fields, a different typed model and consumer. No current open issue covers this residual field omission.
Verified against origin/master: Still present at origin/master `ad959117748181dabe46b8ddc2827de670380cea` at `pkg/config/compiler_validate_strict_application.go:588`. Independently retained in verify-R13-R24.md at the final target SHA.

#### R25: Unnormalized duplicate containers erase BGP export policy, TLS syslog transport, and monitoring state

Title: Unnormalized duplicate containers erase BGP export policy, TLS syslog transport, and monitoring state
Severity: High
Confidence: High
Gate verdict: MATERIAL
Evidence: `pkg/config/compiler_dispatch.go:21-30` promises merge semantics for duplicate roots: ```go // Behavior-preserving invariants (do NOT reorder relative to master): the // iteration is over tree.Children in source order and dispatches to the SAME // compilers in the SAME order as the inline switch it replaces — duplicate // roots (e.g. two `security { }` blocks) still merge in author order, and the // first compiler error is returned unchanged with its `<section>: %w` wrap. // This phase runs AFTER the base *Config skeleton (P2) and the P3 warning // append, and BEFORE the P5 cross-section derivations (the #4329 NodeID stamp // and the fabric fixup), so tree must already be group-expanded and // inactive-pruned and cfg must already carry its initialized maps. It is // covered by the reusable golden-output gate in compile_golden_4406_test.go. ``` `pkg/config/compiler_protocols.go:205-213` reads only the first BGP sibling and replaces the full typed object: ```go bgpNode := node.FindChild("bgp") if bgpNode != nil { proto.BGP = &BGPConfig{} for _, child := range bgpNode.Children { switch child.Name() { case "local-as": if len(child.Keys) >= 2 { // #4713: reject out-of-range/negative AS instead of the ``` `pkg/config/compiler_protocols.go:278-284` shows that a dropped second block can carry the outbound policy: ```go case "export": // Multi-value leaf (#2587): accumulate ALL policies across // both AST shapes via the firewallMatchValues SSOT. proto.BGP.Export = append(proto.BGP.Export, firewallMatchValues(child)...) case "import": proto.BGP.Import = append(proto.BGP.Import, firewallMatchValues(child)...) } ``` `pkg/config/compiler_security_log.go:38-47` allocates a new stream for every same-name hierarchical instance: ```go for _, inst := range namedInstances(node.FindChildren("stream")) { stream := &SyslogStream{ Name: inst.name, Port: 514, // default } for _, prop := range inst.node.Children { switch prop.Name() { case "host": // Flat: host 192.168.99.3; if v := nodeVal(prop); v != "" { ``` `pkg/config/compiler_security_log.go:82-90` parses a valid TLS transport on the first object: ```go case "transport": for _, tc := range prop.Children { switch tc.Name() { case "protocol": stream.Transport.Protocol = nodeVal(tc) case "tls-profile": stream.Transport.TLSProfile = nodeVal(tc) } } ``` `pkg/config/compiler_security_log.go:90-96` then replaces the map entry wholesale: ```go } } } if stream.Host != "" { sec.Log.Streams[stream.Name] = stream } } ``` `pkg/config/dup_named_blocks.go:43-52` proves the duplicate-block gate does not cover either symbol: ```go // earlier block's config silently (#5180, consolidating codex-177 A3-b2-F3 + // A3-b3-F1). Three containers are affected: // //   - groups { <name> { … } }  — expandGroups keeps only the last definition //     (ast_groups.go: groups[name] = g). //   - interfaces { <ifname> { … } } — compileInterfaces overwrites //     Interfaces[ifName] (compiler_interfaces.go). //   - security { screen { ids-option <name> { … } } } — compileScreen overwrites //     Screen[profile.Name]; WITHIN one ids-option it also reads each //     icmp/ip/tcp/udp/limit-session family with FindChild (first sibling only), ``` `pkg/frr/protocols_render.go:501-508` emits no outbound route-map when the erased export chain is empty: ```go // path. A single-policy chain references the standalone // route-map (byte-identical to pre-#5277); a chain of >= 2 // references the composed route-map that preserves the ordered // Junos policy chain (#5277) instead of dropping all but the // last. if rm := bgpRouteMapRef(bgpNeighborExportChain(n, globalExportChain, policyOptions)); rm != "" { fmt.Fprintf(&b, "  neighbor %s route-map %s out\n", n.Address, rm) } ``` `pkg/daemon/daemon_system.go:106-115` turns the erased TLS setting into UDP: ```go var clients []*logging.SyslogClient for name, stream := range cfg.Security.Log.Streams { srcAddr := stream.SourceAddress if srcAddr == "" { srcAddr = globalSourceAddr } protocol := stream.Transport.Protocol if protocol == "" { protocol = "udp" } ```
Trace: A hierarchical parser retains repeated same-key blocks as siblings. For `protocols { bgp { group ... neighbor ...; } bgp { export DENY-EXPORT; } }`, `FindChild("bgp")` returns only the first sibling, so the valid second export never reaches `BGP.Export`. `validateRoutingExportReferencesStrict` walks the compiled slice and therefore cannot reject or recover an erased policy. FRR receives a live neighbor with an empty export chain and emits no `route-map ... out`, advertising every otherwise eligible BGP route instead of applying the authored deny/export policy. Separately, two `security log stream audit` blocks, the first with `host` plus `transport { protocol tls; }` and the second with the same host plus severity, produce two fresh objects; the second map assignment removes TLS and runtime defaults to plaintext UDP. `FormatSet` emits both subtrees as set lines, while `SetPath` reuses matching containers, so parse -> compile differs from FormatSet -> set replay -> compile. Fresh `compileFlowMonitoring`/`compileRPM`/`compileIPMonitoring` objects and `compileAddressBook`'s first `global`/fresh map are lower-impact siblings of the same round-trip violation.
Refutation attempt: I checked `validateDuplicateNamedBlockAST`, all security-log AST gates, routing export-reference validation, flat-set `SetPath`, formatter output, and the runtime consumers. The duplicate gate explicitly enumerates only groups/interfaces/screen; log gates validate each individual stream but do not reject duplicate names; routing gates see only already-compiled exports; and flat set merges rather than replacing. Each individual block is schema-valid, so strict compile passes. The issue is not intended last-wins behavior: the dispatcher and existing #4818/#4820/#4821 fixes explicitly state Junos duplicate blocks merge, and formatter replay changes the result.
HPC/invariant check: The traversals are linear and parser depth-bounded; no race, integer overflow, or hot-path allocation is involved. The violated invariants are dual-AST equivalence, duplicate-root author-order merge, strict-gate visibility, and formatter round-trip equivalence. The fail-open route-policy consequence and TLS downgrade occur on the control plane and live Go/FRR consumers, not retired eBPF/DPDK code.
Why it matters: A syntactically valid hierarchical/load-override config can silently remove an outbound BGP filter and leak routes, or silently send an audit stream without the explicitly configured TLS transport. The same text rendered and replayed as set syntax behaves differently, so backups/edits can change enforcement without an operator-visible semantic change.
Fix direction: Normalize repeated same-key containers before compilation, or make each compiler iterate all matching protocol/service/global blocks and find-or-create named objects with Junos merge rules. Merge list fields, preserve scalar last-wins only where defined, and reject ambiguous duplicate terminal/scalar conflicts at strict commit. Add strict and tolerant tests for repeated BGP/OSPF/RIP blocks, same-name syslog streams, flow-monitor/RPM/IP-monitoring blocks, and global address books; compare hierarchical compilation with equivalent flat-set and `FormatSet` replay, and assert FRR route-map/TLS runtime output.
Labels: `config`, `routing`, `security`, `syslog`, `observability`, `dual-ast`, `formatter-roundtrip`, `fail-open`, `vSRX-parity`

No dedup entry or issue-history item names `compileProtocols` duplicate families, `compileLog` duplicate stream names, or the combined formatter consequence.

#### R26: Untyped flow-export refresh seconds overflow into a 512 ns template ticker

Title: Untyped flow-export refresh seconds overflow into a 512 ns template ticker
Severity: High
Confidence: High
Gate verdict: MATERIAL
Evidence: `pkg/config/schema_system.go:708-716` types adjacent timeouts but leaves refresh seconds untyped and unvalidated: ```go "flow-active-timeout": {desc: "Active flow export timeout in seconds (default 60)", args: 1, placeholder: "<seconds>", valueType: ValueInteger, valueDesc: "Active flow export timeout in seconds (0..4294967295)", valueExamples: []string{"60"}, validator: ValidateInteger(0, maxWireU32), children: nil}, "flow-inactive-timeout": {desc: "Inactive flow export timeout in seconds (default 15)", args: 1, placeholder: "<seconds>", valueType: ValueInteger, valueDesc: "Inactive flow export timeout in seconds (0..4294967295)", valueExamples: []string{"15"}, validator: ValidateInteger(0, maxWireU32), children: nil}, "template-refresh-rate": {desc: "Interval between template re-exports", children: map[string]*schemaNode{ "seconds": {desc: "Template refresh interval in seconds (default 60)", args: 1, placeholder: "<seconds>", children: nil}, }}, ``` `pkg/config/compiler_services.go:1230-1239` accepts any amd64 `int`: ```go case "template-refresh-rate": if v := nodeVal(prop); v != "" { if n, err := strconv.Atoi(v); err == nil { tmpl.TemplateRefreshRate = n } } if secNode := prop.FindChild("seconds"); secNode != nil { if v := nodeVal(secNode); v != "" { if n, err := strconv.Atoi(v); err == nil { tmpl.TemplateRefreshRate = n ``` `pkg/flowexport/manager.go:292-300` performs the overflowing conversion for NetFlow; IPFIX repeats it at lines 321-329: ```go if tmpl.FlowActiveTimeout > 0 { tc.activeTimeout = time.Duration(tmpl.FlowActiveTimeout) * time.Second } if tmpl.FlowInactiveTimeout > 0 { tc.inactiveTimeout = time.Duration(tmpl.FlowInactiveTimeout) * time.Second } if tmpl.TemplateRefreshRate > 0 { tc.refreshRate = time.Duration(tmpl.TemplateRefreshRate) * time.Second } ``` `pkg/flowexport/transport.go:217-226` only repairs nonpositive results: ```go // (#4423 M10). A hand-built ExportConfig (tests, external callers) that left // TemplateRefreshRate at 0 falls back to the default cadence instead of // crashing the Run goroutine — and a panic there is fatal (it runs under // `go e.Run(ctx)`). func templateRefreshInterval(d time.Duration) time.Duration { if d <= 0 { return defaultTemplateRefreshRate } return d } ``` `pkg/flowexport/netflow.go:604-611` feeds any positive wrapped value directly to a ticker: ```go // Run starts the exporter's background goroutines. Blocks until ctx is cancelled. func (e *Exporter) Run(ctx context.Context) { // Send initial template e.sendTemplates() // #4423 M10: clamp a non-positive refresh rate so NewTicker never panics. templateTicker := time.NewTicker(templateRefreshInterval(e.cfg.TemplateRefreshRate)) defer templateTicker.Stop() ``` `pkg/flowexport/netflow.go:616-624` sends templates on every delivered tick: ```go for { select { case <-ctx.Done(): // Flush remaining batches e.flushBatches() return case <-templateTicker.C: e.sendTemplates() case <-batchTicker.C: ```
Trace: Strict schema accepts `services flow-monitoring version9 template t template-refresh-rate seconds 20211507185753197` because `seconds` has arity only. On linux/amd64, `strconv.Atoi` accepts it. The manager checks the original positive `int`, then `time.Duration(n) * time.Second` wraps modulo 2^64 to exactly `512ns` (`20211507185753197 * 1,000,000,000 mod 2^64 = 512`). The #4423 helper sees a positive duration and returns it unchanged. NetFlow and IPFIX each create that ticker and call `sendTemplates` at the maximum rate their loop and UDP writes can sustain.
Refutation attempt: I checked the schema, compiler, typed field (`int` seconds), both manager resolvers, both exporter `Run` loops, and the #4423 clamp. No `ValidateInteger`, `MaxDurationSeconds` check, checked multiplication, or operational minimum exists on this leaf. Adjacent active/inactive fields are typed, proving schema validation is active rather than globally absent. The exact witness is below `MaxInt64`, positive before and after wrap, and was recomputed on the target `GOARCH=amd64`; neither `Atoi` nor the nonpositive fallback rejects it. Existing tests cover only zero and negative ticker inputs.
HPC/invariant check: This is signed duration multiplication overflow and timer/resource amplification, not a data race. Go's ticker channel coalesces missed ticks, preventing queue growth, but that makes the goroutine a continuous template-send loop rather than bounding work. It consumes daemon CPU and emits UDP templates at send throughput. The same arithmetic is duplicated for v9 and IPFIX.
Why it matters: One strict-accepted config value can turn a 60-second housekeeping timer into a near-busy loop, flooding every configured collector and consuming control-plane CPU. On a firewall daemon, sustained control-plane starvation can interfere with apply, HA, and telemetry processing even though forwarding is in userspace.
Fix direction: Give both `seconds` leaves `ValueInteger` plus `ValidateInteger(1, MaxDurationSeconds)` (or a tighter documented Junos operational maximum). Parse into a width-stable integer and use checked duration conversion in `flowexport` as defense in depth. Clamp/reject sub-operational intervals before ticker creation. Add v9/IPFIX tests for exact maximum, maximum+1, the `512ns` witness, strict rejection, tolerant behavior, and a runtime assertion that no wrapped sub-second ticker is constructed.
Labels: `config`, `flowexport`, `netflow`, `ipfix`, `typed-leaf`, `integer-overflow`, `resource-safety`, `observability`, `vSRX-parity`
Dedup note: Closed #1979 typed active/inactive flow timeouts but omitted template refresh. Closed #4423 handles zero/negative `time.NewTicker` panic only; this witness wraps to positive and bypasses that fix. Dedup searches found no template-refresh `time.Duration` overflow entry.
Verified against origin/master: Still present at origin/master `ad959117748181dabe46b8ddc2827de670380cea` at `pkg/config/compiler_services.go:1230`. Independently retained in verify-R25-R36.md at the final target SHA.

#### R29: Unbounded heartbeat threshold overflows the live peer timeout and defeats the cold-boot liveness guard

Title: Unbounded heartbeat threshold overflows the live peer timeout and defeats the cold-boot liveness guard
Severity: High
Confidence: High
Gate verdict: MATERIAL
Evidence: `pkg/config/schema_chassis.go:90-97` accepts every positive signed 64-bit threshold and documents the decision as safe because the count is not wire encoded: > 90 `"heartbeat-threshold": {` > 91 `    desc:          "Missed heartbeats before the peer is declared lost (default 5)",` > 92 `    args:          1,` > 93 `    valueType:     ValueInteger,` > 94 `    valueDesc:     "Missed heartbeats before peer is declared lost (>= 1; xpf default 5, Junos allows 3..8)",` > 95 `    valueExamples: []string{"3", "5", "8"},` > 96 `    validator:     ValidateIntegerMin(1),` > 97 `    children:      nil,`
Trace: On amd64, `ValidateIntegerMin` parses through `math.MaxInt64` (`pkg/config/schema_validators.go:100-120`) and `compileChassis` copies the same value through `strconv.Atoi` into `HeartbeatThreshold` (`pkg/config/compiler_system.go:1823-1827`). `applyConfigLocked` installs it as `m.hbThreshold` (`pkg/cluster/group_state.go:74-80`), and `StartHeartbeat` snapshots it into the receiver (`pkg/cluster/heartbeat_manager.go:56-100`). Both `checkTimeout` and the post-guard freshness recheck calculate `time.Duration(r.threshold) * r.interval` without checked multiplication (`pkg/cluster/heartbeat.go:968-1005,1041-1047`). With the default 100 ms interval, threshold `92233720369` produces `-9223372036809551616ns`. After the 30-second startup grace, every ordinary positive heartbeat age is greater than that negative timeout. `handlePeerTimeout` therefore marks a healthy peer dead, clears peer state, and runs single-node election (`pkg/cluster/heartbeat_manager.go:380-447`); the next heartbeat marks it alive and reruns election (`:314-376`). A symmetric config makes both nodes alternate false loss and recovery, including primary ownership and optional fence activity.
Refutation attempt: The count not being wire encoded does not make the multiplication safe. The interval is individually bounded, but the product is not. The startup grace only delays the first false loss for 30 seconds. The fresh-heartbeat race guard cannot recover because it recomputes the same negative timeout. The transfer-commit suppressor is conditional and temporary; it is not a general liveness guard. The accepted-value test explicitly asserts min-only behavior through 100000 (`pkg/config/schema_validate_chassis_test.go:63-69`) and has no product boundary.
HPC/invariant check: Required invariant: `threshold > 0`, `interval > 0`, and `threshold * interval <= math.MaxInt64 nanoseconds` before constructing a `time.Duration`. At 100 ms the maximum safe threshold is `92233720368`; the first unsafe value is accepted and deterministically wraps negative under Go integer arithmetic. HA failover decisions must never derive from a non-positive configured timeout.
Why it matters: A cleanly committed cluster setting converts fresh heartbeats into repeated peer-loss events after cold boot. That can produce dual-primary churn, RETH/VIP ownership oscillation, GARP churn, and fence attempts against a live peer. This reopens the failure class the cold-boot grace is intended to contain.
Fix direction: Add a cross-field validator that proves the interval/threshold product fits `time.Duration`, and independently use checked or saturating multiplication at every runtime liveness calculation. Reject the unsafe configuration rather than silently clamping operator intent. Add strict-schema boundary tests and a receiver test that advances beyond startup grace while fresh heartbeats continue at the largest accepted product.
Labels: MATERIAL, HA, cold-boot, split-brain, integer-overflow, schema-runtime-contract, userspace-live
Dedup note: No symbol+mechanism+impact match exists in the scratch index or issue history. Closed #1792 involved wall-clock arithmetic at the same timeout expression, not product overflow. Closed #4386 involved the never-seen branch bypassing startup grace. Open #6492 concerns cold-boot fencing gaps. Open #5081 concerns live application of changed timing. None covers an accepted `heartbeat-threshold` overflowing `threshold * interval` into a negative duration.
Verified against origin/master: Still present at origin/master `ad959117748181dabe46b8ddc2827de670380cea` at `pkg/config/schema_chassis.go:90`. Independently retained in verify-R25-R36.md at the final target SHA.

#### R38: An oversized VIP set makes every VRRP advert fail after the node has claimed ownership

Title: An oversized VIP set makes every VRRP advert fail after the node has claimed ownership
Severity: High
Confidence: High
Gate verdict: MATERIAL
Evidence: `pkg/vrrp/vrrp.go:211-220` installs an entire unit address slice into one synthesized RETH instance without a cardinality check: > 211 `instances = append(instances, &Instance{` > 212 `    Interface:         subIface,` > 213 `    GroupID:           100 + rgID,` > 214 `    Priority:          pri,` > 215 `    Preempt:           preemptMap[rgID],` > 216 `    AcceptData:        true,` > 217 `    AdvertiseInterval: advertInterval,` > 218 `    GARPCount:         gc,` > 219 `    VirtualAddresses:  unit.Addresses,` > 220 `})` `pkg/vrrp/packet.go:56-63` then rejects the resulting wire packet once its one-byte address count is exceeded: > 56 `count := len(p.IPAddresses)` > 57 `// Reject before serializing: the count is written to a single u8 wire byte` > 58 `// (buf[3]), so >255 addresses would narrow lossily (256->Count 0) and a` > 59 `// 0-address advert is meaningless per RFC 5798 section 5.2.4. Surface the` > 60 `// misconfiguration instead of emitting an advert with a wrong Count.` > 61 `if count < MinAdvertAddrCount || count > MaxAdvertAddrCount {` > 62 `    return nil, fmt.Errorf("VRRP advert address count %d out of range %d..%d",` > 63 `        count, MinAdvertAddrCount, MaxAdvertAddrCount)` Despite that error, `pkg/vrrp/instance.go:1328-1337` publishes MASTER ownership and starts neighbor-cache announcements unconditionally: > 1328 `vi.vipMu.Unlock()` > 1329 `` > 1330 `vi.sendAdvert(pri)` > 1331 `vi.emitEvent()` > 1332 `vi.garpEpoch.Add(1)` > 1333 `if !vi.suppressGARP.Load() {` > 1334 `    // Non-forced: a routine MASTER transition is rate-limited by the` > 1335 `    // 500ms dampener (the epoch dedup still guarantees one burst per` > 1336 `    // transition). Post-MAC-change reconcile uses the forced path.` > 1337 `    go vi.sendGARP(false)`
Trace: Both collector paths preserve unbounded slices: generic VRRP assigns `vg.VirtualAddresses` directly at `pkg/vrrp/vrrp.go:96-105`, while non-VLAN RETH appends every unit address at `:223-238`. The strict schema marks `virtual-address` as `multi: true` but supplies no count validator (`pkg/config/schema_interfaces.go:290-300`), and `Manager.UpdateInstances` validates family, VRID, duplicate identity, and election domains without validating per-family address cardinality (`pkg/vrrp/manager.go:432-520`). `sendAdvert` partitions the configured list by family and discards each `sendPacket` error after a Debug log (`pkg/vrrp/instance_send.go:38-71`). IPv4 deterministically fails at 256 configured addresses. IPv6 deterministically fails at 255 configured addresses because `sendPacketIPv6` prepends the required link-local address before marshal, producing 256 (`instance_send.go:177-198`); the package README explicitly acknowledges that rejection (`pkg/vrrp/README.md:593-596`). `becomeMaster` first adds all VIPs, then calls the void sender, emits MASTER, and sends GARP/NA. Every periodic advert repeats the same error. A peer therefore receives no advert, its master-down timer expires, and it also adds/announces the same VIP set. Both nodes remain MASTER and neither can converge through VRRP.
Refutation attempt: The packet-layer count guard prevents a malformed Count byte, but it converts the defect into a permanent local silence and does not gate ownership. No strict config validator, collector guard, or manager guard limits the list. VIP netlink actuation is not an implicit bound; Linux can hold hundreds of addresses, and the fail-closed actuation gate treats successful adds or existing addresses as success. A one-family instance removes the possible escape where the other address family still advertises. This is High rather than Critical because the trigger requires an accepted or tolerant configuration and does not cross an authentication or memory-safety boundary.
HPC/invariant check: The cold-path invariant is that an instance must be wire-serializable before it can actuate VIPs or publish MASTER. Required bounds are at most 255 IPv4 addresses and at most 254 configured IPv6 addresses when the sender prepends its link-local. The current code bounds only the final serializer, after ownership state has become externally visible. There is no hot-path reason to defer this validation.
Why it matters: One accepted address-list size produces persistent dual ownership, duplicate ARP/NDP announcements, asymmetric traffic, and session divergence. The state/event plane says MASTER while the election wire is permanently silent, defeating the central split-brain control loop.
Fix direction: Validate the per-family advertised address count in `UpdateInstances` before mutating the live desired set, with the IPv6 link-local included in the bound, and add the same strict commit validation for operator feedback. Make advert construction/sending return an outcome that promotion and retry logic cannot silently treat as publication. Add red-on-revert tests for 256 IPv4 VIPs, 255 configured IPv6 VIPs, no MASTER event/GARP on rejection, and the exact maximum accepted counts.
Labels: MATERIAL, HA, VRRP, split-brain, wire-bound, resource-bound, dual-stack, vSRX-interoperability, userspace-live
Dedup note: `packet_addrcount_5090_test.go` and commit `7b8b5e9d9` cover the packet serializer's lossy one-byte Count conversion. This is a distinct follow-on at `sendAdvert`/`becomeMaster`: the serializer now returns the right error, but the election state machine treats that error as successful publication. No matching symbol+mechanism+impact entry exists in the current scratch index, refreshed open issue list, or checked-in issue history.

#### R41: Invalid RETH redundancy-group values commit as non-HA addresses owned by both nodes

Title: Invalid RETH redundancy-group values commit as non-HA addresses owned by both nodes
Severity: High
Confidence: High
Gate verdict: MATERIAL
Evidence: `pkg/config/schema_interfaces.go:80-85` gives the RETH group leaf arity but no integer or range validator: > 80 `    "link-speed":    {desc: "Member link speed", args: 1, children: nil},` > 81 `    "minimum-links": {desc: "Minimum active member links", args: 1, children: nil},` > 82 `}},` > 83 `"redundant-ether-options": {desc: "Redundant Ethernet interface options", children: map[string]*schemaNode{` > 84 `    "redundancy-group": {desc: "Redundancy group for this RETH", args: 1, children: nil},` > 85 `}},` `pkg/config/compiler_interfaces.go:136-143` silently leaves the zero-value group when parsing fails: > 136 `// Check for redundant-ether-options redundancy-group` > 137 `if reoNode := child.FindChild("redundant-ether-options"); reoNode != nil {` > 138 `    if rgNode := reoNode.FindChild("redundancy-group"); rgNode != nil {` > 139 `        if v, err := strconv.Atoi(nodeVal(rgNode)); err == nil {` > 140 `            ifc.RedundancyGroup = v` > 141 `        }` > 142 `    }` > 143 `}` The assigned collector treats every resulting non-positive value as if no RETH ownership had been configured (`pkg/vrrp/vrrp.go:169-175`): > 169 `var instances []*Instance` > 170 `for _, name := range names {` > 171 `    ifc := cfg.Interfaces.Interfaces[name]` > 172 `    if ifc.RedundancyGroup <= 0 {` > 173 `        continue` > 174 `    }` > 175 `    rgID := ifc.RedundancyGroup`
Trace: The untyped schema accepts arbitrary one-token values. `redundancy-group typo` or an `Atoi` overflow leaves `InterfaceConfig.RedundancyGroup == 0`; explicit zero or a negative integer is stored as non-positive. The strict RETH validator then intentionally skips every `<= 0` interface (`pkg/config/compiler_validate_strict_reth_vrrp.go:69-74`), so strict commit reports success. Member-to-RETH resolution is independent of this field, and the dataplane compiler makes the physical member inherit the logical RETH config (`pkg/dataplane/compiler_iface.go:797-805`). Because it computes `isVRRPReth` as `RedundancyGroup > 0`, the bad value makes it pass the real configured addresses to networkd instead of the per-node link-local base (`:937-958,963-1015`). Both cluster nodes therefore install the same RETH addresses statically on their respective physical members. `CollectRethInstances` skips them, direct ownership has no positive RG event/inventory for them, and RETH MAC programming also skips `<= 0` (`pkg/daemon/daemon_apply_dataplane.go:53-65`). The duplicate addresses are permanent rather than bounded by an election or handoff interval.
Refutation attempt: Generic schema arity only proves that one token exists; without a validator it does not prove numeric syntax. The derived-VRID validator cannot distinguish an absent option from a parse failure because the compiler already collapsed both to zero, and it explicitly exempts non-positive values. A configured chassis RG of the intended number cannot repair the lost interface binding. Manager VRID validation is downstream of the collector skip. This is High rather than Critical because it requires a bad but strictly accepted configuration and does not provide remote code execution or an unauthenticated wire trigger.
HPC/invariant check: Before address application, a present `redundant-ether-options redundancy-group` must satisfy a representable, positive, supported ID and resolve to exactly one ownership engine. Parse failure must never share the zero value used for absence. Validation and presence tracking are cold-path work; no forwarding hot path is affected.
Why it matters: A simple RETH group typo passes commit and puts the same service addresses on both firewalls without VRRP, direct-mode ownership, or virtual-MAC coordination. That produces immediate duplicate ARP/NDP ownership, asymmetric forwarding, and unsynchronized sessions while all configuration/status paths can appear successfully applied.
Fix direction: Type the schema leaf as an integer and validate the base range, then make the semantic validator enforce the mode-dependent maximum (155 for synthesized VRRP, the supported cluster range for direct mode). Preserve presence/parse failure through compilation so tolerant load can warn and quarantine the RETH addresses instead of applying them statically. Add flat, packed, and hierarchical strict tests for nonnumeric, zero, negative, `Atoi` overflow, maximum, and maximum+1 values, plus an apply-model test proving an invalid present binding never reaches networkd as ordinary static addresses.
Labels: MATERIAL, HA, RETH, VRRP, split-brain, strict-commit, parse-failure, config-validation, vSRX-compatibility, userspace-live
Dedup note: Closed #4826 validates only a successfully parsed positive RETH group whose synthesized VRID would exceed 255. Open GH #6543 covers duplicate textual identities in the chassis redundancy-group collection. Neither covers this interface leaf's missing validator, ignored `Atoi` error, collapse to RG0, and static dual ownership. No symbol+mechanism+impact match exists in the scratch index, refreshed open issues, or checked-in history.
