#### R04: Native GRE decapsulation promotes bytes outside the outer IP datagram

Title: Native GRE decapsulation promotes bytes outside the outer IP datagram
Severity: Medium
Confidence: High
Gate verdict: MATERIAL
Evidence: `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/gre.rs:676` then parses options against the entire captured Ethernet frame and treats every byte after them as candidate inner data (7 lines actually read): ```rust if sequence_present { frame.get(inner_offset..inner_offset + 4)?; inner_offset += 4; } let inner_packet = frame.get(inner_offset..)?; let inner_len = packet_trimmed_len(inner_packet, inner_family)?; let inner_packet = &inner_packet[..inner_len]; ```
Trace: RX supplies a full captured Ethernet frame -> XDP `parse_iphdr` records IPv4 `tot_len` but sets `l4_offset` from IHL and does not constrain capture to `tot_len` -> `stage_native_gre_decap` passes the full raw frame -> `try_native_gre_decap_from_frame` checks the outer declared end only in the checksum-present branch -> GRE key/sequence and inner parsing use `frame` to capture end -> `packet_trimmed_len` validates only the inner declaration against that oversized tail -> a synthetic inner frame is accepted and enters normal tunnel-zone processing. For checksum-present GRE, the authenticated region can end before the promoted tail; for checksum-absent GRE, the outer declaration is never consulted at all.
Refutation attempt: Endpoint family/source/destination/key matching, inner family, inner declared length, TCP/UDP/ICMP minimum lengths, ECN rules, and GRE checksum validation were traced. They do not establish that `inner_offset` or `inner_offset + inner_len` lies at or before the outer IPv4 Total Length / IPv6 Payload Length end. `gre_checksum_region` does calculate that end safely with checked addition, but its slice is discarded after checksum verification and the subsequent parse returns to the whole frame. Existing native-GRE tests cover endpoint/key, checksum, ECN, inner truncation, and short L4 headers; none makes the outer declaration shorter than the captured GRE+inner tail. The inner packet still receives tunnel ingress-zone policy, which limits this from being a direct policy bypass and is why the severity is Medium.
HPC/invariant check: No Rust out-of-bounds access occurs; all individual slice operations are guarded and offset additions here are small. The violated invariant is parser authority: bytes outside the outer L3 datagram, including Ethernet padding or a contradictory captured tail, must never become authenticated/forwarded inner packet bytes. Network-byte-order reads are correct. The fix can remain allocation-free and should not add atomics or cache-line traffic.
Why it matters: A malformed outer IPv4/IPv6 packet from an otherwise matching GRE endpoint can declare a datagram that excludes some or all of the GRE options/inner packet while placing a valid inner datagram in captured trailing bytes. Userspace accepts bytes that the outer IP header says are not part of the datagram, diverging from normal IP parsers and, on checksum-present GRE, extending forwarding beyond the checksum's declared envelope. This is a fail-open parser differential at a packet trust boundary.
Fix direction: Compute one outer declared end unconditionally before GRE option parsing. Reject an outer length shorter than the actual outer header, before the complete GRE fixed/options header, or beyond capture. Bound all GRE option reads and the inner candidate to `frame[gre_offset..outer_end]`, then require `inner_offset + inner_len <= outer_end`. Add IPv4 and IPv6 tests for checksum-present and checksum-absent GRE where the captured tail is valid but the outer declaration ends before the GRE header, in GRE options, and before the inner declared end; include benign Ethernet padding controls.

#### R09: A SYN-ACK without the final ACK retains a half-open flow for the established timeout

Title: A SYN-ACK without the final ACK retains a half-open flow for the established timeout
Severity: Medium
Confidence: High
Gate verdict: MATERIAL
Evidence: `userspace-dp/src/session/expire.rs:318-323` applies that veto on the owner/standalone expiry path: ```rust if companion_eligible && self.companion_keeps_alive(&key, e_nat, now_ns) { self.last_pop_stats.kept_alive_by_companion += 1; continue; } if let Some(removed) = self.remove_entry(&key) { self.last_pop_stats.expired += 1; ```
Trace: A client SYN installs forward and reverse entries on the 20-second opening timeout. A real server SYN-ACK hits the reverse entry; lookup marks it established and stamps the 300-second established timeout, while propagation marks the forward entry established but deliberately retains its 20-second deadline pending the final client ACK. If that ACK never arrives, forward expiry runs at about 20 seconds. `companion_keeps_alive` sees the reverse entry still inside its own 300-second window, copies its timestamp to the forward entry, and rebuckets the forward entry. The wheel rechecks and retains it until the reverse established timeout expires, so two half-open slots survive roughly 15 times the intended window.
Refutation attempt: I checked the timer-wheel clamp/rebucket behavior, HA eligibility gates, close propagation, install timeouts, and all handshake tests. The rebucketed already-due forward entry is checked on subsequent ticks, not removed; the same companion predicate keeps succeeding until the reverse timeout. The completed-handshake test sends the final ACK, and the no-SYN-ACK test never creates this mixed-timeout state. No test expires SYN/SYN-ACK without final ACK. The interaction survives.
HPC/invariant check: A two-row flow needs one flow-level handshake/expiry class. Companion retention is off hot path and may do one bounded index lookup, but it must compare a shared effective timeout/state, not let a long-timeout half extend a handshake-incomplete peer. An explicit compact handshake state is preferable to additional per-packet allocation or cross-worker atomics.
Why it matters: A remote client can send SYNs to responsive internal listeners, let legitimate SYN-ACKs return, and never finish the handshake. Each attempt pins two bounded session-table slots for the established timeout, weakening the #3152 half-open DoS bound and denying legitimate session creation at a much lower sustained rate.
Fix direction: Track `SYN seen / SYN-ACK seen / final ACK seen` as flow-level state and keep both halves on the opening deadline until the final ACK. At minimum, make companion retention refuse to extend an entry when the flow has not completed the handshake or use the minimum timeout class across the pair. Add a timer-wheel regression for SYN, reverse SYN-ACK, no final ACK at opening and established deadlines.
Labels: bug, userspace-dp, TCP, session-GC, resource-exhaustion, syn-check, vsrx-parity
Dedup note: Final searches used `companion_keeps_alive`, `half-open`, `SYN-ACK`, `opening timeout`, `handshake timeout`, and `established`. #3152/#4109 fixed bare-SYN and client-only-ACK promotion; #4380 introduced companion retention for genuine asymmetric traffic. This is the opposite mixed-timeout interaction created by combining those fixes, with a distinct resource-exhaustion consequence. No exact current-index/history item exists.

#### R11: HTTP DDNS cache ignores a changed resolved bind device

Title: HTTP DDNS cache ignores a changed resolved bind device
Severity: Medium
Confidence: High
Gate verdict: MATERIAL
Evidence: `pkg/ddns/backend_http.go:467-475` resolves a fresh bind config but keys and returns the cached client only by raw provider leaves:

```go
key := bindCacheKey(p)
c.mu.Lock()
defer c.mu.Unlock()
if cl, ok := c.clients[key]; ok {
    return cl, nil
}
cl := newHTTPClientBound(b)
c.clients[key] = cl
return cl, nil
```
Trace: 1. Each live Surface A reconcile refreshes `cfg.ResolveKernelIfName`. 2. `clientFor` resolves the current `bindConfig`, then derives its cache key only from the raw source-address, destination-interface, and routing-instance leaves. 3. On a cache hit it discards the newly resolved bind and returns a transport whose dial closure captured the old device/address. 4. A reth, VLAN, tunnel, or bridge remap can change the kernel device without changing those raw leaves. 5. Reap builds the same raw-key live set, so it preserves the stale client. 6. Recurring updates and check-IP probes continue through the old device or fail there indefinitely.
Refutation attempt: Raw-leaf invalidation works when a configured binding leaf changes, but it does not cover a stable leaf resolving to a new device. Per-pass backend reconstruction still reuses this cache. Reap retains the stale entry because it uses the same raw identity. Bind validation fails malformed bindings closed, but a valid newly resolved bind is computed and then ignored on cache hit. A review-only test changed resolver output while preserving `DestinationInterface` and observed the same cached client. Origin/master remains byte-identical at the cited path.
HPC/invariant check: A transport-cache identity must include every resolved value captured by its dial closure, and an active committed binding must not preserve an older SO_BINDTODEVICE target
Why it matters: A topology commit can leave recurring Surface A updates and check-IP probes pinned to a removed or wrong WAN device until restart or an unrelated binding-leaf change, causing indefinite publish failure or publishing/checking through the wrong WAN
Fix direction: Key the cache on a canonical resolved bind identity, or compare the newly resolved bindConfig with cached metadata and close/rebuild on change. Build the Reconcile live set from the same resolved identity so reap and lookup agree

#### R12: Cross-surface DDNS co-ownership treats equal RR data at different authorities as one wire resource

Title: Cross-surface DDNS co-ownership treats equal RR data at different authorities as one wire resource
Severity: Medium
Confidence: High
Gate verdict: MATERIAL
Evidence: `pkg/ddns/state.go:342` (5 lines) and `pkg/ddns/surface_a.go:1722` (7 lines) ```go type WireRRClaim struct { FQDN        string // canonical form (dnsCanonicalFQDN) ForwardType string // "A" | "AAAA" Rdata       string // textual published address (the rdata) } ``` ```go want := wireRRClaim(fqdn, forwardType, rdata) for _, c := range m.leaseCoowners() { if c == want { return true } } return false ```
Trace: Medium MATERIAL: `daemon_run_bringup.go:96-103` cross-wires the two managers; each advertises only `{canonical FQDN, RR type, rdata}`. A Surface A teardown that matches an unrelated Surface B authority enters `surface_a.go:1538-1563`, re-UPSERTs through A's backend, retains the claim, and can defer forever (`:1597-1611`). The converse lease teardown suppresses its delete at `manager.go:1080-1107`. Equal data in split DNS views, routing instances, or distinct update servers is therefore mistaken for shared ownership.
Refutation attempt: The review checked whether endpoint identity is globally fixed or implicitly shared. It is not: Surface A supports RFC 2136 and HTTP providers, Surface B resolves RFC 2136, both support endpoint/routing identity, and both already compute durable backend fingerprints (`surface_a.go:1779-1813`, `manager.go:1768-1800`). Those fingerprints are omitted from `WireRRClaim`. Surface A's sibling-family guard explicitly requires the same provider because a different provider is a different authority (`surface_a.go:1731-1740`).
HPC/invariant check: The ownership invariant must be keyed by the actual mutable wire resource, including canonical authority/view identity. Atomic snapshot reads and lock ordering remain sound; the defect is semantic key under-specification, not a race.
Why it matters: Removing one binding can preserve or re-publish stale DNS at the wrong authority. After address reuse, clients in that view can be directed to a different host, and ownership can remain stuck until the unrelated lease disappears.
Fix direction: Add a credential-free, normalized authority/view identifier to cross-surface claims and suppress only when both surfaces target the same resource. Define a cross-surface canonical fingerprint because the current `fp1-` and `fpb1-` encodings are not directly comparable. Add same-tuple/different-authority negative tests and same-authority positive tests.
Labels: `ddns`, `ownership`, `split-horizon`, `routing-instance`, `correctness`

#### R13: Malformed or zero-length RFC 3442 option presence falls through to the forbidden Router option

Title: Malformed or zero-length RFC 3442 option presence falls through to the forbidden Router option
Severity: Medium
Confidence: High
Gate verdict: MATERIAL
Evidence: `pkg/dhcp/dhcpv4.go:410` (9 lines) ```go libRoutes := ack.ClasslessStaticRoute() // option 121 if len(libRoutes) == 0 { // Legacy option 249 (Microsoft), identical RFC 3442 encoding. if raw := ack.Options.Get(dhcpv4.GenericOptionCode(249)); len(raw) > 0 { var r dhcpv4.Routes if err := r.FromBytes(raw); err == nil { libRoutes = r } } ```
Trace: Medium MATERIAL: `leaseFromACKv4` calls `classlessStaticRoutes`; the dependency's `ClasslessStaticRoute` returns `nil` both when option 121 is absent and when `Routes.FromBytes` fails (`dhcpv4.go:608-617`). This helper then treats zero decoded routes as `present=false` at `:420-421`; the caller enters `:371-378` and installs option 3. Thus malformed/empty 121, or malformed/empty 249 when 121 is absent, is semantically converted into absence.
Refutation attempt: The dependency was inspected rather than inferred. Its `Options.Has` method (`options.go:73-76`) distinguishes key presence, while `ClasslessStaticRoute` intentionally collapses decode errors to nil. Existing tests cover valid 121, valid 249, and option-3-only ACKs, but no empty or malformed classless option. RFC 3442 requires Router-option suppression when the classless-route option is supplied; see [RFC 3442](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3442).
HPC/invariant check: Presence and decoded cardinality are separate domains. `len(decoded)==0` cannot encode absent, present-empty, and present-malformed without violating the precedence invariant.
Why it matters: A malformed ACK can silently install the option-3 default route that the classless option was meant to supersede, causing wrong-path routing or loss on DHCP uplinks.
Fix direction: Check `ack.Options.Has(OptionClasslessStaticRoute)` and generic 249 presence before decode, preserving 121 precedence over 249. Reject the ACK on malformed data, or at minimum mark the classless option present and suppress option 3 while surfacing the parse failure. Add zero-length, truncated-prefix, truncated-gateway, and 121-malformed-plus-valid-249 tests.
Labels: `dhcpv4`, `rfc3442`, `fail-open`, `routing`, `vsrx-parity`

#### R20: Staged-generation GC discards current-gen resolution errors and proceeds to destructive deletion

Title: Staged-generation GC discards current-gen resolution errors and proceeds to destructive deletion
Severity: Medium
Confidence: High
Gate verdict: MATERIAL
Evidence: pkg/upgrade/stagedgen/stagedgen.go:320 (7 lines) ```go 320 extraProtected := map[string]bool{} 321 for g := range protected { 322     extraProtected[g] = true 323 } 324 if cur, rerr := c.ResolveCurrent(); rerr == nil && cur != "" { 325     extraProtected[cur] = true 326 } ```
Trace: `ResolveCurrent` deliberately distinguishes absent (`"", nil`) from unsafe, dangling, unreadable, or unstatable current state (`error`) at `stagedgen.go:247-280`. GC drops that error, sorts generations by wall-clock-prefixed name, preserves only the newest two, and removes every older unprotected directory at `:348-369`. A current generation can be older in name after an NTP backward step (explicitly supported by the comments) or an operator rollback. A transient symlink/stat error then removes the active source instead of skipping GC.
Refutation attempt: A normal `Publish` makes the new current and usually places it in the retained name window, but GenID order is explicitly non-monotonic and GC is also called from cut/runtime paths. The existing old-current test covers successful resolution only. Missing current is already a clean no-generation case; returning on non-nil error does not impede first install. Candidate survives.
HPC/invariant check: A collector may delete an object only after positively excluding all live owners. Unknown current ownership is not absence. This is infrequent filesystem work, so failing closed has no dataplane cost.
Why it matters: The running process may continue, hiding the damage until restart or the next cut, when the active staged source has vanished and recovery/rollback loses its durable input.
Fix direction: Resolve and validate current-gen before any deletion; on non-nil error, return it and perform no generation removal. Keep missing-current as the existing nil case. Add tests for an older current with readlink/stat failure and for a backward-clock current outside the retention window.
Labels: upgrade, GC, crash-consistency, filesystem, fail-open, rollback

Confidence: High

Why it matters: Any co-located user can race a documented secret-bearing artifact and recover long-lived authentication material despite the final mode appearing correct in audits and tests.
Fix direction: Build to a random path inside a 0700 directory on the destination filesystem (and/or run the child with umask 0077), chmod/fsync there, then atomically replace the requested output and fsync its directory. #### R24: Wildcard `apply-groups` cloning bypasses the expansion work budget and can build a quadratic AST

Title: Wildcard `apply-groups` cloning bypasses the expansion work budget and can build a quadratic AST
Severity: Medium
Confidence: High
Gate verdict: MATERIAL
Evidence: The wildcard branch at `pkg/config/ast_groups.go:377` clones the complete source subtree once per matching destination, with no budget charge for the match, clone, recursive merge, or retained output: ```go 377         // Check if source keys contain wildcards (<*>). 378         if keysContainWildcard(s.Keys) { 379             // Wildcard merge: apply to all matching containers in dst. 380             for _, d := range *dst { 381                 if !d.IsLeaf && keysMatchWildcard(d.Keys, s.Keys) { 382                     cloned := cloneNodes(s.Children) 383                     mergeNodes(&d.Children, cloned, appendPath(ancestorPath, d.Keys)) 384                 } 385             } ```
Trace: (1) A candidate contains `N` concrete destination containers and one applied group whose `<*>` container has an `M`-node subtree. (2) `expandGroupsRecursive` increments `budget.work` once for that group reference. (3) `mergeNodes` matches all `N` containers and deep-clones/merges `M` nodes for each, retaining distinct inherited children when they are absent inline. (4) Expanded size and work become `O(N*M)` while the budget remains 1; the 64-depth cap is irrelevant. (5) Strict commit, tolerant boot, and HA SyncApply all execute this path before section compilation, and later prepasses/compiler walks traverse the amplified tree. A generated but accepted candidate can consume excessive CPU/memory or terminate the daemon through OOM.
Refutation attempt: Not required at Medium, but I checked the intended guards. The recursion cap handles depth only. `maxGroupExpandWork` counts references, not allocations/output nodes. Memoization caches an expanded group body but the wildcard branch deliberately calls `cloneNodes` for every destination, so it does not cap cloning. The 16 MiB ingress limit bounds raw `N+M`, not the expansion product, and incremental candidate edits are not an output-cardinality proof. The batch's depth test exercises a long chain and a shallow control, not wildcard fan-out.
HPC/invariant check: No atomic/cache-line/endianness concern. The resource invariant is that every expansion budget must upper-bound work and retained output. Here one charged operation can perform and retain `N*M` node copies, so the advertised total-work counter is not a bound.
Why it matters: Config commit and HA sync are control-plane availability paths. An authenticated operator mistake, generated config, or hostile/corrupt HA peer can cause disproportionate allocation and latency, blocking configuration convergence or crashing the daemon instead of returning a bounded compile error.
Fix direction: Replace the reference counter with a shared budget that charges visited, cloned, merged, and retained nodes, using checked arithmetic before allocation. Abort before cloning when the remaining output budget cannot cover `subtreeSize * matchCount`; include all per-node prepass expansions. Add near-limit/over-limit wildcard tests and assert a clean error on strict and tolerant entrypoints.
Labels: availability, resource-exhaustion, config-compiler, apply-groups, ha, performance, vsrx-parity

Closed #1914 is wildcard tunnel-ID collision admission; closed #4070 is leaf-list inheritance; history #4474 is transitive group content loss. None covers one wildcard reference bypassing the resource budget. The in-code #5194 depth/reference fix is precisely the incomplete guard, not an indexed open duplicate.

#### R27: Source-NAT range endpoints discard non-host masks before strict validation

Title: Source-NAT range endpoints discard non-host masks before strict validation
Severity: Medium
Confidence: High
Gate verdict: MATERIAL
Evidence: `pkg/config/compiler_nat_helpers.go:303-312` states `/32` is required but only appends a mask when absent: ```go // expandAddressRange expands "low/mask to high/mask" into individual IP strings. // Both low and high must be /32 CIDRs. Max 256 IPs. func expandAddressRange(low, high string) ([]string, error) { lowCIDR := low if !strings.Contains(lowCIDR, "/") { lowCIDR += "/32" } highCIDR := high if !strings.Contains(highCIDR, "/") { highCIDR += "/32" ``` `pkg/config/compiler_nat_helpers.go:314-321` parses but discards both `*IPNet` masks: ```go lowIP, _, err := net.ParseCIDR(lowCIDR) if err != nil { return nil, fmt.Errorf("invalid low address %q: %w", low, err) } highIP, _, err := net.ParseCIDR(highCIDR) if err != nil { return nil, fmt.Errorf("invalid high address %q: %w", high, err) } ``` `pkg/config/compiler_nat_helpers.go:341-347` rewrites the surviving host IPs as valid `/32` members: ```go var result []string buf := make(net.IP, 4) // count is bounded by 256 here, so the uint32 loop bound cannot wrap. for i := uint32(0); i < uint32(count); i++ { binary.BigEndian.PutUint32(buf, lowN+i) result = append(result, buf.String()+"/32") } ``` `pkg/config/compiler_validate_strict_nat.go:825-833` validates only that rewritten typed slice: ```go // Mirror the snapshot builder's live address set: the DNAT-compat // single Address (unused by source pools today, but included for // parity) plus the source pool Addresses. var addrs []string if pool.Address != "" { addrs = append(addrs, pool.Address) } addrs = append(addrs, pool.Addresses...) if len(addrs) == 0 { ``` `pkg/config/compiler_validate_strict_nat.go:841-849` therefore sees only valid `/32` values and accepts: ```go for _, a := range addrs { if reason, ok := sourceNATPoolAddressReason(a); !ok { return fmt.Errorf( "source-nat pool %q (referenced by rule-set %q rule %q): "+ "address %q %s; a single malformed or over-capacity member "+ "poisons the whole pool — the rule commits but the dataplane "+ "marks the pool unusable (InvalidPool) and drops it at runtime, "+ "silently stopping translation", name, rs.Name, rule.Name, a, reason) ```
Trace: `address 192.0.2.1/24 to 192.0.2.2/24` reaches `expandAddressRange`. `net.ParseCIDR` returns each original host IP separately from its network mask; the helper ignores the masks, compares `.1` to `.2`, and emits two `/32` strings. The source-pool grammar/cardinality gates run later over those rewritten values and pass. Both strict and tolerant compilers therefore accept a malformed range and install a two-host pool rather than rejecting the non-host endpoints. Flat and hierarchical forms share the helper; formatter replay preserves the malformed source text but repeats the same silent canonicalization.
Refutation attempt: I checked whether source-pool prefixes are generally legal, whether an earlier schema validator inspects authored range endpoints, whether the allocator interprets range endpoint masks, and whether the post-compile strict gate can recover them. Standalone source-pool prefixes are intentionally valid after #3049, but this function's own contract specifically requires `/32` for the `low to high` form. `address` remains unmodeled in the schema, and the original masks are irretrievably gone before strict validation. The 256-address cap prevents expansion DoS but does not validate endpoint masks.
HPC/invariant check: The #5194 `uint64` inclusive count and 256 bound are sound, and the `uint32` loop cannot wrap under that bound. No concurrency or allocation-amplification finding remains. The failed invariant is malformed-input fail-closed behavior and validation of authored data before canonicalization.
Why it matters: A typo or imported vSRX range using non-host CIDRs commits cleanly with materially different pool capacity and egress identities. The pool can exhaust ports early or translate through addresses the operator did not intend, while every strict gate reports success.
Fix direction: Parse each endpoint with `netip.ParsePrefix`/`ParseAddr`; accept bare IPv4 or require `Bits()==32` for a CIDR endpoint before extracting its address. Reject any non-host mask in the helper on both paths, retain the 256 cap, and add strict/tolerant tests for `/24`, mixed bare/`/32`, IPv6, reversed, and valid endpoints in flat, hierarchical, and formatter-round-trip forms.
Labels: `config`, `nat`, `source-nat`, `parser`, `validation`, `fail-closed`, `integer-safety`, `vSRX-parity`

#### R28: Hierarchical duplicate event trigger siblings bypass validation and compilation silently drops every trigger after the first

Title: Hierarchical duplicate event trigger siblings bypass validation and compilation silently drops every trigger after the first
Severity: Medium
Confidence: High
Gate verdict: MATERIAL
Evidence: At the reviewed base, `pkg/config/event_options_within.go:190-199` validates only the first child named `trigger`: ```go // trigger — a within clause with no trigger gates nothing; the engine // would treat it as an unconditional match (fail-open), so require one. trigNode := w.FindChild("trigger") if trigNode == nil { return emit("event-options policy %q within %d: missing a `trigger on|until "+ "<count>` (a within clause with no trigger gates nothing)", policy, sec) } specs, unknown := parseEventTriggerSpecs(trigNode) ``` The compiler independently repeats the same first-child selection at `pkg/config/compiler_services.go:1790-1799`: ```go case "within": w := &EventWithin{} if v := nodeVal(child); v != "" { if n, err := strconv.Atoi(v); err == nil { w.Seconds = n } } if trigNode := child.FindChild("trigger"); trigNode != nil { // trigger on N or trigger until N for i := 1; i < len(trigNode.Keys)-1; i++ { ``` `pkg/config/ast.go:181-188` explicitly defines `FindChild` as returning the first match. `pkg/config/parser.go:215-229,393-402` appends each hierarchical statement as its own leaf node, so this valid parser shape is reachable: ```text within 60 { trigger on 3; trigger until 5; } ```
Trace: 1. The hierarchical parser creates two children under the same `within` node: `Keys=["trigger","on","3"]` and `Keys=["trigger","until","5"]`. It appends rather than coalesces statements. 2. With no groups, `ExpandGroupsWithVars` only checks for stale `apply-groups` references and preserves those siblings. Schema declares `trigger` as an open leaf and has no sibling-cardinality check. 3. `validateEventOptionsWithinAST` reaches the `within`, calls `FindChild("trigger")`, validates `on 3`, and returns success. Strict commit therefore accepts. The tolerant path also sees no defect, so it emits no warning. 4. `compileEventOptions` again calls `FindChild("trigger")`, sets `EventWithin.TriggerOn=3`, and never reads the `until 5` sibling. Reversing the statements retains only `TriggerUntil=5`; a malformed or out-of-range second sibling is likewise never converted or rejected. 5. `pkg/eventengine/engine.go:1323-1393` evaluates only the compiled field. The operator-authored second bound is absent, so automated `then change-configuration` behavior executes under a materially different temporal policy than the committed configuration expresses.
Refutation attempt: I checked for later normalization, schema cardinality validation, a second compiler pass, and a runtime backstop. Direct hierarchical siblings survive group expansion; the schema relies on this custom validator; both validator and compiler use the same first-only helper; the runtime receives only typed `EventWithin` fields and cannot recover the discarded AST node. Existing `event_options_within_3751_test.go` covers flat-set commands that merge beneath one trigger node and a single hierarchical leaf `trigger on 3 until 5;`, but not two hierarchical trigger statements. The full Go tests pass because that shape is absent.
HPC/invariant check: This is not a hot-path/HPC issue. Parser recursion and numeric ranges are bounded. The violated compiler invariant is: every authored trigger statement in an accepted `within` clause must be validated and represented exactly once, and strict/recovery compilation must not silently select a subset.
Why it matters: `event-options` drives autonomous configuration changes. A strict-valid configuration can silently omit a stop or start threshold and run remediation under a different event count than the operator authored. That can produce unintended route/failover/config commits and makes configuration round-trip intent diverge from runtime behavior.
Fix direction: Replace first-child reads with one shared normalization helper over `w.FindChildren("trigger")`. Enforce exactly one trigger statement, or aggregate all specs and reject duplicate/contradictory `on`/`until` forms. Have compilation consume the validated normalized result rather than reparsing independently. On tolerant load, warn and compile an invalid duplicate clause to no usable threshold so the engine's existing zero-threshold guard fails closed. Add strict and tolerant tests for two hierarchical siblings in both orders, a malformed/out-of-range second sibling, and a fail-on-revert assertion that no partial trigger reaches `EventWithin`.
Labels: `bug`, `config`, `event-options`, `reliability`, `go`, `vsrx-parity`
Dedup note: Not a restatement of closed #3751: that issue fixed ignored numeric conversion and combined `on`/`until` specs inside one trigger node; this defect is sibling cardinality plus first-child truncation after that fix. Not the #5250/`ps-review-042` multi-clause latch item, which is runtime state sharing between distinct `within` clauses. Searches of the fresh open issue list and targeted all-state event-options/trigger searches found no issue for this AST shape.
Verified against origin/master: Still present at origin/master `ad959117748181dabe46b8ddc2827de670380cea` at `pkg/config/ast.go:181`. Independently retained in verify-R25-R36.md at the final target SHA.

#### R30: DDNS TTL schemas admit values that wrap to zero at the RFC2136 uint32 boundary

Title: DDNS TTL schemas admit values that wrap to zero at the RFC2136 uint32 boundary
Severity: Medium
Confidence: High
Gate verdict: MATERIAL
Evidence: Surface A is min-only in `pkg/config/schema_interfaces.go:553-557`, while the live RFC2136 backend narrows the resulting `int` in `pkg/ddns/backend_rfc2136.go:493-497`: > 553 `    args:          1,` > 554 `    valueType:     ValueInteger,` > 555 `    valueDesc:     "Record TTL in seconds (>= 1; default 300 when unset)",` > 556 `    valueExamples: []string{"300", "3600"},` > 557 `    validator:     ValidateIntegerMin(1),` > 493 `// forwardRR builds the A or AAAA RR for a record.` > 494 `func (u *rfc2136Updater) forwardRR(rec LeaseDNSRecord) (dns.RR, error) {` > 495 `    name := dns.Fqdn(rec.FQDN)` > 496 `    ttl := uint32(rec.TTL) //nolint:gosec // TTL is a small positive config value` > 497 `    if rec.Addr.Is4() {`
Trace: Both operator surfaces use the same unsafe contract: interface Surface A uses `ValidateIntegerMin(1)` (`pkg/config/schema_interfaces.go:551-558`) and DHCP Surface B does too (`pkg/config/schema_system.go:767-774`). Their compilers preserve an amd64 `int` through `strconv.Atoi` (`pkg/config/compiler_interfaces.go:1336-1339`, `pkg/config/compiler_services.go:615-618`). `LeaseDNSRecord.TTL` is also `int` (`pkg/ddns/backend.go:22-29`). The RFC2136 A/AAAA builder narrows it to `uint32` at `backend_rfc2136.go:496`, and the PTR builder repeats the cast at `:517-524`. Thus configured `4294967296` is positive at every default/fallback check but becomes TTL 0 on all emitted RRs. Values `2^32+n` become `n`, so the stored config, owned-record state, and wire records disagree.
Refutation attempt: `buildLeaseRecord` only defaults values `<= 0`; the oversized value remains positive until the final cast. The linter suppression assumes exactly the property the schema fails to establish. Cloudflare and Route53 using an `int` does not protect the RFC2136 backend, which is the live DHCP DDNS backend and an available Surface A provider. Existing DDNS schema tests cover hostname canonicality and source-address parsing, not TTL width.
HPC/invariant check: DNS RR TTL is an unsigned 32-bit wire field. Required invariant: `1 <= TTL <= math.MaxUint32` before any `uint32` conversion. On amd64, `ValidateIntegerMin(1)` accepts `2^32`; Go conversion yields `uint32(2^32) == 0`. No fallback or checked conversion intervenes.
Why it matters: A strict commit can claim a large positive TTL while RFC2136 publishes a zero or unrelated small TTL. Zero-TTL records are not cacheable, increasing authoritative query load and making DDNS behavior and status contradict operator intent for A, AAAA, and PTR records.
Fix direction: Bound both DDNS schema leaves to `[1, math.MaxUint32]` and add a checked conversion in the RFC2136 builder as defense in depth. Preserve the hostname and source-address cases already covered; add max, max+1, and `2^32+n` tests for Surface A, DHCPv4/v6 Surface B, A/AAAA, and PTR construction.
Labels: MATERIAL, DDNS, RFC2136, integer-narrowing, observability, performance, schema-runtime-contract, userspace-live
Dedup note: No scratch-index or issue-history entry matches DDNS TTL narrowing. Open #6555 is transient interface-address withdrawal; #6218's DDNS item is quarantine filename collision; prior `ps-review-038-A7` concerns `ForcedRefreshSeconds` to `time.Duration`. Those differ by symbol, mechanism, and impact.
Verified against origin/master: Still present at origin/master `ad959117748181dabe46b8ddc2827de670380cea` at `pkg/config/schema_interfaces.go:553`. Independently retained in verify-R25-R36.md at the final target SHA.

#### R31: Strict schema validation rejects the compiler-supported Junos hierarchical default-policy form

Title: Strict schema validation rejects the compiler-supported Junos hierarchical default-policy form
Severity: Medium
Confidence: High
Gate verdict: MATERIAL
Evidence: `pkg/config/schema_security.go:215-220` declares only a token-valued typed leaf, while `pkg/config/compiler_security_policy.go:9-12` explicitly supports the block spelling: > 215 `    args:          1,` > 216 `    valueType:     ValueEnumOf,` > 217 `    valueDesc:     "No-match default action (permit-all | deny-all | reject-all)",` > 218 `    valueExamples: []string{"deny-all", "permit-all", "reject-all"},` > 219 `    validator:     ValidateEnum([]string{"permit-all", "deny-all", "reject-all"}),` > 220 `    children:      nil,` > 9 `        policyStr = child.Keys[1]` > 10 `    } else if len(child.Children) > 0 {` > 11 `        // Hierarchical form: default-policy { deny-all; }` > 12 `        policyStr = child.Children[0].Name()`
Trace: The parser represents `default-policy { deny-all; }` as a node with `Keys == ["default-policy"]` and a child named `deny-all`; assigned parser fixtures use this exact vSRX shape (`pkg/config/parser_ast_test.go:74-80`, `pkg/config/parser_stray_brace_4862_test.go:55-61`). `walkSchemaNode` dispatches a typed leaf to `validateTypedLeaf` (`pkg/config/schema_walk.go:328-358`), which takes values only from `node.Keys[1:]` and returns `missing value` when that slice is empty (`:668-676`). The config store invokes `SchemaValidateWithDefinitions` on the expanded AST before compilation for strict commit/check (`pkg/configstore/store.go:585-627`). The compiler's hierarchical branch is therefore unreachable through the strict production path even though direct compiler tests and tolerant loading can use it.
Refutation attempt: Open-world handling does not help because `default-policy` is a known typed leaf, so validation fails before its child can be treated as an unknown extension. Parser acceptance is not commit acceptance. Setting `multi: true` alone would be unsafe because the generic block-list path permits multiple values while the compiler consumes only the first child. The default remains fail-closed when omitted; this finding is vSRX grammar completeness and schema/compiler disagreement, not a default-deny bypass.
HPC/invariant check: For this singleton verdict, the schema and compiler must accept exactly one of three values from either `Keys[1]` or one presence-only child, reject mixed or multiple forms, and compile the same selected value. Current schema accepts only the first representation while the compiler claims both.
Why it matters: A normal Junos/vSRX hierarchical configuration containing an explicit default deny cannot pass strict import, commit-check, or a later strict commit after tolerant boot. The failure occurs on a security posture statement the compiler is already designed to honor, blocking migration and creating two grammar sources of truth.
Fix direction: Add a purpose-built dual-shape tree/tail validator for `default-policy` that accepts exactly one flat token or exactly one child verdict and rejects duplicates, mixed forms, descendants, and unknown values. Keep the compiler and completion behavior aligned. Add config-store strict tests for all three verdicts in both forms and negative multi-child/mixed cases; retain parser-only coverage.
Labels: MATERIAL, security-policy, default-policy, vSRX-completeness, schema-compiler-drift, strict-commit, fail-closed
Dedup note: Closed #3065 added default-deny semantics, `reject-all`, and the missing schema entry; it did not cover rejection of the compiler-supported hierarchical shape after the leaf became typed. Prior `ps-review-042` covers absent-default handling. No index/history record matches this representation mismatch.
Verified against origin/master: Still present at origin/master `ad959117748181dabe46b8ddc2827de670380cea` at `pkg/config/compiler_security_policy.go:9`. Independently retained in verify-R25-R36.md at the final target SHA.

#### R33: Malformed encrypted-envelope fields bypass decryption and boot as an empty committed configuration

Title: Malformed encrypted-envelope fields bypass decryption and boot as an empty committed configuration
Severity: Medium
Confidence: High
Gate verdict: MATERIAL
Evidence: `pkg/configstore/db.go:373-380` accepts the raw object shape and uses a normal struct decode, which ignores all envelope keys because `ConfigTree` contains only `Children`: ```go if err := requireJSONObject(data); err != nil { return nil, true, fmt.Errorf("parse %s: %w", path, err) } tree := &config.ConfigTree{} if err := json.Unmarshal(data, tree); err != nil { return nil, true, fmt.Errorf("parse %s: %w", path, err) } ```
Trace: 1. A current outer config envelope contains a valid JSON object such as `{"format":1,"prf":"sha256","salt":"AAAA","nonce":"AAAA","data":"AAAA"}`. An all-empty or all-`null` reserved-field object is a second trigger. 2. `stripEnvelope` accepts the current outer header and passes the inner object to `unmarshalEnvelope`. 3. The numeric `format` produces `json.UnmarshalTypeError`; line 372 classifies it as plaintext. For `null`/empty values, decoding succeeds but line 385 sees only zero-value strings and line 389 also classifies it as plaintext. 4. AES-GCM key lookup and `Open` are never reached, so ciphertext integrity cannot fail the load. 5. `requireJSONObject` accepts the leading `{`. `json.Unmarshal` into `ConfigTree` ignores `format`/`prf`/`salt`/`nonce`/`data` and returns a zero-child tree without error. 6. `Store.Load` leniently compiles that empty tree and honors the outer `committed=1`, accepting policy-absent state instead of returning `ErrConfigDBUnreadable`.
Refutation attempt: I checked the #4888 unknown-format guard and both assigned #4888 tests; they cover non-empty string discriminators only. I checked `requireJSONObject`; it rejects a top-level `null`, not an object containing null/typed reserved fields. I checked `config.ConfigTree` and found no custom decoder or unknown-field rejection. I also followed `Store.Load`; an empty tree is a valid bootstrap-shaped compile. The semantic checks in `ReadConfirm` do reject an empty confirm record, but active/candidate/rollback tree reads share `readTreeMeta` and do not have an equivalent non-empty semantic gate.
HPC/invariant check: This is off the packet hot path. It violates the fail-closed persistent-state invariant: any object carrying an encryption-envelope field must either authenticate and decrypt or fail; it must never enter the plaintext AST decoder. No integer cast or alignment issue is involved.
Why it matters: A malformed restore, future inner-envelope schema using a non-string discriminator, or deliberate/corrupt root-owned DB can be accepted as a committed empty configuration. Startup proceeds after silently dropping firewall policy and other configured controls rather than stopping on unreadable authoritative state.
Fix direction: Probe the top-level object into `map[string]json.RawMessage` first. If any reserved key (`format`, `prf`, `salt`, `nonce`, `data`) is present, require the complete current envelope, exact string types, supported PRF, and non-empty fields; return an error on every typed decode failure. Pass through as plaintext only when none of those keys is present. Add end-to-end outer-envelope tests for numeric, boolean, `null`, and empty reserved values and require `ErrConfigDBUnreadable`.
Labels: `bug`, `configstore`, `crypto`, `firewall`, `fail-closed`, `persistence`
Dedup note: Closed #4888 fixed a non-empty unknown/missing string `format`; its implementation and tests do not cover decode errors or reserved-field presence hidden by empty/`null` values. Closed #5474 covers a non-object top-level body. Open #5523 C179-053 covers the unauthenticated outer `committed` marker, not this inner typed-object fallback. Exact symbol/mechanism searches in `dedup-index.tsv`, `docs/issues/issue-history.md`, and fresh issues found no match.
Verified against origin/master: Still present at origin/master `ad959117748181dabe46b8ddc2827de670380cea` at `pkg/configstore/db.go:373`. Independently retained in verify-R25-R36.md at the final target SHA.

#### R34: Archive reseeding performs contextless remote `ReadDir` while holding the global store mutex and can wedge cold boot

Title: Archive reseeding performs contextless remote `ReadDir` while holding the global store mutex and can wedge cold boot
Severity: Medium
Confidence: High
Gate verdict: MATERIAL
Evidence: `pkg/configstore/store_persist.go:632-636` performs a contextless filesystem call: ```go func maxArchiveSeq(dir string) (uint64, error) { entries, err := archiveDirReader(dir) if err != nil { return 0, err } ```
Trace: 1. The committed configuration names a custom archive directory on a hard-mounted NFS/compliance share; the repository's own factory-reset test explicitly documents remote/NFS as supported custom-path shapes. 2. On cold boot, `daemon_run_bringup.go:516-520` synchronously applies the active config before cluster communications and later control-plane startup. 3. Apply tail calls `SetArchiveConfig`; a fresh process has no `archiveSeedDir`, so it acquires `Store.mu` and enters `os.ReadDir` through `archiveDirReader`. 4. A hung hard mount leaves the goroutine in the kernel indefinitely. There is no context, timeout, or caller-visible error path. 5. `Store.mu` remains held, the daemon-wide apply semaphore remains held, boot never reaches cluster communications, and all configstore readers/mutators queue behind the same mutex. The day-2 path similarly wedges the commit/apply transaction after active state has already advanced.
Refutation attempt: I checked the same-dir fast path, but it cannot help the first scan on every process boot or a directory change. I checked the scan-error retry path; it handles returned errors only and cannot handle a syscall that never returns. I checked the daemon apply context and found `context.Background()` at boot, and `SetArchiveConfig` accepts no context. `archive_offlock_6403_test.go:201-217` deliberately blocks `archiveDirReader` while the store lock is held to assert exclusivity, confirming rather than refuting the lock scope.
HPC/invariant check: No packet-loop cache-line concern applies. The violated invariant is that remote or potentially blocking filesystem I/O must not run under the single configstore mutex or in an unbounded cold-boot critical section. The mutex is also the serialization point for HA sync and applied-state accounting.
Why it matters: Loss of an optional archive share can prevent the firewall daemon from completing cold boot and starting HA cluster communications or management services. On a live commit it can freeze every config operation while leaving the operator without a bounded failure result.
Fix direction: Move seeding out of `Store.mu` using a two-phase path token/generation: capture desired dir, scan outside the lock, then publish `max(current, scanned)` only if the path generation still matches. Do not block boot on optional archive storage; use one bounded worker and keep archival unready/skipped with degraded health until seeding completes. Avoid spawning a new waiter for each retry if the underlying filesystem call is permanently stuck. Preserve #6403's monotonic claim invariant with generation validation or a durable local sequence/unique filename scheme.
Labels: `bug`, `configstore`, `availability`, `cold-boot`, `ha`, `performance`
Dedup note: Closed #6403 is an archive sequence race and closed #6404 is reseed retry/readiness correctness; neither tracks a stuck scan under `Store.mu` or cold-boot impact. Open #5523 C179-059 tracks unbounded archive writer goroutines/full snapshots under stalled storage, not this synchronous seed scan, mutex ownership, or startup ordering. Open #5609's custom-archive item concerns retained remote secrets. Exact fresh searches found no matching issue.
Verified against origin/master: Still present at origin/master `ad959117748181dabe46b8ddc2827de670380cea` at `pkg/configstore/store_persist.go:632`. Independently retained in verify-R25-R36.md at the final target SHA.

#### R36: Graceful RA withdrawal discards the final goodbye failure and clears its retry debt

Title: Graceful RA withdrawal discards the final goodbye failure and clears its retry debt
Severity: Medium
Confidence: High
Gate verdict: MATERIAL
Evidence: `pkg/ra/ra.go:266-274` detects failure of the fresh-connection backstop, but only logs it: > 266 `if cfg != nil {` > 267 `    // Surface a failed backstop goodbye (#5093): this is the last` > 268 `    // retry the graceful-withdraw path has, so a swallowed write` > 269 `    // error here would silently leave the stale router live on hosts.` > 270 `    if err := m.sendOneGoodbye(cfg); err != nil {` > 271 `        slog.Warn("ra: standalone goodbye failed",` > 272 `            "interface", name, "err", err)` > 273 `    }` > 274 `}` The manager then removes the only tombstone and returns only a replacement-start error at `pkg/ra/ra.go:291-300`: > 291 `if onProvenClose != nil && m.epoch == startEpoch &&` > 292 `    m.ifaceEpoch[name] == e.startIfaceEpoch && !e.goodbyeWanted {` > 293 `    // Old conn PROVEN closed + tombstone still held → ≤1 live conn.` > 294 `    if startErr = onProvenClose(); startErr == nil {` > 295 `        repl = m.senders[name]` > 296 `    }` > 297 `}` > 298 `delete(m.draining, name)` > 299 `m.mu.Unlock()` > 300 `return repl, startErr` The public full-withdraw entry point also discards every `releaseDrain` result and reports success at `pkg/ra/ra.go:634-643`: > 634 `func (m *Manager) Withdraw() error {` > 635 `    m.mu.Lock()` > 636 `    m.bumpEpoch()` > 637 `    owned, epoch := m.collectGracefulWithdrawLocked()` > 638 `    m.mu.Unlock()` > 639 `    for _, o := range owned {` > 640 `        // nil onProvenClose: a withdraw never starts a replacement.` > 641 `        m.releaseDrain(o.name, o.s, epoch, nil)` > 642 `    }` > 643 `    return nil`
Trace: On demotion or config removal, the live sender first attempts its owner-only lifetime-zero burst in `sender.finishShutdown`. A failed write leaves `goodbyeEmitted=false` (`pkg/ra/sender.go:609-622`), so `releaseDrain` correctly invokes `sendOneGoodbye` on a fresh socket. If that bind or write also fails, `finishDrainDecision` logs the error, marks the one-shot claim consumed, deletes `m.draining[name]`, and returns nil because `startErr` covers only replacement startup. `Apply(nil)`, `Withdraw`, and `WithdrawInterfaces` therefore retain neither the failed config nor an error. The cluster caller treats `Apply` as successful and advances `lastRAReconcileHash` (`pkg/daemon/daemon_ra_reconcile.go:64-81`); later periodic reconciles see an equal desired hash and do not retry. Standalone config removal and shutdown likewise receive nil from `Withdraw`. Hosts can keep the demoted node as an IPv6 default router for the configured lifetime, 1800 seconds by default (`pkg/ra/sender.go:26`).
Refutation attempt: The owner attempt plus fresh-socket backstop handles a transient failure that clears between the two writes, and the cold-boot `WithdrawOnce` path now returns `[]GoodbyeResult` so its caller retries. Neither protects the graceful path when both attempts fail during the same interface outage. Re-running `Apply(nil)` is not sufficient after the tombstone is deleted because there is no sender or retained config from which to construct another goodbye. The periodic cluster reconciler is also explicitly hash-idempotent after the false nil result. Hard crash failover is a separate architectural limitation; this finding is the avoidable false-success path during graceful demotion/removal.
HPC/invariant check: RA withdrawal is cold control-plane work. The required invariant is that a requested terminal lifetime-zero action remains pending until one write succeeds or newer ownership supersedes it. Retaining a bounded per-interface debt record does not add packet-path locks. A retry must be fenced by the manager/interface epoch so a later promotion cannot emit a stale goodbye.
Why it matters: A controlled HA demotion, config removal, or shutdown can report a successful withdrawal while clients continue forwarding through an inactive router identity for up to 30 minutes. That causes IPv6 blackholing or asymmetric traffic precisely when the graceful path is expected to shorten failover.
Fix direction: Return the backstop error through `finishDrainDecision`, `releaseDrain`, `Apply`, and `Withdraw`, and retain `{interface, cfg, ownership epoch}` as pending-goodbye debt after a failed final write. Re-drive it with bounded backoff from reconciliation until success or supersession; do not advance `lastRAReconcileHash` while debt remains. Add a red-on-revert test where both owner and standalone writes fail, the first reconcile returns failure, a later reconcile retries and succeeds, and a repromotion cancels stale debt.
Labels: MATERIAL, HA, RA, IPv6, graceful-failover, retry-debt, false-success, observability, dual-stack, userspace-live
Dedup note: Closed #5093 named the same broad failure class and requested structured results through `Withdraw`, but its shipped fix completed retry debt only for cold-boot `WithdrawOnce`. The exact graceful `finishDrainDecision` mechanism above is still present after #5093 closed, and no open issue tracks it. Closed #2033 concerns ordering of normal versus goodbye RAs, not loss of the final failed action. The current index, issue history, and refreshed open issue list contain no open symbol+mechanism+consequence match.
Verified against origin/master: Still present at origin/master `ad959117748181dabe46b8ddc2827de670380cea` at `pkg/ra/ra.go:266`. Independently retained in verify-R25-R36.md at the final target SHA.

#### R37: A full config-apply queue strands the newest generation without retry or health debt

Title: A full config-apply queue strands the newest generation without retry or health debt
Severity: Medium
Confidence: High
Gate verdict: MATERIAL
Evidence: The receive path advances its authoritative received high-water before attempting a nonblocking enqueue at `pkg/cluster/sync_conn_read.go:304-330`: > 304 `// #5563: advance the received-config high-water BEFORE enqueue. This is` > 305 `// the receiver's view of the peer's current committed generation and` > 306 `// gates manual-failover readiness against lastAppliedConfigGen. Record it` > 307 `// even if the enqueue below drops the payload (queue full) so the standby` > 308 `// stays flagged config-stale until the apply actually lands on a re-push.` > 312 `if gen > s.lastRecvConfigGen.Load() {` > 313 `    s.lastRecvConfigGen.Store(gen)` > 321 `if s.configApplyCh != nil {` > 322 `    select {` > 323 `    case s.configApplyCh <- configApplyItem{gen: gen, text: configText}:` > 324 `    default:` > 325 `        // Ordered apply queue full — practically impossible (commits` > 326 `        // are seconds apart, apply is sub-second). Drop with an alarm;` > 327 `        // the next commit / reconnect re-push (fresh higher gen)` > 328 `        // re-converges the standby.` > 329 `        s.stats.Errors.Add(1)` > 330 `        slog.Error("cluster sync: config apply queue full, dropping config (will re-converge on next push)", "gen", gen, "size", len(configText))` The sender-side level reconciler suppresses that promised same-connection re-push at `pkg/daemon/daemon_ha_sync.go:474-489`: > 474 `// Check-and-claim the (epoch × generation) marker under one lock so two` > 475 `// concurrent triggers (e.g. a promotion racing the safety-net tick) push` > 476 `// at most once. Claim the marker BEFORE the push: a failed/dropped send` > 477 `// disconnects, and the next (re)connect bumps the epoch so the reconciler` > 478 `// re-pushes on the fresh connection.` > 479 `d.configSyncMu.Lock()` > 480 `if d.configSyncHasPushed && d.configSyncPushedEpoch == epoch && d.configSyncPushedGen == gen {` > 481 `    d.configSyncMu.Unlock()` > 482 `    slog.Debug("cluster: config-sync reconcile no-op (already pushed for epoch/generation)",` > 483 `        "reason", reason, "epoch", epoch, "generation", gen)` > 484 `    return`
Trace: `SessionSync` allocates a 64-entry `configApplyCh` (`pkg/cluster/sync.go:847-857`). Let the single `OnConfigReceived` consumer block or run slower while a connected peer delivers valid generations G1 through G65. G1 is in progress and G2..G65 can exhaust the channel; the next generation that observes a full queue is dropped after `lastRecvConfigGen` advances. The consumer eventually applies every queued item, leaving `lastAppliedConfigGen < lastRecvConfigGen`, but the dropped payload no longer exists. `noteConfigApplyFailure` is called only after an invoked callback returns an error (`sync_conn_config.go:351-379`), so a pre-callback queue drop never arms the 30-second config-sync health timer. `TransferReadiness` exposes the mismatch and blocks planned failover (`sync_bulk.go:235-242`), but unplanned peer-loss promotion deliberately does not use that gate. On the healthy connection, the daemon's `(connection epoch, config hash)` marker makes every 30-second reconcile a no-op; only a new commit or reconnect supplies another payload.
Refutation attempt: The bounded queue correctly prevents config application from blocking heartbeat/session reads, and the received/applied mismatch prevents a planned promotion. Those are partial mitigations, not convergence: there is no config ACK, receiver NACK, queue-overflow debt timer, or same-generation retry. A warning and error counter do not repair state. The 65-message trigger is high-cardinality for normal human commits but is reachable under commit automation, a slow dependency during apply, or an authenticated faulty peer; each message is a full snapshot and validly authenticated frames are accepted by this path. This is Medium rather than High because the burst plus apply lag is unusual and planned failover remains blocked.
HPC/invariant check: Config snapshots are complete and cold-path, so intermediate queued generations can be coalesced while preserving a monotonically newest pending generation. The receive loop must remain nonblocking, but the invariant is that accepting a newer receive high-water creates durable apply/retry debt until that exact or a newer generation succeeds. A one-slot latest-wins mailbox plus a wake channel, or an explicit config ACK/NACK protocol, avoids unbounded memory and does not affect packet processing.
Why it matters: The standby can remain indefinitely on an older security policy while transport health and CF health stay green. If the primary then fails unexpectedly, the stale node is eligible for unplanned takeover, reopening traffic denied by the lost tightening commit or denying traffic allowed by a loosening commit.
Fix direction: Replace drop-on-full with bounded latest-wins coalescing or add receiver ACK/NACK and sender retry. Advance/retain received high-water only together with durable pending debt, arm the existing config-health grace when enqueue cannot retain the payload, and clear it only after an equal-or-newer apply. Add a test that blocks the real consumer, overfills 64 entries, releases it, and proves the newest config applies without a reconnect and health/debt converges.
Labels: MATERIAL, HA, config-sync, security-policy, bounded-queue, retry-debt, cold-boot, failover-readiness, authentication, userspace-live
Dedup note: Closed #3931 fixed racing unordered config goroutines; closed #4151 retained applied high-water on callback failure; closed #5563 added the planned-failover received/applied gate; #6387 added health debt for callback errors. Open #5084 concerns stale queued items crossing a peer boot/connection epoch, #6368 concerns config-epoch install atomicity, #6419 concerns directional namespaces, and #6173 concerns the committed-but-not-yet-received window. None covers a payload dropped after `lastRecvConfigGen` advances, with no callback, health timer, or stable-connection re-push. No current open issue or history entry matches symbol+mechanism+consequence.

#### R39: Tolerated nil config slots panic both RETH ownership modes before fail-closed reconciliation

Title: Tolerated nil config slots panic both RETH ownership modes before fail-closed reconciliation
Severity: Medium
Confidence: High
Gate verdict: MATERIAL
Evidence: `pkg/vrrp/vrrp.go:150-159` dereferences every redundancy-group slice element: > 150 `if cc := cfg.Chassis.Cluster; cc != nil {` > 151 `    if cc.RethAdvertiseInterval > 0 {` > 152 `        advertInterval = cc.RethAdvertiseInterval` > 153 `    }` > 154 `    for _, rg := range cc.RedundancyGroups {` > 155 `        if rg.GratuitousARPCount > 0 {` > 156 `            garpCounts[rg.ID] = rg.GratuitousARPCount` > 157 `        }` > 158 `        preemptMap[rg.ID] = rg.Preempt` > 159 `    }` The same collector immediately dereferences interface map values at `pkg/vrrp/vrrp.go:169-175`: > 169 `var instances []*Instance` > 170 `for _, name := range names {` > 171 `    ifc := cfg.Interfaces.Interfaces[name]` > 172 `    if ifc.RedundancyGroup <= 0 {` > 173 `        continue` > 174 `    }` > 175 `    rgID := ifc.RedundancyGroup` The direct-ownership walker repeats the interface dereference at `pkg/vrrp/vrrp.go:254-263`: > 254 `result := make(map[string][]string)` > 255 `for _, name := range sortedIfNames(cfg) {` > 256 `    ifc := cfg.Interfaces.Interfaces[name]` > 257 `    if ifc.RedundancyGroup != rgID {` > 258 `        continue` > 259 `    }` > 260 `    // Only include actual RETH interfaces - skip fabric, control,` > 261 `    // and management interfaces that default to RedundancyGroup 0.` > 262 `    if !strings.HasPrefix(name, "reth") {` > 263 `        continue`
Trace: Nil typed slots are an established tolerant/programmatic/HA-snapshot premise in the checked-in #3474/#3476/#3492/#3499/#3501 issue family. The #3501 fix makes `Config.RethToPhysical` skip a nil interface (`pkg/config/types.go:71-74`), so it now returns successfully to these assigned walkers, which dereference the same slot next. `CollectRethInstances` also dereferences nil unit values in both VLAN and non-VLAN paths (`pkg/vrrp/vrrp.go:201-205,223-226`), and `RethVIPsForRG` repeats both forms (`:278-283,290-294`). On runtime apply, `applyTailReconciles` calls `CollectRethInstances` at `pkg/daemon/daemon_apply_tail.go:42-50`, before the later cluster `UpdateConfig` at `:221-223`, so a nil RG/interface/unit can panic before the manager can return a fail-closed update error. When `NoRethVRRP` or `PrivateRGElection` disables that collector, direct ownership and readiness call `RethVIPsForRG` from `pkg/daemon/daemon_ha_vip.go`, preserving the nil-interface/unit crash in the alternate mode. A panic in either path terminates xpfd rather than retaining the last known-good ownership set.
Refutation attempt: Strict text compilation normally constructs non-nil entries, but production explicitly supports tolerant boot and HA-derived snapshots and has repeatedly hardened sibling walkers for this exact representation. The newly nil-safe `RethToPhysical` is not a defense because these functions walk the original maps again. Manager family/VRID validation is downstream and never receives a desired set. The finding is Medium, not High, because it requires malformed internal/tolerant state rather than an ordinary valid strict commit, although a synchronized bad snapshot can still remove both HA members.
HPC/invariant check: These are cold config walks, so nil checks have negligible cost. The invariant is that every tolerant typed collection walker either skips nil entries with an observable warning/debt record or rejects the desired snapshot without changing live ownership. No pointer obtained from a map/slice of config pointers may be dereferenced before that check.
Why it matters: A no-brick/tolerant snapshot can crash the daemon during cold boot or commit reconciliation exactly where the node is rebuilding RETH ownership. On an HA pair, propagation of the same snapshot can turn a recoverable malformed entry into loss of both control planes and all VIP ownership.
Fix direction: Add nil guards for redundancy groups, interfaces, and units in both collectors, sharing a nil-safe RETH walker so the two ownership modes cannot drift. Surface skipped desired objects as warnings and reconciliation/readiness debt rather than silently claiming complete coverage. Add table tests for each nil slot in VRRP-backed and direct modes, plus an `applyTailReconciles` test proving the old live desired set is retained and an error is returned instead of panicking.
Labels: MATERIAL, HA, VRRP, cold-boot, tolerant-load, nil-safety, direct-ownership, availability, userspace-live
Dedup note: Closed #3501 is the earlier `Config.RethToPhysical` dereference and now supplies the nil-safe predecessor that exposes this residual. `codex-review-175` covers nil routing-instance/redundancy-group values in operational completion code, a different symbol and operator-display impact. No index/history/open-issue entry covers `CollectRethInstances` or `RethVIPsForRG` crashing HA ownership reconciliation.
Verified against origin/master: Still present at origin/master `ad959117748181dabe46b8ddc2827de670380cea` at `pkg/vrrp/vrrp.go:150`. Independently retained in verify-R37-R48.md at the final target SHA.

#### R40: VRRP-backed and direct RETH modes disagree on non-reth interfaces carrying a redundancy group

Title: VRRP-backed and direct RETH modes disagree on non-reth interfaces carrying a redundancy group
Severity: Medium
Confidence: High
Gate verdict: MATERIAL
Evidence: `pkg/vrrp/vrrp.go:169-175` treats any interface with a positive `RedundancyGroup` as a synthesized VRRP instance, without checking RETH identity: > 169 `var instances []*Instance` > 170 `for _, name := range names {` > 171 `    ifc := cfg.Interfaces.Interfaces[name]` > 172 `    if ifc.RedundancyGroup <= 0 {` > 173 `        continue` > 174 `    }` > 175 `    rgID := ifc.RedundancyGroup` If no RETH mapping exists, `pkg/vrrp/vrrp.go:182-189` deliberately leaves the physical interface name in place: > 182 `gc := garpCounts[rgID] // 0 = use default (3)` > 183 `` > 184 `// Resolve reth -> physical member (no bond device)` > 185 `physName := ifc.Name` > 186 `if phys, ok := rethToPhys[ifc.Name]; ok {` > 187 `    physName = phys` > 188 `}` > 189 `linuxName := config.LinuxIfName(physName)` By contrast, `pkg/vrrp/vrrp.go:255-263` explicitly excludes the same interface in direct mode: > 255 `for _, name := range sortedIfNames(cfg) {` > 256 `    ifc := cfg.Interfaces.Interfaces[name]` > 257 `    if ifc.RedundancyGroup != rgID {` > 258 `        continue` > 259 `    }` > 260 `    // Only include actual RETH interfaces - skip fabric, control,` > 261 `    // and management interfaces that default to RedundancyGroup 0.` > 262 `    if !strings.HasPrefix(name, "reth") {` > 263 `        continue`
Trace: The interface schema is wildcard-based and exposes `redundant-ether-options` to every interface name (`pkg/config/schema_interfaces.go:36,83-85`). The compiler copies its `redundancy-group` into any `InterfaceConfig` (`pkg/config/compiler_interfaces.go:136-141`), and the strict derived-VRID validator checks only nil and numeric range, not the `reth` prefix (`compiler_validate_strict_reth_vrrp.go:50-86`). Thus a strict config can attach the option to `ge-0/0/0`. In normal VRRP-backed mode, `CollectRethInstances` builds an instance on `ge-0-0-0`, copies all unit addresses as VIPs, and the instance startup path removes those addresses while BACKUP (`pkg/vrrp/instance.go:941-950`). In `no-reth-vrrp`/private-election mode the collector returns nil, while `RethVIPsForRG` filters the same name out, so direct ownership never treats the addresses as VIPs. A mode toggle therefore changes static physical addresses into floating ownership or vice versa; peers with transient mode/config skew can disagree about whether that interface belongs to the RG.
Refutation attempt: The presence of `redundant-ether-options` might be interpreted as defining a RETH regardless of its name, but the direct walker explicitly states and enforces that only `reth*` is an actual RETH. `Config.RethToPhysical` likewise maps logical RETH names through member `RedundantParent`, and project/vSRX examples put `redundant-ether-options` on `rethN` while physical members use `redundant-parent`. The strict schema cannot both accept a non-reth name and let the two ownership engines assign contradictory semantics. This is Medium rather than High because it requires a vSRX-invalid contextual configuration or a mode transition, not the normal supported RETH shape.
HPC/invariant check: RETH inventory is a cold config operation. The invariant is that VRRP-backed and direct ownership consume the same canonical set of logical RETH interfaces, and strict commit rejects unsupported interface/type combinations. Prefix/type validation and a shared iterator have no forwarding hot-path cost.
Why it matters: A strict commit can cause an ordinary physical interface address to disappear on the BACKUP, float as a VIP, or stop floating when the ownership mode changes. That creates mode-dependent reachability, breaks vSRX configuration parity, and can make cluster peers reason from different ownership inventories during failover.
Fix direction: Add a contextual strict validator requiring `redundant-ether-options` only on canonical `rethN` interfaces, with tolerant-load warning/skip behavior. Route `CollectRethInstances` and `RethVIPsForRG` through one nil-safe logical-RETH iterator. Add strict accept/reject tests and a parity test asserting both ownership modes derive the same interfaces/VIPs.
Labels: MATERIAL, HA, VRRP, RETH, mode-parity, vSRX-compatibility, config-validation, ownership-invariant, userspace-live

Open #6177 concerns the bounded handoff overlap for valid RETHs; it does not cover contradictory inventory selection. Closed #4826 concerns derived VRID range, not interface type/context.

#### R43: Fresh userspace-manager restarts do not reconcile retained classifier rows

Title: Fresh userspace-manager restarts do not reconcile retained classifier rows
Severity: Medium
Confidence: High
Gate verdict: MATERIAL
Evidence: The loader pins both classifier maps, and normal close explicitly preserves pinned state for restart (`pkg/dataplane/loader_userspace_shim.go:562-570`, `pkg/dataplane/loader.go:1203-1218`): ```go 562         "userspace_ctrl", 563         "userspace_bindings", 564         "userspace_ingress_ifaces", 565         "userspace_heartbeat", 566         "userspace_xsk_map", 567         "userspace_local_v4", 568         "userspace_local_v6", 569         "userspace_interface_nat_v4", 570         "userspace_interface_nat_v6", ``` ```go 1203 // Close releases Go handles for eBPF resources but leaves pinned maps 1204 // and links in the kernel for the next daemon to reuse. This enables 1205 // hitless restarts — sessions survive and XDP/TC programs keep running. 1206 func (m *Manager) Close() error { 1207     for ifindex, l := range m.xdpLinks { 1208         if err := l.Close(); err != nil { 1209             slog.Error("failed to close XDP link handle", "ifindex", ifindex, "err", err) 1210         } ``` The live userspace manager takes that normal-close path after stopping the helper (`pkg/dataplane/userspace/manager.go:471-475`): ```go 471 func (m *Manager) Close() error { 472     m.mu.Lock() 473     defer m.mu.Unlock() 474     m.stopLocked() 475     return m.bpfShim.Close() ``` A new `Manager` has only volatile prior-key inventories (`pkg/dataplane/userspace/manager.go:163-179`). Bootstrap calls a clear that can visit only `lastBindingIndices`, then forgets it (`maps_sync.go:178-194,852-870`): ```go 162     fabricSnapshotBuilder func(*config.Config) []FabricSnapshot 163     lastIngressIfaces     []uint32 164     lastRSTv4             []netip.Addr 165     lastRSTv6             []netip.Addr 166     lastRSTAttempt        time.Time 167     lastRSTInstallOK      bool ``` ```go 175     // is replaced. Read under m.mu (existing snapshot lock). 176     neighborIndex map[neighborIndexKey]*NeighborSnapshot 177     // #1197: ifindex set for listener filter; rebuilt on config commit. 178     monitoredIfindexes      map[int]struct{} 179     lastBindingIndices      []uint32 180     neighborsPrewarmed      bool 181     ctrlEnableAt            time.Time 182     ctrlWasEnabled          bool 183     initialCtrlCleanupDone  bool ``` ```go 862     if bindingsMap == nil { 863         m.lastBindingIndices = nil 864         return 865     } 866     var zeroBinding userspaceBindingValue 867     for _, idx := range m.lastBindingIndices { 868         _ = bindingsMap.Update(idx, zeroBinding, ebpf.UpdateAny) 869     } 870     m.lastBindingIndices = nil ``` The ingress hash similarly deletes only keys remembered by this process and then replaces the volatile inventory (`maps_sync.go:961-989`): ```go 980     for _, k := range m.lastIngressIfaces { 981         if _, keep := newIngressSet[k]; keep { 982             continue 983         } 984         if err := ifaceMap.Delete(k); err != nil && !errors.Is(err, ebpf.ErrKeyNotExist) { 985             return fmt.Errorf("delete userspace_ingress_ifaces %d: %w", k, err) 986         } 987     } 988     m.lastIngressIfaces = newIngress 989     return nil ``` The live XDP shim trusts any retained ingress key, derives a binding-array index, and accepts a retained READY row when its referenced slot has a current heartbeat (`userspace-xdp/src/lib.rs:426-453,471-518,724-735`): ```rust 426     let ingress_ifindex = unsafe { (*ctx.ctx).ingress_ifindex }; 427     if unsafe { USERSPACE_INGRESS_IFACES.get(&ingress_ifindex) }.map_or(true, |v| *v == 0) { 428         return Ok(cpumap_or_pass(ctrl)); 429     } 430     let native_gre = 431         parsed.protocol == PROTO_GRE && (ctrl.flags & USERSPACE_CTRL_FLAG_NATIVE_GRE) != 0; 432 433     let rx_queue_index = unsafe { (*ctx.ctx).rx_queue_index }; 434     let selected_queue = select_userspace_queue(ctrl, rx_queue_index, &parsed); ``` ```rust 445     let binding_idx = ingress_ifindex * BINDING_QUEUES_PER_IFACE + selected_queue; 446     let mut binding = USERSPACE_BINDINGS.get(binding_idx); 447     // Treat zero-flags (unpopulated Array entry) as missing. 448     if binding.map_or(true, |b| b.flags == 0) && selected_queue != rx_queue_index { 449         let fallback_idx = ingress_ifindex * BINDING_QUEUES_PER_IFACE + rx_queue_index; 450         binding = USERSPACE_BINDINGS.get(fallback_idx); 451     } 452     let binding = match binding { 453         Some(b) if b.flags != 0 => b, ```
Trace: 1. Daemon generation A has an XDP-attached netdev classified as userspace ingress. Its ingress hash key and READY binding-array row are pinned. 2. A config transition changes that netdev's role, or a partial apply leaves the old row, and the daemon exits before same-process stale-key debt is completed. `Close` retains maps and links. 3. Generation B constructs a fresh Go `Manager`; `lastIngressIfaces` and `lastBindingIndices` are nil because neither is reconstructed from the pinned maps. 4. Bootstrap disables `userspace_ctrl`, but `clearAllBindingRowsLocked` iterates zero remembered rows. `syncIngressIfaceMapLocked` writes current keys and iterates zero old keys. Both stale rows remain. 5. The new helper registers current slots and refreshes their heartbeat/XSK entries, then status re-enables `userspace_ctrl`. 6. A packet on the still-attached netdev finds the stale ingress key. If the retained binding's slot was reused, the fresh heartbeat makes the old READY row look live and the shim redirects the packet to an XSK owned by a different current binding. If it was not reused, the stale row instead drives degraded transit drop. Neither result reflects generation B's snapshot.
Refutation attempt: I checked bootstrap control-disable and heartbeat zeroing, attachment lifecycle, current binding writes, same-process stale-row retry tests, and full teardown. Control-disable only protects the bootstrap interval; current helper heartbeat refresh makes a reused stale slot live after enable. `#5697` retains failed clear debt only in the same `Manager`; `#5486` clears only its in-memory binding inventory; full `Cleanup` removes pins only on decommission, while normal restart deliberately calls `Close`. No startup iterator or persisted inventory reconstructs kernel truth. A removed netdev may be detached by a clean compile, but the defect remains reachable for a still-attached netdev whose role changed and after crash/partial-apply residue.
HPC/invariant check: The vulnerable work is cold control-path map reconciliation, not packet processing. The fix should run while `userspace_ctrl` is disabled and must not add packet-path allocation or locking. Binding index multiplication remains bounded by the existing interface/queue caps; the fault is lifecycle ownership, not arithmetic. Iterating a large array at every 1 Hz status tick would be inappropriate, but a one-time bootstrap sweep or fresh classifier-map recreation is outside the hot path.
Why it matters: After an ordinary crash/restart boundary, packets can be redirected under a classifier state that the active config never published. Reused slots can send traffic into the wrong interface/queue context; unreused slots produce a persistent transit outage. The daemon reports the new snapshot and healthy current bindings even though the kernel classifier still contains generation-A rows.
Fix direction: 1. Treat classifier pins separately from session-retention pins. While control is disabled, iterate and delete every ingress hash key not in the new set. 2. Recreate/zero the binding classifier map, or iterate every nonzero row and clear rows not written by the new generation; do not rely on fresh-process memory. 3. Preserve failed delete/update keys as explicit retry debt and only enable control after reconciliation succeeds. 4. Add a fail-on-revert test that prepopulates both pinned maps, constructs a new `Manager` with nil inventories, publishes a smaller/different interface set, and proves stale keys/READY rows cannot redirect. Include one failed-delete retry case.
Labels: `bug`, `dataplane`, `userspace`, `xdp`, `lifecycle`, `restart`, `partial-apply`, `operator-truth`
Dedup note: Checked `#6537` (same-process partial ingress install loses delete inventory), `#5697` (same-process failed binding clear debt), `#5486` (teardown clearing), `#5363` (pin ABI remediation), and fresh `#6741` (obsolete retained registry handles/close-in-use). None covers a new process starting with empty volatile inventories while compatible classifier pins retain old keys. Fixing `#6537` does not reconstruct keys after restart, and fixing F1 does not repair `#6537`'s partial-update debt before restart.
