
`pkg/dataplane/userspace/maps_sync.go:809` commits the enable before returning to the caller that will issue `syncHAStateLocked`:

```go
	if ctrl.Enabled == 1 {
		if err := ctrlMap.Update(zero, ctrl, ebpf.UpdateAny); err != nil {
			return m.failClosedUserspaceCtrlLocked(ctrlMap, ctrl, fmt.Errorf("enable userspace_ctrl from helper status: %w", err))
		}
		m.ctrlWasEnabled = true
	}
```

Trace:

1. On helper cold start, `HaState::new` publishes an empty RG map. Snapshot application synchronously builds forwarding, starts/binds workers, and returns status to Go.
2. In a cluster, `Manager.apply` invokes `applyHelperStatusLocked` before replaying `rg_active` and calling `syncHAStateLocked`.
3. If returned bindings are registered/armed and neighbor generation is ready, `applyHelperStatusLocked` writes `userspace_ctrl.Enabled=1`. The cold path does not set `rgTransitionInFlight`; that fence is for explicit RG transitions.
4. Kernel packet processing is concurrent with the manager lock/RPC sequence. A packet redirected by the live interface-NAT/native-GRE maps can therefore enter XSK after the ctrl update and before the first HA RPC completes.
5. An interface-NAT destination resolves to `LocalDelivery` with the real RG-owned interface as egress. `enforce_ha_resolution_snapshot` sees the empty map and returns before `owner_rg_for_resolution`, so an inactive standby is not converted to `HAInactive`/fabric redirect.
6. Host-inbound/junos-host policy still runs, but it answers only whether that service is allowed, not whether this node owns the RG. If permitted, this packet reaches the local stack on the standby.
7. The later HA RPC populates inactive groups and subsequent resolution/cache checks fail closed. That bounds the exposure window but cannot revoke a UDP/IKE/ICMP packet already reinjected.

Refutation attempt:

I checked the startup readiness delay, transition fence, later session revalidation, and host-inbound policy. The 15-second HA delay is bypassed as soon as `probeBindingsReady && neighborSyncReady`; it is not an HA-snapshot-ready predicate. `rgTransitionInFlight` is not initialized for cold replay. Session hits are re-enforced once HA arrives, so the flaw does not persist, but one-shot/local UDP traffic does not need persistence. Host-inbound default deny narrows the exposed services but is orthogonal to RG ownership. I also checked the prior ifindex-0 concern: this trace uses interface NAT's real nonzero egress ifindex, so the owner is knowable and the only bypass is the empty-map sentinel.

HPC/invariant check:

The ArcSwap read and publication are memory-safe and coherent. The defect is a semantic state collapse: empty means both `standalone, HA intentionally absent` and `clustered, first HA state not received`. No extra packet-path lock is needed. A tri-state initialization flag or startup control-plane fence preserves the existing single ArcSwap load and cache-line behavior.

Why it matters:

An HA standby can accept an RG-owned local packet during every clustered helper cold boot. For permitted UDP/control services, one accepted datagram is a complete action; for IKE or management traffic it can create split-brain behavior or leak service availability from the inactive node. The system otherwise promises fail-closed packet handling until ownership is known.

Fix direction:

On clustered startup, mark HA replay in flight before `applyHelperStatusLocked` and keep `userspace_ctrl` disabled until `syncHAStateLocked` succeeds; a replay failure must leave ctrl disabled and retry debt armed. For defense in depth, represent worker HA state as `Standalone | UninitializedCluster | Ready(map)` (or publish an explicit initialization/cluster bit) and allow empty-map LocalDelivery only for `Standalone`. Add a cold-start integration test that makes bindings/neighbors ready while HA is still withheld and asserts ctrl stays zero and RG-owned LocalDelivery resolves inactive.

`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/poll_stages.rs:1148` performs the global-table call directly in the packet stage:

The stated upstream rate bound is optional. `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/poll_stages.rs:488` passes immediately when no screen profile exists:

```rust

    screen: &mut ScreenState,
    counters: &mut BatchCounters,
    worker_ctx: &WorkerContext,

        return StageOutcome::Continue(ScreenCheckOutcome::Pass);
    }
```

`userspace-dp/src/screen/packet.rs:86` also defines a configured zero UDP threshold as disabled:

```rust
    pub syn_frag: bool,
    pub source_route: bool,
    pub icmp_flood_threshold: u32, // packets per second, 0 = disabled
    pub udp_flood_threshold: u32,  // packets per second, 0 = disabled
    pub syn_flood_threshold: u32,  // SYN packets per second per zone, 0 = disabled
```

Trace:

1. A DNAT/static-NAT-to-self or native-GRE-inner IKE endpoint is permitted by the ingress zone's host-inbound IKE service. This is the documented AF_XDP secondary path.
2. An attacker sends syntactically valid zero-responder-SPI initiations and varies the 64-bit initiator SPI. Stage 11 admits and seeds each unique key.
3. After 4,096 keys, every additional initiation acquires the node-global mutex and iterates the entire `FastMap` to compute the minimum timestamp, then removes and inserts.
4. Concurrent packet workers targeting any secondary-path IKE exchange block on the same cache line/mutex. The attack therefore converts line-rate admitted UDP into serialized O(4,096) work before reinjection to the kernel IKE daemon.
5. With no screen profile, or `udp_flood_threshold=0`, stage 10 imposes no rate bound. Host-inbound IKE permission is an access policy, not a flood limiter.

Refutation attempt:

I checked whether the cap, lazy expiry, screen stage, primary-path nftables, or strongSwan cost bounded the Rust work. The cap bounds memory but is exactly what activates the repeated full scan. Lazy expiry occurs on lookup and does not make full-table seed eviction O(1). Screen profiles are optional and zero disables UDP flood control. Direct interface-IP IKE uses the primary path, but the documented DNAT/static-NAT/native-GRE secondary path is live. Kernel IKE processing may itself be expensive, but this scan happens first and adds a global cross-worker serialization point.

HPC/invariant check:

There is no memory-unsafety or integer overflow. The violated performance invariant is `bounded control table must have bounded per-packet maintenance independent of occupancy`. A `FastMap` iteration touches thousands of noncontiguous cache lines under a single mutex; every worker then contends on that mutex's cache line. The key clone is allocation-free, but lock hold time and cache misses are attacker-amplified.

Why it matters:

An operator must be able to permit IKE without making the userspace packet workers vulnerable to deterministic global lock contention. Saturating this secondary-path table can consume packet cores and delay unrelated IKE/control processing, causing tunnel setup/rekey/DPD failures and broader packet-loop latency on affected workers.

Fix direction:

Replace the full scan with bounded eviction metadata: an indexed min-heap (`O(log n)`), timing wheel, or generation-tagged FIFO/LRU queue with stale-node validation and a strict bounded-node budget. Sharding by local endpoint can reduce mutex contention, but each shard still needs bounded eviction. Add a full-cap benchmark/test that asserts one new seed does not visit all entries and a multi-thread contention benchmark independent of optional screen configuration.

Labels: `ipsec`, `ike`, `dos`, `performance`, `lock-contention`, `packet-latency`, `vsrx-parity`

The historical O(4096) item concerns a rejected V_min bucket scan, a different subsystem and call path. No issue covers the global IKE exchange eviction scan.


`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/binding_state/tx_inbox.rs:113` drops `req` immediately when the soft admission is full; dropping the request drops its `Vec<u8>` rather than returning it to the TLS pool:

```rust

        if self.try_acquire_pending_tx_admission(None, true).is_err() {

```

`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/cos/redirect_pool.rs:60` allocates once that pool has been consumed:

```rust
pub(in crate::afxdp) fn checkout(src: &[u8]) -> Vec<u8> {
    POOL.with(|pool| {
        let mut buf = pool.borrow_mut().pop().unwrap_or_default();
        buf.clear();
        buf.extend_from_slice(src);
        buf
    })
```

Trace:

Not required for `COHORT`. Mechanism: cross-worker prepared redirect checks out/copies bytes; destination inbox admission fails; infallible enqueue drops the `TxRequest` and reports `Ok`; source UMEM is recycled correctly, but the owned vector is freed. Repetition drains the source TLS pool, after which each still-doomed packet allocates/copies/frees a fresh vector.

Refutation attempt:

The packet loss is intentional and correctly counted, the MPSC admission counter is released exactly once, and Rust ownership prevents leaks/use-after-free. Successful queue service eventually recycles vectors, but the overflow path never reaches those settle sites. The issue therefore survives only as overload allocation amplification, not a correctness or memory-safety bug.

HPC/invariant check:

The warmed-path invariant promised by `redirect_pool.rs` is allocation-free cross-worker copies after warmup. Inbox saturation violates it precisely when allocator pressure is least desirable. The queue remains lock-free and bounded; no atomics ordering change is needed.

Why it matters:

Sustained destination-worker pressure turns deliberate bounded packet drops into allocator traffic and full-frame copies, adding CPU and tail latency during overload. The scope is performance-only and self-recovers after pressure, so this belongs in the existing warmed-path allocation cohort rather than an individual issue.

Fix direction:

Reserve destination inbox admission before checking out/copying the frame, then commit the owned request through `PendingTxAdmission`; or use the fallible owned enqueue and recycle the returned request's byte vector on failure. Recycle the source UMEM only after enqueue commit. Add a saturated-inbox test that warms N buffers, sends N failed redirects, and asserts the TLS pool count/capacity is conserved with no allocator fallback.

## Material findings

### M-01

Title: Native GRE decapsulation promotes bytes outside the outer IP datagram

Severity: Medium

Confidence: High

Gate verdict: MATERIAL

Evidence: `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/gre.rs:654` computes the outer-declared checksum region only when the optional GRE checksum bit is set (8 lines actually read):

```rust
    if checksum_present {
```

Evidence: `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/gre.rs:676` then parses options against the entire captured Ethernet frame and treats every byte after them as candidate inner data (7 lines actually read):

```rust

        frame.get(inner_offset..inner_offset + 4)?;
        inner_offset += 4;
    }

    let inner_len = packet_trimmed_len(inner_packet, inner_family)?;
    let inner_packet = &inner_packet[..inner_len];
```

Trace: RX supplies a full captured Ethernet frame -> XDP `parse_iphdr` records IPv4 `tot_len` but sets `l4_offset` from IHL and does not constrain capture to `tot_len` -> `stage_native_gre_decap` passes the full raw frame -> `try_native_gre_decap_from_frame` checks the outer declared end only in the checksum-present branch -> GRE key/sequence and inner parsing use `frame` to capture end -> `packet_trimmed_len` validates only the inner declaration against that oversized tail -> a synthetic inner frame is accepted and enters normal tunnel-zone processing. For checksum-present GRE, the authenticated region can end before the promoted tail; for checksum-absent GRE, the outer declaration is never consulted at all.

Refutation attempt: Endpoint family/source/destination/key matching, inner family, inner declared length, TCP/UDP/ICMP minimum lengths, ECN rules, and GRE checksum validation were traced. They do not establish that `inner_offset` or `inner_offset + inner_len` lies at or before the outer IPv4 Total Length / IPv6 Payload Length end. `gre_checksum_region` does calculate that end safely with checked addition, but its slice is discarded after checksum verification and the subsequent parse returns to the whole frame. Existing native-GRE tests cover endpoint/key, checksum, ECN, inner truncation, and short L4 headers; none makes the outer declaration shorter than the captured GRE+inner tail. The inner packet still receives tunnel ingress-zone policy, which limits this from being a direct policy bypass and is why the severity is Medium.

HPC/invariant check: No Rust out-of-bounds access occurs; all individual slice operations are guarded and offset additions here are small. The violated invariant is parser authority: bytes outside the outer L3 datagram, including Ethernet padding or a contradictory captured tail, must never become authenticated/forwarded inner packet bytes. Network-byte-order reads are correct. The fix can remain allocation-free and should not add atomics or cache-line traffic.

Why it matters: A malformed outer IPv4/IPv6 packet from an otherwise matching GRE endpoint can declare a datagram that excludes some or all of the GRE options/inner packet while placing a valid inner datagram in captured trailing bytes. Userspace accepts bytes that the outer IP header says are not part of the datagram, diverging from normal IP parsers and, on checksum-present GRE, extending forwarding beyond the checksum's declared envelope. This is a fail-open parser differential at a packet trust boundary.

Fix direction: Compute one outer declared end unconditionally before GRE option parsing. Reject an outer length shorter than the actual outer header, before the complete GRE fixed/options header, or beyond capture. Bound all GRE option reads and the inner candidate to `frame[gre_offset..outer_end]`, then require `inner_offset + inner_len <= outer_end`. Add IPv4 and IPv6 tests for checksum-present and checksum-absent GRE where the captured tail is valid but the outer declaration ends before the GRE header, in GRE options, and before the inner declared end; include benign Ethernet padding controls.

### M-02

Title: Successful local TX drains discard both reusable deques and allocate again on the next drain

Severity: Low

Confidence: High

Gate verdict: MATERIAL

Evidence: `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/tx/drain/mod.rs:577` transfers the worker-owned deque out and leaves a new zero-capacity deque in the worker (8 lines actually read):

```rust
pub(super) fn take_pending_tx_requests(binding: &mut BindingWorker) -> VecDeque<TxRequest> {
    // Reuse the worker-owned `pending_tx_local` buffer as the drain
    // target so the owner-worker hot path stays allocation-free. `pop`
    // from the lock-free inbox appends into the same buffer without a
    // queue-to-queue copy.
    let mut out = core::mem::take(&mut binding.tx_pipeline.pending_tx_local);
    binding.live.take_pending_tx_into(&mut out);
    out
```

Evidence: `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/tx/drain/phase_backup.rs:162` creates a second empty deque and pushes every nonempty drain through it (8 lines actually read):

```rust
    let mut retry = VecDeque::new();
    while let Some(req) = pending.pop_front() {
        retry.push_back(req);
        if retry.len() >= TX_BATCH_SIZE
            || binding.tx_pipeline.free_tx_frames.is_empty()
            || pending.is_empty()
        {
            match transmit_batch(binding, &mut retry, ctx.now_ns, shared_recycles) {
```

Trace: Local/copy TX requests accumulate in persistent `pending_tx_local` or the bounded inbox -> `take_pending_tx_requests` moves the persistent deque and its allocation out, leaving `VecDeque::new()` in the binding -> `backup_drain_local` allocates another deque on the first `retry.push_back` -> successful `transmit_batch` empties it -> restore runs only when `retry` is nonempty -> both the old `pending` capacity and the successful retry deque capacity are dropped at function exit -> the next nonempty sparse drain allocates again. `transmit_batch` already caps work by `TX_BATCH_SIZE`, free frames, and pending length, so the extra batching deque is not needed for correctness.

Refutation attempt: `VecDeque::new()` itself does not allocate, and prepared/direct TX requests can bypass this path. However, every nonempty invocation executes `retry.push_back`, and the success path at lines 209-211 restores nothing. `mem::take` therefore also makes the original worker deque's capacity transient. Retry/backpressure does restore a nonempty deque, so the defect is specifically the common successful local fallback path. Focused drain/transmit tests pass but assert ordering/counters, not allocator calls or retained capacity.

HPC/invariant check: Ownership, FIFO order, retry behavior, atomics, and frame recycling remain correct. The violated hot-path invariant is stable worker-owned storage: successful steady-state TX should not allocate/free queue backing memory per sparse packet or per drain pass. This creates allocator metadata/cache traffic and variable latency on a packet worker; no lock-free correctness defect or memory unsafety was found.

Why it matters: NAT64 output, generated/prebuilt traffic, direct-build fallback, and cross-owner local requests can use this drain. Sparse traffic can pay roughly one or two deque allocations per packet; sustained traffic pays per drain pass. The allocator and cache churn adds avoidable packet-worker tail latency and can amplify contention under multi-worker load even though forwarding remains functionally correct.

Fix direction: Drain `pending` directly through `transmit_batch`, which already enforces `TX_BATCH_SIZE`, and restore the emptied deque to `binding.tx_pipeline.pending_tx_local` on every exit so its capacity remains worker-owned. Alternatively add a persistent worker scratch deque, but do not add another transient container. Add an allocation-count or capacity-retention test for repeated successful one-request drains and full batches, plus retry-order controls.

Labels: performance, dataplane, rust, tx, allocation, latency, cache, hpc

That mechanism is fixed at this setup tip: `finalise.rs:39-56` reverse-pops the staged vector without a new `retry_tail`. M-02 is unconditional on the successful local backup drain and has a different function, trigger, and fix locus. No matching current record was found.

Title: Shared-session poison recovery is not surfaced as a metric

Severity: Low

Confidence: High

Gate verdict: DUP

Evidence: `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/shared_ops.rs:7` says the counter is retained for future wiring rather than current status export (10 lines actually read):

```rust
/// publish, remove, lookups, owner-RG index maintenance). Each recovery
/// means a worker thread panicked while holding one of the shared-session
/// mutexes; the map still holds every committed insert, so the HA
/// promotion/demotion path proceeds with the EXISTING sessions instead of
/// silently treating the table as empty (which dropped all synced sessions
/// at failover — the #2402 bug). Mirrors the worker-command-queue policy
/// (`worker_queue::lock_recover`, #1807). Each recovery also emits a sparse
/// journald line so operators see that a worker panicked (the root cause);
/// the counter is kept for tests and future status wiring.
pub(crate) static SHARED_SESSION_POISON_RECOVERIES: AtomicU64 = AtomicU64::new(0);
```

Trace: Not required for a DUP gate.

Refutation attempt: Not required for a DUP gate. A sparse log is useful but is not a scrapeable/aggregatable dataplane health signal.

HPC/invariant check: Increment uses relaxed ordering correctly and occurs only on poison. Surfacing the value adds no packet-path synchronization.

Why it matters: Operators cannot alert on a contained panic that compromised shared HA session state unless they happen to retain and correlate the log line.

Fix direction: Export the cumulative counter in binding/coordinator status and the normal metrics surface, with a recovery-rate alert.

Labels: rust, ha, observability, mutex-poison, metrics

Dedup note: Exact match to current open issue GH#6641.

Verified against origin/master: Yes; `origin/master` is the setup SHA and the comment/counter remain unsurfaced.

### D-11

Title: The screen extractor accepts IPv4 IHL below the mandatory five words

Severity: Medium

Confidence: High

Gate verdict: DUP

Evidence: `userspace-dp/src/screen/extract.rs:108` reads and uses the IHL nibble without a minimum check (9 lines actually read as the narrow contract called by the batch's poll stages):

```rust
        // IPv4: extract IHL, total_len, frag_off from the fixed 20-byte
        // base header. frag_off is bytes 6-7, big-endian.
        let ip_hdr = &frame[l3_offset..];
        info.ip_ihl = ip_hdr[0] & 0x0F;
        info.ip_total_len = u16::from_be_bytes([ip_hdr[2], ip_hdr[3]]);
        info.ip_frag_off = u16::from_be_bytes([ip_hdr[6], ip_hdr[7]]);
        // Fragment if MF bit (0x2000) set OR fragment offset (0x1FFF) > 0.
        // First fragment: MF=1 AND offset==0 (#1137, mirrors BPF #866).
        info.is_fragment = (info.ip_frag_off & 0x3FFF) != 0;
```

Evidence: `userspace-dp/src/screen/extract.rs:119` checks only whether the claimed IHL extends past capture (10 lines actually read):

```rust
        // FAIL-CLOSED (#4167): the header's own IHL claims a header
        // (`ihl*4`) longer than the captured frame, so the options
        // region — and thus any LSRR/SSRR source-route option — cannot
        // be parsed. Drop rather than silently skip the scan below,
        // which would leave `saw_ipv4_source_route=false` for a route
        // the extractor was UNABLE to read (a fail-open on the
        // `source-route` screen). Mirrors the IPv6 extension-header
        // overshoot fail-closed check. A minimal IHL=5 header always
        // survives — `l3_offset + 20 <= frame.len()` was just asserted.
        let ihl_bytes = (info.ip_ihl as usize) * 4;
```

Trace: Not repeated for a DUP gate; the canonical report covers how the undersized offset makes screen TCP reads come from IPv4 header bytes.

Refutation attempt: Not required for a DUP gate. The base capture has 20 bytes, but that does not validate the packet's encoded IHL, and downstream XDP validation is not a valid substitute for this reusable parser contract.

HPC/invariant check: A single predictable `ihl < 5` branch is sufficient. Parser fail-closed correctness outweighs negligible cost.

Why it matters: Malformed packets can feed IP-header bytes to TCP flag/port screen logic and obtain a disposition based on invented L4 semantics.

Fix direction: Reject IPv4 version/IHL mismatch and `IHL < 5` before deriving any L4 or option offset; add IHL 0-4 tests through the poll-stage screen path.

Labels: dataplane, rust, ipv4, parser, screen, bounds, fail-closed, vsrx-parity

Dedup note: Exact match to `ps-review-038-A1_rust_dataplane_packet-b2` dedup row 643.

Verified against origin/master: Yes; `origin/master` is the setup SHA and has no minimum-IHL check at this contract.

### D-12

Title: `FlowRrRing` overflow protection disappears in release builds

Severity: Medium

Confidence: High

Gate verdict: DUP

Evidence: `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/types/cos.rs:447` guards capacity only with `debug_assert!` before indexing and incrementing (10 lines actually read as the narrow ring contract called by `phase_shaped.rs`):

```rust
    pub(in crate::afxdp) fn push_back(&mut self, bucket: u16) {
        debug_assert!(
            usize::from(self.len) < COS_FLOW_FAIR_BUCKETS,
            "FlowRrRing overflow: len={} cap={}",
            self.len,
            COS_FLOW_FAIR_BUCKETS
        );
        let tail = (usize::from(self.head) + usize::from(self.len)) & COS_FLOW_FAIR_BUCKET_MASK;
        self.buf[tail] = bucket;
        self.len += 1;
```

Trace: Not repeated for a DUP gate; the canonical report covers duplicate active-bucket insertion and release-build corruption consequences.

Refutation attempt: Not required for a DUP gate. The caller intends one active entry per bucket, but the ring API itself can silently overwrite/wrap when that distributed invariant is violated.

HPC/invariant check: This is a fixed-size cache-friendly ring, but release correctness cannot rely solely on debug assertions at an externally mutable scheduling boundary.

Why it matters: An invariant violation corrupts the active CoS set in release, potentially starving queues or servicing overwritten buckets with no immediate diagnostic.

Fix direction: Make push return failure or perform a hard bounded guard in release, record the invariant violation, and add adversarial duplicate/full-ring tests around every phase-shape insertion path.

Labels: dataplane, rust, cos, ring, bounds, release-build, queue-correctness

Dedup note: Exact match to `ps-review-038-A1_rust_dataplane_packet-b2` dedup row 644.

Verified against origin/master: Yes; `origin/master` is the setup SHA and retains the debug-only checks.

## Cohort findings

### C1

**Title:** Output-filter TX-selection and cached evaluators retain a fall-through log's placeholder Accept after terminal discard/reject

**Severity:** Medium

**Confidence:** High

**Gate verdict:** COHORT

**Evidence:** `userspace-dp/src/filter/engine/tx_selection.rs:223-231` returns immediately after replacing only `acc.action`:

```rust
            record_filter_counter(&term.counter, packet_bytes);
        }
        merge_matched_tx_modifiers(&mut acc, filter, term, now_ns, packet_bytes);
        if !term.continue_term {
            acc.action = term.action;
            return acc;
        }
    }
    acc
```

The cached twin does the same at `userspace-dp/src/filter/engine/cache_sensitive.rs:74-82`:

```rust
            continue;
        }
        merge_matched_cached_modifiers(&mut acc, filter, term);
        if !term.continue_term {
            acc.action = term.action;
            return acc;
        }
    }
    acc
```

The full evaluator's contrasting fix is at `userspace-dp/src/filter/engine/eval.rs:149-155`:

```rust
        if !term.continue_term {
            acc.action = term.action;
            normalize_log_match_action(&mut acc);
            return acc;
        }
    }
    normalize_log_match_action(&mut acc);
```

**Trace:** Not required for COHORT. A modifier/log term records `FilterLogMatch { action: Accept }`, evaluation continues, a later output term terminates with Discard/Reject, enforcement drops because `output_result.action` is correct, but `output_result.log_match` is emitted unchanged and reports permit.

**Refutation attempt:** Not required for a COHORT, but callers and tests were checked. `cos_classify.rs:782-792` derives drop/reject from `output_result.action` and separately forwards `output_result.log_match`; enforcement is not bypassed. Existing `fallthrough_log_action` tests cover only the full evaluator, whose normalization call is present.

**HPC/invariant check:** The fix is one branch-local scalar assignment; it requires no allocation, lock, extra packet parse, or atomic operation. Preserve the current Arc-backed log metadata and do not clone a String.

**Why it matters:** RT_FLOW/filter telemetry can claim Accept for an output-filter packet that was actually discarded or rejected, corrupting incident evidence and policy validation while enforcement remains fail closed.

**Fix direction:** Apply the same final-verdict normalization to `TxSelectionFilterResult` in both terminal-return and fall-through-return paths; add output TX-selection and cached-output regressions for `log; next term` followed by discard and reject.

**Labels:** `rust`, `userspace-dp`, `firewall-filter`, `observability`, `vsrx-parity`, `cohort`

**Dedup note:** Current 721-row index has no open issue with this symbol/mechanism. Closed issue #2616 described the same root and explicitly required cached-output regressions, but closed issues are not DUP gates; this is a recurrence/residual and is cohort-level because packet enforcement remains correct.

**Verified against origin/master:** Yes. `git show origin/master:userspace-dp/src/filter/engine/tx_selection.rs` at origin/master `ad959117748181dabe46b8ddc2827de670380cea` still returns at lines 226-228 without normalization. Setup tip is the same SHA.

### C2

**Title:** Event-stream connection discards `set_nonblocking(true)` failure even though all stop/deadline guarantees require a nonblocking socket

**Severity:** Low

**Confidence:** Medium

**Gate verdict:** COHORT

**Evidence:** `userspace-dp/src/event_stream/connection.rs:20-28` ignores the only transition from a blocking `UnixStream` to the mode assumed by the write/read loops:

```rust
    while !shared.stop.load(Ordering::Acquire) {
        // ---- Connect phase ----
        let stream = match try_connect(&socket_path, &shared) {
            Some(s) => s,
            None => break, // stop requested during connect
        };
        stream.set_nonblocking(true).ok();
        // #5267: `connected` stays set BEFORE `replay_buffered`. It gates only
```

**Trace:** Not required for COHORT. If `fcntl(F_SETFL)` fails (for example under a restrictive runtime policy or fault), the socket remains blocking; a later `read`/`write` can sleep in the kernel instead of returning `WouldBlock`, so stop/deadline polling and thread join can wedge.

**Refutation attempt:** Not required for COHORT. A valid ordinary Unix socket makes this failure rare, and EBADF would generally make later I/O fail rather than block. No type-level guarantee or follow-up mode probe establishes nonblocking behavior, however, and the code deliberately relies on `WouldBlock` for bounded shutdown.

**HPC/invariant check:** This is connection setup, not packet/event hot-path work. Propagating the one syscall error adds no steady-state latency or allocation.

**Why it matters:** The #2877 stop-aware replay/drain fix is conditional on nonblocking mode; silently violating that prerequisite can reintroduce an unbounded helper stop/demotion wait.

**Fix direction:** Treat `set_nonblocking(true)` failure as a connection failure: close/reconnect with a bounded backoff and a counter/log. Add a test seam that injects the setup error and proves the loop never enters blocking I/O.

**Labels:** `rust`, `userspace-dp`, `event-stream`, `resource-safety`, `ha`, `cohort`

**Dedup note:** Closed #2877 covered explicit blocking replay/drain writes, not failure to establish nonblocking mode. The current 721-row index and issue history contain no open owner for this setup error; low reachability makes it cohort-level defense in depth.

**Verified against origin/master:** Yes. `git show origin/master:userspace-dp/src/event_stream/connection.rs` at `ad959117748181dabe46b8ddc2827de670380cea` still contains `.ok()` at line 26. Setup tip is the same SHA.

### C3

**Title:** Lenient/HA WireGuard duplicate pubkeys are not inert: release reconcile creates inconsistent peer and AllowedIPs indexes

**Severity:** Medium

**Confidence:** High

**Gate verdict:** COHORT

**Evidence:** `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/wg/engine.rs:879-887` documents the corruption but enforces uniqueness only with a release-disabled assertion:

```rust
            // r7 Codex/Claude nit: duplicate pubkeys in `configs`
            // leave an orphan `Peer` in `new_peers` (unreachable via
            // pubkey lookup) and make `new_allowed` carry entries
            // indexed at the earlier duplicate's slot. The Go control
            // plane is supposed to reject duplicate pubkeys at config
            // validation; this `debug_assert` keeps the engine-side
            // invariant visible during development without panicking
            // production builds if the validation layer is bypassed.
            let prior = new_index.insert(cfg.pubkey, idx);
```

The next lines, `engine.rs:887-894`, keep the later pubkey index while inserting each duplicate's AllowedIPs against its own slab slot:

```rust
            let prior = new_index.insert(cfg.pubkey, idx);
            debug_assert!(
                prior.is_none(),
                "duplicate peer pubkey in reconcile_peers configs (prior idx={prior:?}, new idx={idx})"
            );
            for cidr in &cfg.allowed_ips {
                new_allowed.insert(*cidr, idx);
            }
```

**Trace:** Not required for COHORT. Tolerant load/peer-sync downgrades duplicate-pubkey validation to a warning, snapshot hydration pushes both peers, release reconcile stores both slab entries, pubkey lookup resolves only the later entry, and AllowedIPs can still point to the earlier orphan. Handshake/session lookup and cryptokey routing then disagree, blackholing or misapplying per-peer endpoint/PSK settings.

**Refutation attempt:** Not required for COHORT, but the strict and tolerant contracts were read. Strict commit rejects duplicates at `compiler_validate_wireguard.go:169-172`; `compiler_opts.go:1099-1110` explicitly downgrades that gate for tolerant load/HA and claims the Rust reconcile is duplicate-safe. Hydration at `forwarding_build/tunnels.rs:249-313` validates key shape but does not deduplicate, so the candidate survives only on the lenient/HA path.

**HPC/invariant check:** Reconcile is cold path. Rejecting the whole WG row or canonicalizing duplicates before publication adds no packet-path lookup, lock, or allocation. The live peer slab/LPM should remain immutable and internally one-to-one after publication.

**Why it matters:** A no-brick tolerant boot can bring up an apparently configured WireGuard interface whose cryptokey routes and handshake identity disagree, causing silent tunnel blackholes after cold boot or peer sync.

**Fix direction:** Preflight pubkeys before mutating any new engine table. For lenient input, drop the entire WG row (matching malformed-key fail-closed behavior) and emit one observable warning; for strict/direct engine construction, return a typed error. Add a release-mode duplicate regression covering distinct AllowedIPs and distinct endpoint/PSK settings.

**Labels:** `rust`, `userspace-dp`, `wireguard`, `ha`, `cold-boot`, `snapshot-integrity`, `cohort`

**Dedup note:** Closed #2445 is exact-duplicate AllowedIPs across different peers, not duplicate pubkey identity. No current index row owns this pubkey/slab mechanism. It is COHORT by the mandatory lenient-HA-sync materiality rule, despite live tunnel impact.

**Verified against origin/master:** Yes. `git show origin/master:userspace-dp/src/afxdp/wg/engine.rs` at `ad959117748181dabe46b8ddc2827de670380cea` shows the same debug-only check at lines 879-894; `git show origin/master:pkg/config/compiler_opts.go` shows tolerant downgrade at lines 1099-1110. Setup tip is the same SHA.

### C4

**Title:** Fairness evaluator accepts unbounded u32 flow counts, allowing release wrap or tiny-input-to-huge-heap Cstruct amplification

**Severity:** Low

**Confidence:** High

**Gate verdict:** COHORT

**Evidence:** `userspace-dp/src/fairness_eval/per_worker.rs:73-78` adds valid parsed u32 counts in a u32 accumulator:

```rust
        *per_ts_worker
            .entry((row.timestamp, row.worker_id))
            .or_insert(0) += row.count;
    }

    let distribution_a_i = median_per_worker_zero_filled(&per_ts_worker, n_total_workers);
```

`userspace-dp/src/fairness.rs:24-33` then expands each count into that many heap elements:

```rust
pub fn compute_cstruct(distribution: &[u32]) -> f64 {
    let mut shares: Vec<f64> = Vec::new();
    for &a_i in distribution {
        if a_i == 0 {
            continue;
        }
        let share = 1.0_f64 / (a_i as f64);
        for _ in 0..a_i {
            shares.push(share);
        }
```

**Trace:** Not required for COHORT. A small TSV can provide `count=4294967295`; aggregation either wraps when same-worker rows sum in release (debug panics) or passes the huge median to `compute_cstruct`, which attempts roughly 32 GiB of `f64` storage before the later sum guard can reject the evidence.

**Refutation attempt:** Not required for COHORT. Worker IDs and zero worker count are validated, malformed numerics are skipped with warnings, and expected-flow sum tolerance is checked in verdict evaluation. None caps a syntactically valid u32 count or avoids expanding it before rejection. The tool is offline/operator-facing, which bounds severity.

**HPC/invariant check:** This is not the packet path, but it is a merge-gating utility. Cstruct can be computed in O(number of workers) time and O(1) extra memory: `N=sum(a_i)`, `sum(shares)=active_workers`, and `sum(shares^2)=sum(1/a_i)`.

**Why it matters:** A corrupt scrape or accidental counter spike can abort the evaluator through allocation failure, while a release-mode addition wrap can instead produce a plausible but false fairness verdict.

**Fix direction:** Use checked u64 accumulation; reject totals above the expected-flow count plus explicit tolerance before Cstruct; replace the expanded vector with weighted moments. Add max-u32 and two-row-overflow tests that fail cleanly without allocating by count.

**Fix direction:** Define node-vs-worker semantics. Prefer pre-dividing configured limits across active workers with deterministic remainder, or explicitly expose/document the multiplier and effective limit.

**Title:** `WorkerUmemInner` drops mapped memory before the libxdp UMEM object that borrows it

**Severity:** Low

**Evidence:** Field declaration order at `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/umem/mod.rs:6-10` drops `area` before `umem`:

```rust

    umem: Umem,

```

The narrow called contract at `userspace-dp/src/xsk_ffi.rs:384-390` requires the opposite lifetime:

```rust

```

**Trace:** Not required for DUP. Final Rc drop runs fields in declaration order; `MmapArea::drop` munmaps, then `Umem::drop` calls libxdp teardown while retaining the now-dangling area pointer.

**Refutation attempt:** Not required for DUP. Current libxdp teardown reportedly does not dereference the area, making this latent rather than a demonstrated UAF, but the Rust unsafe precondition is still violated.

**HPC/invariant check:** Reordering fields changes only destruction order, with no packet-path cost or layout contract exposed externally.

**Why it matters:** A library upgrade that reads registration memory during teardown can turn a latent lifetime violation into use-after-unmap.

**Fix direction:** Declare `umem` before `area` (or implement explicit Drop with `Option<Umem>`), document the order, and add a teardown-order test seam.

### D17

**Title:** Event-stream idle keepalive append bypasses the 16 MiB pending-write cap

**Severity:** Low

**Confidence:** High

**Gate verdict:** DUP

**Evidence:** `userspace-dp/src/event_stream/connection.rs:339-346` appends every keepalive without checking `WRITE_BACKLOG_MAX_BYTES`:

```rust
                // socket-error / EOF path rather than by a false reconnect on
                // transient fullness.
                if last_write.elapsed() >= keepalive_interval {
                    let mut ka = [0u8; FRAME_HEADER_SIZE];
                    ka[4] = MSG_KEEPALIVE;
                    write_buf.extend_from_slice(&ka);
                    last_write = Instant::now();
                }
```

**Trace:** Not required for DUP. A connected local consumer stops reading; producer drain stops at the cap, but periodic keepalives continue extending the same Vec, permitting growth beyond the cap for the life of the stalled connection.

**Refutation attempt:** Not required for DUP. Growth is slow and the frame is small, but the connection can remain alive indefinitely and the cap's resource invariant is absolute.

**HPC/invariant check:** If pending data exists at cap, it already supplies liveness; skipping keepalive avoids allocation/copy and requires one length comparison.

**Why it matters:** A slow local observer can cause unbounded helper memory growth despite the documented fixed backlog ceiling.

**Fix direction:** Do not append keepalive when pending bytes are nonzero or would cross the cap; add a repeated-idle-at-cap test asserting stable capacity/length.

**Labels:** `rust`, `userspace-dp`, `event-stream`, `resource-safety`, `allocation`

**Dedup note:** Exact item A1-b10-F4 is open GH#5189 (current dedup row 250).

**Verified against origin/master:** Yes. Origin/master equals setup SHA and the keepalive append remains uncapped.

Severity: High

Confidence: High

Gate verdict: MATERIAL

Evidence: `userspace-dp/src/server/helpers/status.rs:274-281` makes one such slot disable global forwarding:

```rust
    state.status.enabled = state.status.forwarding_armed
        && state.status.capabilities.forwarding_supported
        && !state.status.bindings.is_empty()
        && state
            .status
            .bindings
            .iter()
            .all(|b| b.registered && b.armed);
```

Evidence: the narrow live manager contract at `pkg/dataplane/userspace/manager_ha.go:601-607` suppresses the only global re-arm because it compares only the retained global bit:

```go
func (m *Manager) syncDesiredForwardingStateLocked() error {
	if m.proc == nil || m.proc.Process == nil {
		return nil
	}
	desired := m.desiredForwardingArmedLocked()
	if m.lastStatus.ForwardingArmed == desired {
		return nil
```

Trace: Start with forwarding globally armed and every existing binding armed. Apply a valid snapshot that increases the binding plan, for example by adding a data interface or increasing the common RX-queue count. `snapshot.rs:344-350` replaces the old bindings with this replan. Existing numeric slots retain `armed=true`; each appended slot becomes `registered=true, armed=false`. Reconcile can bind its worker, but status computes `enabled=false` because the all-bindings predicate fails. The Go manager applies that disabled status, then its periodic desired-state loop sees `ForwardingArmed == desired == true` and sends no `set_forwarding_state`; therefore `set_bindings_forwarding_armed` never runs. The retained shim keeps transit fail closed until an operator explicitly toggles forwarding or another path happens to re-arm every binding.

Refutation attempt: I traced both snapshot branches, `replan_queues`, reconciliation, status refresh, BPF-manager status application, and the one-second desired-state loop. There is no post-replan propagation of global arm state. Existing planner tests cover only a same-identity/same-cardinality slot and manual unregistration, not plan expansion. The manager's skip predicate has no per-binding or `Enabled` condition. The candidate survives.

HPC/invariant check: Planning is cold-path, so the fix must not add packet work. Binding state must be preserved by stable `(interface/ifindex, queue_id)` identity, and every newly valid binding must initialize `armed` from the accepted global forwarding intent. A map built during replanning is acceptable; no atomics, locks, or per-packet allocation are needed.

Why it matters: A routine live config expansion or queue-count change causes a total, persistent transit outage on standalone and HA nodes. The posture is fail closed rather than fail open, but it can leave an HA standby permanently not takeover-ready and can drop traffic on the active node after commit.

Fix direction: Key preserved state by stable binding identity, not slot. Initialize a genuinely new valid binding as `registered=true` and `armed=guard.status.forwarding_armed`; clear all live socket fields when identity changes. Alternatively call a single arm-projection helper immediately after every replan. Add expansion, contraction, reorder, and armed-HA snapshot tests plus a Go test proving the periodic loop does not strand `Enabled=false` when global intent is true.

Trace: On a disarmed helper with an accepted snapshot, request `armed=true`. The handler sets the global and binding bits, then reconcile can fail during mandatory-map/integrity preflight or post-teardown worker bring-up. It returns `ok=false`, so Go discards the response status, but the Rust state retains the requested bits. The next status poll receives `ForwardingArmed=true`; `refresh_status` updates live fields but does not roll back desired `registered/armed`. Manager status application keeps binding rows non-READY/fail closed, records this status, and `syncDesiredForwardingStateLocked` returns early because global desired and reported arm bits now match. No automatic arm reconcile is retried. Queue registration failures similarly report requested bits rather than applied state.

Refutation attempt: I checked `requestDetailedLocked`: it discards an `OK:false` response, so the immediate caller cannot accidentally repair from its status. I then traced the periodic status poll, map application, busy-binding rebind watchdog, deferred-worker debt, and desired forwarding loop. None records debt for this handler error; the busy watchdog only handles its own error class, while desired forwarding compares only the retained global bit. The #6135 test asserts `ok=false` and error text but deliberately seeds/retains `forwarding_armed=true`; it has no rollback or retry assertion. The candidate survives.

HPC/invariant check: This is cold-path transactionality. The invariant is `reported applied state == successfully reconciled runtime state`; failed desired changes must either roll back or create explicit retry debt. Snapshotting a few booleans/BindingStatus entries is acceptable off path and adds no packet latency, lock, allocation, or cache-line traffic.

Why it matters: A transient pin, integrity, spawn, or bind fault can become a permanent total transit outage and an HA cold-boot/takeover-readiness failure even after the underlying fault clears. Status misleadingly says forwarding is armed, preventing the reconciler designed to heal desired-state drift from running.

Fix direction: Stage requested control state separately and commit it only after successful reconcile, or restore the previous global/per-binding values on every `Err`. Prefer explicit desired-vs-applied fields plus retry debt if asynchronous convergence is intended. Apply the same transaction helper to forwarding and queue/binding state handlers. Add fail-on-revert tests that inspect retained state and exercise the next manager poll/retry.

Trace: Internal hosts A and B use the same source port and protocol to the same external server. Interface-mode SNAT rewrites only both source IPs to the same interface address, preserving the port; their external 5-tuples and return `SessionKey` are identical. Both handles occupy the same bucket, and `reply_matches_forward_session` recomputes the same identical key for both, so the first-installed session wins. The live reverse path synthesizes and installs its reverse decision from that match. A reply belonging to B is therefore rewritten/delivered to A (especially direct for UDP; TCP may subsequently reject on sequence state, but only after cross-host misdelivery/disruption).

Refutation attempt: I read all forward/reverse/canonical key transforms, the local and shared lookup order, and the reverse-install consumer. No ingress field, NAT binding ID, TCP sequence state, or other discriminator survives on the wire or enters `SessionKey`. Pool SNAT is safe because it allocates a unique translated port; interface SNAT does not. Scanning more candidates cannot recover information absent from the packet. The source test itself proves both candidates validate. The candidate survives.

HPC/invariant check: NAT admission must preserve a bijection for every simultaneously live translated tuple. Do not add an unbounded per-packet candidate scan; on collision at session-install time, allocate PAT for the later interface-SNAT flow or fail its install closed. The common noncollision hot lookup should remain one inline SmallVec element with no allocation or shared lock.

Why it matters: Concurrent ordinary client flows can suffer cross-host reply delivery, session hijacking, or deterministic denial. The bug is reachable without malformed packets and violates vSRX stateful NAT isolation.

Fix direction: Detect translated-tuple collision before publishing a no-PAT interface-SNAT session. Allocate a unique translated source port/ICMP identifier for the later flow, using the existing pool allocator discipline, or reject the flow if interface mode is contractually forbidden to PAT. Replace the current test's first-installed expectation with two uniquely reversible sessions and add UDP/TCP live-path tests across local/shared scopes and HA import.

```rust
                // active; keep this half. Otherwise fall through: both halves
```

Evidence: `userspace-dp/src/session/expire.rs:318-323` applies that veto on the owner/standalone expiry path:

```rust

                        continue;
                    }
                    if let Some(removed) = self.remove_entry(&key) {
                        self.last_pop_stats.expired += 1;
```

Trace: A client SYN installs forward and reverse entries on the 20-second opening timeout. A real server SYN-ACK hits the reverse entry; lookup marks it established and stamps the 300-second established timeout, while propagation marks the forward entry established but deliberately retains its 20-second deadline pending the final client ACK. If that ACK never arrives, forward expiry runs at about 20 seconds. `companion_keeps_alive` sees the reverse entry still inside its own 300-second window, copies its timestamp to the forward entry, and rebuckets the forward entry. The wheel rechecks and retains it until the reverse established timeout expires, so two half-open slots survive roughly 15 times the intended window.

Refutation attempt: I checked the timer-wheel clamp/rebucket behavior, HA eligibility gates, close propagation, install timeouts, and all handshake tests. The rebucketed already-due forward entry is checked on subsequent ticks, not removed; the same companion predicate keeps succeeding until the reverse timeout. The completed-handshake test sends the final ACK, and the no-SYN-ACK test never creates this mixed-timeout state. No test expires SYN/SYN-ACK without final ACK. The interaction survives.

HPC/invariant check: A two-row flow needs one flow-level handshake/expiry class. Companion retention is off hot path and may do one bounded index lookup, but it must compare a shared effective timeout/state, not let a long-timeout half extend a handshake-incomplete peer. An explicit compact handshake state is preferable to additional per-packet allocation or cross-worker atomics.

Why it matters: A remote client can send SYNs to responsive internal listeners, let legitimate SYN-ACKs return, and never finish the handshake. Each attempt pins two bounded session-table slots for the established timeout, weakening the #3152 half-open DoS bound and denying legitimate session creation at a much lower sustained rate.

Fix direction: Track `SYN seen / SYN-ACK seen / final ACK seen` as flow-level state and keep both halves on the opening deadline until the final ACK. At minimum, make companion retention refuse to extend an entry when the flow has not completed the handshake or use the minimum timeout class across the pair. Add a timer-wheel regression for SYN, reverse SYN-ACK, no final ACK at opening and established deadlines.

This is the opposite mixed-timeout interaction created by combining those fixes, with a distinct resource-exhaustion consequence. No exact current-index/history item exists.

Refutation attempt: Not required for DUP. Alias/key validation proves tuple identity but no TCP sequence/ack acceptability state is stored or checked here.

HPC/invariant check: Sequence validation must be bounded and allocation-free on session hit, preferably compact state in the existing entry/cache line.

Why it matters: An off-path attacker who can guess a tuple can disrupt a live TCP flow.

Fix direction: Track sufficient TCP sequence-window state and accept RST/FIN close transitions only when the segment is in-window, matching vSRX stateful behavior.

Trace: Gated duplicate. A malformed snapshot numeric value reaches capacity multiplication, nested construction, and later narrowing before AF_XDP/platform bounds reject it.

Refutation attempt: Not required for DUP. Normal Go production inputs are constrained, but the independent Rust HA/control boundary accepts the numeric field and mixed-version/corrupt input remains relevant.

HPC/invariant check: Bound queue count at decode/preflight and use checked multiplication; this is cold-path and should never affect packet latency.

Why it matters: A malformed control/HA snapshot can panic, over-allocate, or consume excessive reconciliation time.

## Validation

- `cargo test --manifest-path userspace-dp/Cargo.toml session::tests:: -- --test-threads=1`: 172 passed.
- `cargo test --manifest-path userspace-dp/Cargo.toml server::tests:: -- --test-threads=1`: 75 passed.
- `slowpath::tests::`: 41 passed; `state_writer::tests::`: 13 passed; `tcp_flags::tests::`: 7 passed; `xsk_ffi::tests::`: 9 passed.
- Batch integration targets: `cos_doc_drift` 8 passed; `fairness_eval_blackbox` 22 passed; `runtime_view_publish_canary` 31 passed; `vrf_session_identity_doc_guard` 2 passed.
- Focused existing tests for handshake promotion, NAT reverse collision, #6135 reconcile error reporting, and planner state preservation all pass. These do not refute the findings: M3's test explicitly expects first-installed ambiguous selection, while M1/M2/M4 lack the failing expansion/rollback/incomplete-handshake cases.
- `cargo test --manifest-path userspace-xdp/Cargo.toml` is not a valid host test harness: compilation requires build-time `MAX_INTERFACES`, and linking `std` tests conflicts with the no-std BPF panic handler. No `make generate`/kernel-verifier run was performed because no source was changed.
- `git show origin/master:<path> | cmp - <path>` matched all 22 material/duplicate evidence and narrow-contract paths checked. `origin/master`, detached `HEAD`, and setup tip are the same immutable SHA.

## Final assessment

The batch is generally disciplined about bounds, ownership, fail-closed packet handling, timer-wheel scan bounds, io_uring buffer lifetime, and avoiding packet-path allocation. The material defects are cross-module state-machine failures: desired/applied forwarding state is conflated, per-direction TCP timeout state is not coherent at GC, and interface SNAT admits a wire tuple that no lookup structure can demultiplex. These require invariant-level fixes and regression tests; adding more status refreshes or multimap scanning will not resolve them.

## Findings By Confidence

### High Confidence

#### Material Finding

Title: Changed SNAT/NAT64 pools reissue live translated tuples on retained addresses

Severity: High

Confidence: High

Gate verdict: MATERIAL

Evidence: `userspace-dp/src/nat/source.rs:327` makes allocator identity include the exact name, ordered address vectors, and port range:

```rust
#[derive(Clone, Debug, Hash, PartialEq, Eq)]
struct SourceNatPoolAllocatorKey {
    pool_name: String,
    pool_addresses_v4: Vec<Ipv4Addr>,
    pool_addresses_v6: Vec<Ipv6Addr>,
    port_low: u16,
    port_high: u16,
}
```

Evidence: `userspace-dp/src/nat/source.rs:726` falls back to the newly constructed empty allocator whenever that exact key is absent:

```rust
if let Some(key) = rule.allocator_key() {
    if let Some(existing) = pool_allocators.get(&key) {
        rule.pool_allocator = existing.clone();
    } else {
        let allocator = previous_allocators
            .get(&key)
            .cloned()
            .unwrap_or_else(|| rule.pool_allocator.clone());
        rule.pool_allocator = allocator.clone();
        pool_allocators.insert(key, allocator);
```

Evidence: NAT64 has the same all-or-nothing rule at `userspace-dp/src/nat64.rs:980`:

```rust
/// #4518: find a previous NAT64 prefix whose prefix bytes AND source pool
/// are byte-identical, returning its `Arc`-backed [`PortAllocator`] so live
/// translated-port reservations survive a config reload.
///
/// Order-sensitive `Vec` equality on `pool_v4` is deliberate: the
/// allocator's per-address counters are indexed by pool position, so any
/// change to the pool set OR its order must NOT reuse the old allocator (see
/// [`from_snapshots_with_previous`]). Returns `None` when no compatible
/// prefix exists (rule added, prefix changed, or pool changed) — the caller
/// then builds a fresh allocator.
```

Evidence: the purported add/remove/reorder regression at `userspace-dp/src/nat64_tests.rs:4161` allocates from the old pool but only changes to a disjoint address:

```rust
// A pool CHANGE (addresses added/removed/reordered) must NOT reuse the old
// allocator — the round-robin counters are pool-position indexed, so stale
// reservations against a different pool must not be replayed. The new flow
// therefore starts fresh at the low port on the new pool address.
#[test]
fn nat64_4518_pool_change_resets_allocator() {
    let state1 = Nat64State::from_snapshots(&[single_addr_prefix()]);
    let dst_v4 = Ipv4Addr::new(8, 8, 8, 8);
    let c1: Ipv6Addr = "2001:db8::1".parse().unwrap();
```

Trace:

1. Under pool `[A]`, flow F1 to remote tuple `(R, rport)` is the first allocation. `AddressOccupancy::claim` starts at cursor zero, so F1 receives `(A, port_low)` (`nat/allocator.rs:589-617`). Its forward session remains installed.
2. An in-process config refresh adds/reorders an address, renames the pool, or changes an overlapping port range. The refresh passes `Some(&self.forwarding)` into the builder (`afxdp/coordinator/snapshot_refresh.rs:273-288`), but source NAT reuses state only for the exact allocator key and NAT64 only for a byte-identical ordered pool. A changed pool containing A therefore starts a new zeroed allocator.
3. The refresh purges remapped tunnel sessions and swaps forwarding state (`snapshot_refresh.rs:371-380`); it does not purge sessions using the replaced NAT allocator. F1 continues forwarding with its stored `NatDecision`.
4. The first suitable post-refresh flow F2 to the same `(R, rport)` selects retained address A and `port_low`, because the new allocator has no occupancy record for F1. F1 and F2 now have an identical translated source tuple and identical remote tuple.
5. Both forward handles enter the 1:N NAT reverse bucket. `reply_matches_forward_session` compares only the complete derived wire key (`session/key.rs:19-26`); both candidates match the same reply. `find_forward_nat_match` returns the first match (`session/lookup.rs:222-249`), so replies can be delivered to the wrong internal flow or the other flow can blackhole.
6. Teardown is not a repair: source release scans allocators in the current rule set (`source.rs:781-826`), so an old-generation allocation cannot be found after replacement.

Refutation attempt:

- I checked the #4518 compatible-reload fix. It correctly preserves the `Arc<PortAllocator>` for a byte-identical pool, but deliberately creates a fresh allocator on add/remove/reorder; it does not cover an address retained across the two generations.
- I checked the changed-pool test. It changes `198.51.100.1` to disjoint `203.0.113.9`, where tuple collision is impossible, and then explicitly expects reuse of the old low port. It does not exercise `[A] -> [A,B]`, `[A,B] -> [A]`, reordering, pool rename, or overlapping range change.
- I checked snapshot strict-overlap validation. It can reject duplicate ownership domains inside one incoming snapshot, but it has no inventory of sessions and allocations owned by the previous live generation.
- I checked #4399/#4438's multimap indexes. They retain both handles, but validation cannot disambiguate two forward sessions whose complete translated and remote tuples are identical; both pass the same equality predicate.
- I checked the refresh commit path for a NAT-session purge or migration. The only pre-swap session purge there is tunnel-remap-specific. HA reservation fixes operate on peer imports, not same-process local refresh.

HPC/invariant check: The broken invariant is one live owner per `(protocol, translated source address, translated source port/identifier, remote address, remote port)` across all active config generations. Current reset is cheap but discards that ownership. The fix belongs on the cold snapshot path and must not add a per-packet lock. Migrate/reserve old live tuples by actual address and port into the new allocator, remapping positional address indexes, or synchronously purge every session tied to the replaced allocation domain before publishing the new state. Migration should remain O(live allocations in changed pools), bounded outside packet processing.

Why it matters: A routine pool add/remove/reorder, pool rename, or port-range change can immediately duplicate a still-live public 5-tuple. Replies can cross internal sessions, reset an established connection, or expose one client's reply traffic to another client able to target the same remote endpoint. This violates the core NAT BIB/tuple-uniqueness contract and persists until the old session ages or is removed.

Fix direction: Add generation-aware allocator migration keyed by actual `(pool address, port)` rather than old vector index. Carry `live_by_flow`, address-only owners, persistent leases/expiry indexes, deterministic ownership, cursors, and HA reservations for retained addresses and overlapping ports. For removed domains, either retain a draining allocator referenced by old sessions or purge those sessions before the swap and propagate closes. Add source-NAT and NAT64 integration tests for `[A] -> [A,B]`, removal retaining A, reorder, rename, and overlapping range changes, with two internal flows to one remote endpoint and reverse lookup assertions. Also assert old-session teardown releases the correct generation.

Labels: `userspace-dp`, `nat`, `nat64`, `allocation-lifecycle`, `tuple-uniqueness`, `session-integrity`, `config-reload`, `vsrx-parity`

GH#6600 and the historical #4512/#4388 class concern peer-import reservation ordering; GH#6522 concerns sibling-holder release; GH#6528 concerns wrong-mode teardown; #4518 preserves only byte-identical reloads. The mechanism and trigger here are distinct: local in-process state replacement loses old occupancy while sessions survive.

The finding is still present.

#### Cohort Issue: NAT vSRX-Parity and Observability Residuals (2 Survivors)

Title: DNAT cross-tier specificity overrides earlier Junos rules

Severity: Medium

Confidence: High

Gate verdict: COHORT

Evidence: `userspace-dp/src/nat/destination.rs:745` explicitly documents the divergent selection rule:

```rust
// #3844: WITHIN a tier the first matching entry (zone-specific, then
// zone-wildcard) determines the outcome via `to_outcome` — a `then
// destination-nat off` entry yields `Exempt` (no translation), any
// other entry yields `Translate`. An `Exempt` (a `Some(..)`) halts the
// cross-tier `.or_else` chain, so it short-circuits the LOWER tiers.
// NOTE ON PRECEDENCE: across tiers this is MOST-SPECIFIC-WINS (exact
// (proto,dst,port) > wildcard-port > proto-any > prefix-LPM), NOT strict
// Junos config order. A more-specific *later* translate rule beats a
// broader *earlier* off rule (same tier-precedence the DnatTable applies
// to translate-vs-translate, #3164). To exempt traffic that a translate
```

Trace: Not required for COHORT. The direct case is an earlier broad `destination-nat off` rule followed by a later exact-port translate rule; lookup probes exact before wildcard/prefix and translates despite the earlier exemption.

Refutation attempt: Not required for COHORT. I nevertheless checked same-tier insertion order and the #3844 `off` implementation; they are correct. The divergence is specifically cross-tier and is acknowledged in the production comment. Existing tests cover the opposite, more-specific-off case but not broad-earlier-off.

HPC/invariant check: The vSRX invariant is rule-set context precedence followed by first matching configured rule, not packet-tuple specificity invented by the runtime table. A fix can probe the existing bounded tier set and choose the lowest config ordinal among matching candidates, preserving fixed-cost lookup and avoiding allocation.

Why it matters: Migrated vSRX configurations can translate traffic explicitly exempted by an earlier rule, or choose a different backend solely because a later rule has a more specific tuple shape. This is a behavioral parity and policy-intent defect, but the code documents the limitation and it belongs with the existing parity backlog.

Fix direction: Carry a stable config ordinal into each `DnatEntry`/prefix slot and select the earliest matching ordinal across applicable exact, wildcard, protocol-any, and prefix candidates after applying the proper rule-set scope precedence. Add inverse-order tests for broad-off/exact-translate and broad-translate/exact-off, including prefix and protocol-any tiers.

Labels: `userspace-dp`, `nat`, `dnat`, `rule-ordering`, `policy-intent`, `vsrx-parity`, `cohort`

Dedup note: #3844 fixed missing `destination-nat off` representation and same-tier short-circuiting. Closed #4161 covers the sibling source-NAT rule-set scope precedence and explicitly notes DNAT's different tier model. No exact current issue was found, but this documented parity residual belongs under GH#2008/GH#4422 rather than a separate issue.

Title: NAT counter clear can retain a packet while erasing its bytes

Severity: Low

Confidence: High

Gate verdict: COHORT

Evidence: `userspace-dp/src/nat/mod.rs:166` updates the two dimensions independently:

```rust
impl NatRuleCounter {
    /// Count one committed translated flow: +1 packet and +packet_len bytes.
    /// Per-flow semantic (not per-packet) — fired once when a new translated
    /// session is installed, so the bytes are the trigger packet's length.
    #[inline]
    pub(crate) fn add(&self, packet_len: u64) {
        self.packets.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed);
        if packet_len != 0 {
            self.bytes.fetch_add(packet_len, Ordering::Relaxed);
        }
```

Evidence: `userspace-dp/src/nat/mod.rs:191` observes packets before bytes and then subtracts both observations:

```rust
let observed_packets = self.packets.load(Ordering::Relaxed);
let observed_bytes = self.bytes.load(Ordering::Relaxed);
self.subtract_observed(observed_packets, observed_bytes);
}

/// #3830: remove exactly `observed_*` from the shared totals with atomic
/// `fetch_sub`s rather than a `store(0)` (see [`reset`](Self::reset) for
/// why). Split out as the clear's subtraction step so the reset/increment
/// interleaving can be driven deterministically in tests: the invariant is
```

Evidence: `userspace-dp/src/nat/tests_counter.rs:308` loads both fields before injecting the concurrent hit, so it cannot exercise an add between those loads:

```rust
// === reset() stage 1: OBSERVE the pre-clear totals — exactly what reset()
// reads before its subtraction. ===
let observed_packets = counter.packets.load(Ordering::Relaxed);
let observed_bytes = counter.bytes.load(Ordering::Relaxed);
assert_eq!(observed_packets, 100, "observed pre-clear packet total");
assert_eq!(observed_bytes, 100 * 64, "observed pre-clear byte total");

// === Concurrent cold-path worker: a LEGITIMATE post-clear translated flow
// is counted in the window between reset's observation and its
```

Trace: Not required for COHORT. With initial `(P,B)`, reset loads `P`; `add(L)` increments packets and bytes; reset then loads `B+L`; subtracting `(P,B+L)` leaves `(1,0)`. The displayed pair cannot describe any real positive-length translated trigger packet.

Refutation attempt: Not required for COHORT. I checked clear serialization and underflow: the registry mutex serializes reset calls and each field remains atomically monotonic between resets, so there is no integer underflow. That does not make the two-field snapshot linearizable. The existing test drives add only after both observations and therefore proves only the old store-clobber fix.

HPC/invariant check: Individual `AtomicU64` RMWs are memory-safe and cheap, but the invariant `bytes correspond to the same set of hits as packets` is not atomic across the pair. Because increments are once per new translated flow, a small per-counter lock or epoch/seqlock protocol can preserve coherence without touching the established per-packet fast path. Avoid a global registry lock on every add.

Why it matters: Immediately after `clear security nat ...`, operators and automation can observe a packet with zero bytes or other mixed-epoch packet/byte totals. This is audit/telemetry accuracy, not enforcement, so it is cohort material rather than individually fileable.

Fix direction: Give add/reset a common pair-level linearization protocol, such as a per-counter lock on the cold flow-install path or an epoch-based accumulator swap. Add a deterministic test that pauses reset after the packet load, performs a positive-length add, then resumes the byte load and asserts a coherent post-clear pair.

Labels: `userspace-dp`, `nat`, `observability`, `counters`, `concurrency`, `cohort`

Dedup note: Closed #3830 replaced `store(0)` with observe-and-subtract and preserved a hit added after both observations. This is the residual between-observation pair race, not the same lost-atomic-update mechanism. It belongs in current counters cohort GH#6566; #3782 is the related policy-counter predecessor.

Verified against origin/master: `git show origin/master:userspace-dp/src/nat/mod.rs` at setup tip `ad959117748181dabe46b8ddc2827de670380cea` still has independent packet/byte loads and subtractions at lines 166-214. `tests_counter.rs:308-323` still injects only after both loads.
