## Findings - High confidence

### F1

Title: Conflicting `icmp-type` and `icmp-code` leaves inside inline application terms bypass the duplicate-scalar gate

Severity: High

Confidence: High

Gate verdict: MATERIAL

Evidence: In `/tmp/review-wt-opus-001-A3-b1/pkg/config/compiler_applications.go:649`, each valid repeat simply overwrites the pointer; unlike the immediately following port cases, there is no first-value flag or append to `dupTermLeaves`:

```go
649         case "icmp-type":
650             if i+1 < len(keys) {
651                 i++
652                 if t, ok := parseICMPTypeCode(keys[i]); ok {
653                     icmpType = t
654                 } else {
655                     // #3348: a malformed inline-term icmp-type. The schema does
656                     // NOT validate inside an opaque `term`, so silently dropping
657                     // it would leave the term UNCONSTRAINED (matches all ICMP) —
658                     // a fail-open widening. Record it for the strict gate.
```

Evidence: The strict gate at `/tmp/review-wt-opus-001-A3-b1/pkg/config/compiler_validate_strict_application.go:588` enumerates only port, timeout, and ALG leaves, so no later validation recovers the missing ICMP duplicate:

```go
588             if len(app.DuplicateTermLeaves) > 0 {
589                 return fmt.Errorf(
590                     "application %q: conflicting duplicate %q inside `term`; a single-valued "+
591                         "term leaf (destination-port / source-port / inactivity-timeout / "+
592                         "timeout / alg) may carry only one value — a repeat with a different "+
593                         "value is last-writer-wins and silently overrides the earlier one by "+
594                         "token order (use repeated `protocol` only for an intentional "+
595                         "multi-protocol term)",
596                     name, app.DuplicateTermLeaves[0])
```

Trace: (1) A hierarchical application term, or a packed flat term, reaches `applicationTermKeys`, which deliberately reassembles both AST shapes. (2) `parseApplicationTerms` parses two valid `icmp-type` or `icmp-code` tokens and overwrites `icmpType`/`icmpCode` with the last value. (3) Because no duplicate marker is recorded and `schema_security.go:1282` declares `term` opaque (`children:nil`), strict `CompileConfig` returns success. (4) The generated `Application` carries only the final pointer. (5) `pkg/dataplane/userspace/capabilities.go:323-333` copies that pointer into the live policy snapshot; `userspace-dp/src/policy.rs:953-971` installs only that final ICMP constraint. A deny application authored with types 8 then 3 therefore denies only type 3; echo traffic can fall through to a later permit or explicit default permit.

Refutation attempt: I checked the typed schema, direct-application duplicate tracking, strict application semantic validators, application collision pass, snapshot builder, Rust matcher, and relevant tests. The direct-body path explicitly tracks ICMP duplicates, proving repeats are not intended as a list; the inline-term duplicate table omits them. The schema cannot help because term contents are opaque. Downstream code does not retain a union. The #3366 regression table tests destination/source port, timeout, and ALG only. The candidate survived each attempted guard.

HPC/invariant check: No concurrency, cache-line, atomic, or byte-order issue is involved. The violated compiler invariant is: every conflicting repeat of a single-valued term leaf must either be rejected or represented without loss. Values themselves are safely bounded to `uint8`; the defect occurs before wire encoding.

Why it matters: This is a strict-commit policy widening. A configuration that Junos-style scalar semantics should reject is accepted while an earlier deny constraint is discarded, allowing traffic outside the last ICMP type/code to reach a permit/default-permit path.

Fix direction: Add `icmpTypeSet`/`icmpCodeSet` plus first parsed values in `parseApplicationTerms`; append `icmp-type`/`icmp-code` to `DuplicateTermLeaves` on a conflicting repeat while allowing identical repeats. Update the strict error text and add hierarchical, packed flat-term, apply-groups, idempotent-repeat, and deny-policy regression cases for both fields.

Labels: security, config-compiler, application-matching, policy-widening, ast-dual-shape, vsrx-parity

Dedup note: The refreshed 721-row index contains `codex-review-180` for conflicting **direct** application scalars and GH#6564 for compact-leaf operand loss; neither covers valid repeated ICMP scalars inside an inline term. Closed history #3366 is the incomplete predecessor: it names only destination-port, source-port, ALG, and timeout at `issue-history.md:54223-54227`. Closed #2545 concerns multi-valued firewall-filter fields, a different typed model and consumer. No current open issue covers this residual field omission.

Verified against origin/master: `git show origin/master:pkg/config/compiler_applications.go` still has the untracked assignments at lines 649-669, and `git show origin/master:pkg/config/compiler_validate_strict_application.go` still omits ICMP at lines 588-596. `origin/master` and setup tip are both `ad959117748181dabe46b8ddc2827de670380cea`; still present.

### F2

Title: Wildcard `apply-groups` cloning bypasses the expansion work budget and can build a quadratic AST

Severity: Medium

Confidence: High

Gate verdict: MATERIAL

Evidence: `/tmp/review-wt-opus-001-A3-b1/pkg/config/ast_groups.go:226` charges one unit per referenced group, independent of how many nodes that reference creates:

```go
226         // #5194 A3-b2-F1: bound the TOTAL expansion work so a wide shallow
227         // fan-out (many groups, each referenced from many contexts) that stays
228         // under the depth cap still cannot spin unbounded on commit / HA sync.
229         budget.work++
230         if budget.work > maxGroupExpandWork {
231             return fmt.Errorf("apply-groups expansion exceeds maximum work budget of %d (possible generated or pathological config)", maxGroupExpandWork)
232         }
```

Evidence: The wildcard branch at `/tmp/review-wt-opus-001-A3-b1/pkg/config/ast_groups.go:377` clones the complete source subtree once per matching destination, with no budget charge for the match, clone, recursive merge, or retained output:

```go
377         // Check if source keys contain wildcards (<*>).
378         if keysContainWildcard(s.Keys) {
379             // Wildcard merge: apply to all matching containers in dst.
380             for _, d := range *dst {
381                 if !d.IsLeaf && keysMatchWildcard(d.Keys, s.Keys) {
382                     cloned := cloneNodes(s.Children)
383                     mergeNodes(&d.Children, cloned, appendPath(ancestorPath, d.Keys))
384                 }
385             }
```

Trace: (1) A candidate contains `N` concrete destination containers and one applied group whose `<*>` container has an `M`-node subtree. (2) `expandGroupsRecursive` increments `budget.work` once for that group reference. (3) `mergeNodes` matches all `N` containers and deep-clones/merges `M` nodes for each, retaining distinct inherited children when they are absent inline. (4) Expanded size and work become `O(N*M)` while the budget remains 1; the 64-depth cap is irrelevant. (5) Strict commit, tolerant boot, and HA SyncApply all execute this path before section compilation, and later prepasses/compiler walks traverse the amplified tree. A generated but accepted candidate can consume excessive CPU/memory or terminate the daemon through OOM.

Refutation attempt: Not required at Medium, but I checked the intended guards. The recursion cap handles depth only. `maxGroupExpandWork` counts references, not allocations/output nodes. Memoization caches an expanded group body but the wildcard branch deliberately calls `cloneNodes` for every destination, so it does not cap cloning. The 16 MiB ingress limit bounds raw `N+M`, not the expansion product, and incremental candidate edits are not an output-cardinality proof. The batch's depth test exercises a long chain and a shallow control, not wildcard fan-out.

HPC/invariant check: No atomic/cache-line/endianness concern. The resource invariant is that every expansion budget must upper-bound work and retained output. Here one charged operation can perform and retain `N*M` node copies, so the advertised total-work counter is not a bound.

Why it matters: Config commit and HA sync are control-plane availability paths. An authenticated operator mistake, generated config, or hostile/corrupt HA peer can cause disproportionate allocation and latency, blocking configuration convergence or crashing the daemon instead of returning a bounded compile error.

Fix direction: Replace the reference counter with a shared budget that charges visited, cloned, merged, and retained nodes, using checked arithmetic before allocation. Abort before cloning when the remaining output budget cannot cover `subtreeSize * matchCount`; include all per-node prepass expansions. Add near-limit/over-limit wildcard tests and assert a clean error on strict and tolerant entrypoints.

Labels: availability, resource-exhaustion, config-compiler, apply-groups, ha, performance, vsrx-parity

Dedup note: The refreshed index/history searches for `apply-groups`, `wildcard`, `ExpandGroups`, `work budget`, and amplification found no output-cardinality issue. Closed #1914 is wildcard tunnel-ID collision admission; closed #4070 is leaf-list inheritance; history #4474 is transitive group content loss. None covers one wildcard reference bypassing the resource budget. The in-code #5194 depth/reference fix is precisely the incomplete guard, not an indexed open duplicate.

Verified against origin/master: `git show origin/master:pkg/config/ast_groups.go` still charges only lines 226-232 and performs the uncharged wildcard clone loop at lines 377-385. `origin/master` and setup tip are both `ad959117748181dabe46b8ddc2827de670380cea`; still present.

## Cohort issue - A3 parser/compiler hardening survivors

These five real defects are grouped into one cohort because they are limited to lenient migration input, local malformed state, display/export behavior, client-side mutation, or operator-facing text. They should not be filed as five independent security issues.

### C1

Title: Tolerant interface compilation narrows malformed GRE keys with unchecked `int` to `uint32` casts

Severity: Medium

Confidence: High

Gate verdict: COHORT

Evidence: Both interface shapes use the same unchecked conversion; the physical form is at `/tmp/review-wt-opus-001-A3-b1/pkg/config/compiler_interfaces.go:183`:

```go
183                 case "key":
184                     if len(prop.Keys) >= 2 {
185                         if v, err := strconv.Atoi(prop.Keys[1]); err == nil {
186                             tc.Key = uint32(v)
187                         }
188                     }
```

Evidence: The strict schema at `/tmp/review-wt-opus-001-A3-b1/pkg/config/schema_interfaces.go:421` knows the exact wire domain, but Store.Load/SyncApply only warn and continue:

```go
421             "key": {
422                 desc:          "Tunnel key",
423                 args:          1,
424                 placeholder:   "<key>",
425                 valueType:     ValueInteger,
426                 valueDesc:     "GRE key (0..4294967295; 32-bit wire field)",
427                 valueExamples: []string{"100"},
428                 validator:     ValidateInteger(0, 4294967295),
429                 children:      nil,
```

Evidence: The live Rust consumer at `/tmp/review-wt-opus-001-A3-b1/userspace-dp/src/afxdp/gre.rs:497` treats wrapped zero as an unkeyed endpoint:

```rust
497         let key_ok = if endpoint.key == 0 {
498             !key_present || key == 0
499         } else {
500             key_present && endpoint.key == key
501         };
502         if key_ok {
503             return Some(endpoint);
```

Trace: Not required for COHORT. On 64-bit builds, tolerated `4294967296` becomes key 0 and `-1` becomes `0xffffffff`; the snapshot copies the narrowed value unchanged.

Refutation attempt: Not required for COHORT. Strict operator commits are protected by `ValidateInteger`; this survives only on the explicit lenient boot/HA-sync path, which is why it is cohort-gated rather than material.

HPC/invariant check: This is a wire-width invariant, not a concurrency issue. Endianness is handled downstream with `to_be_bytes`; the defect is unchecked range narrowing before that encoding.

Why it matters: A malformed legacy/peer key can silently select different GRE decapsulation/encapsulation semantics instead of being dropped or quarantined; wrap-to-zero accepts unkeyed traffic and emits no key.

Fix direction: Parse with `strconv.ParseUint(raw, 10, 32)` in a shared helper. Strict mode should reject; tolerant mode should warn and leave the tunnel inert or omit the malformed key without wrapping. Cover physical/unit and zero/max/negative/overflow cases.

Labels: config-compiler, integer-truncation, gre, tolerant-load, ha, vsrx-parity

Title: Nested JSON `null` nodes reach nil-unsafe AST walkers and panic instead of failing closed

Severity: Medium

Confidence: Medium

Gate verdict: COHORT

Evidence: `/tmp/review-wt-opus-001-A3-b1/pkg/config/ast.go:244` preserves slice length and dereferences every node without a nil check:

```go

247     }
248     result := make([]*Node, len(nodes))
249     for i, n := range nodes {

252             Children:      cloneNodes(n.Children),
```

Evidence: The narrow persistence contract at `/tmp/review-wt-opus-001-A3-b1/pkg/configstore/db.go:353` checks only the top-level JSON token before ordinary `json.Unmarshal`, which accepts `{"Children":[null]}`:

```go
353     // Reject a body whose top-level JSON is not an OBJECT (#5474 fail-open).
354     // Go's json.Unmarshal([]byte("null"), &ConfigTree{}) returns NO error and
355     // leaves the tree at its zero value — a semantically EMPTY config. A
356     // legacy/plaintext (or enveloped-but-unencrypted) active body of literal
357     // `null` would therefore decode to an empty tree and Store.Load would
358     // compile+boot it normally, so the firewall comes up with policy ABSENT
359     // (fail-open) instead of failing closed. Syntactically-invalid bodies and
360     // top-level arrays/scalars already error against the struct target, but
```

Trace: Not required for COHORT. A plaintext/corrupt active DB with a valid object and nested null decodes successfully; `Store.Load` first reaches nil-unsafe sanitization and, absent that, clone/compile walkers, causing a nil-pointer panic rather than `ErrConfigDBUnreadable`/`ErrConfigCompile`.

Refutation attempt: Not required for COHORT. The top-level #5474 guard, AES-GCM integrity when encryption is enabled, parser-produced-tree shape, and nil-aware inactive pruning were checked. None recursively validates decoded node pointers before Store.Load's walkers. Reachability requires local persisted-state corruption/tampering or a trusted in-process producer, so materiality is not claimed.

HPC/invariant check: No concurrency or integer concern. The structural invariant `ConfigTree.Children and Node.Children contain no nil elements` is assumed globally but not enforced at the serialization boundary.

Why it matters: Malformed authoritative state can crash startup rather than enter the documented fail-closed recovery/lifeline path.

Fix direction: Add a recursive structural validator immediately after JSON decode that rejects nil nodes and impossible leaf/container shapes with a typed unreadable-config error. Also make generic clone/navigation/format walkers nil-safe as defense in depth. Add nested-null tests at root and multiple depths.

For old roots `[security A, security B]` and new roots `[security B]`, `oldByKey["security"]` is B, the new B compares equal, and the `seen` map suppresses A's removal; the compare can be empty while compiled policy changed. JSON output retains only one same-key block.

Refutation attempt: Not required for COHORT. `compileSections` explicitly iterates duplicate roots in author order, so duplicates are legitimate and semantically active. The issue is confined to compare/display JSON callers; persistence uses structured marshaling rather than this formatter.

HPC/invariant check: No concurrency/endianness issue. The broken invariant is one-to-one key identity: `KeyPath` is not unique among sibling roots, so a map cannot represent the multiset/order being compared or rendered.

Why it matters: Operators can receive a false-empty `show | compare`, and display-JSON export/reload is lossy for a configuration shape the compiler honors.

Fix direction: Compare duplicate siblings as ordered/multiset buckets per key, preserving occurrence identity; represent repeated JSON containers as arrays or merge their children under explicit conflict rules. Add duplicate-root compare and JSON round-trip tests.

Labels: formatter, ast, observability, round-trip, vsrx-parity

Dedup note: GH#6668 covers bracketed zone-body `FormatSet`, not duplicate-root map collapse. Closed #3562 validates duplicate security compilation, which establishes the legitimate input shape but does not cover formatter output. No refreshed-index entry covers `FormatCompare` or `nodesToJSON` duplicate keys.

Verified against origin/master: `git show origin/master:pkg/config/ast_format.go` retains the collapsing maps at lines 257-265. Base and `origin/master` are identical; still present but display-only.

Severity: Low

Confidence: High

Gate verdict: COHORT

```go

555             return deletePath(&n.Children, path, childSchema, i)
556         }
557     }
558 
559     // #4423 M9: wrap ErrPathNotFound here too. This return fires when an
560     // INTERMEDIATE container in the delete path is absent (more tokens remain
```

Evidence: Activate/deactivate repeats the first-hit behavior at `/tmp/review-wt-opus-001-A3-b1/pkg/config/ast_edit.go:665`:

```go
665     // More tokens remain: find matching container and descend.

669         }
670     }
671
```

Trace: Not required for COHORT. A parsed candidate with two `security` roots, where only the second contains the target policy, descends into the first and returns not-found without examining the second.

Refutation attempt: Not required for COHORT. `ConfigTree.FindChildren` and `compileSections` explicitly support duplicate roots; no normalization merges them before candidate edit operations. The result is an edit failure, not silent dataplane enforcement, so this is cohort-only.

HPC/invariant check: No concurrency/integer concern. The traversal invariant is existential: a path lookup over duplicate containers must succeed if any matching container has the remainder. First-hit recursion violates it.

Why it matters: An operator may be unable to delete or deactivate a policy/interface subtree in a later duplicate block, delaying remediation and diverging from Junos path semantics.

Fix direction: Continue across same-key containers on `ErrPathNotFound`, return the first success, and preserve hard errors. Define whether whole-container operations affect one or all duplicates, then pin delete/activate/deactivate/copy/rename behavior with duplicate-root tests.


### Narrow called-contract reads

Only the contracts needed to prove or refute assigned-code behavior were read outside the assignment: parser sibling preservation and depth cap (`parser.go`); `Node.FindChild`/`FindChildren` (`ast.go`); flat-set container reuse and `FormatSet` (`ast_edit.go`, `ast_format.go`); duplicate named-block coverage (`dup_named_blocks.go`); source-NAT and flow-monitor schema leaves (`schema_security.go`, `schema_system.go`); typed routing-reference validation; FRR BGP render; daemon syslog apply; and flowexport template resolution/ticker code. Parser nesting is capped at 256, config input is capped at 16 MiB, group expansion has depth/work budgets, application/address-set expansion is bounded, and F3's range expansion is capped at 256. No unbounded recursion survivor was found.

### Dedup dispositions

- Policy terminal conflict on tolerant load is the exact #3043 mechanism; not re-reported.
- Malformed chassis RG/node identity coercion is #5694/codex-review-182 and is prewalk-guarded.
- NAT mixed-scope tolerant widening is #4881; mixed Keys/child address truncation is GH#6693; duplicate NAT match/then is #3850.
- Packed host-inbound and named-instance shapes are GH#6736/GH#6705/GH#6662; no restatement was promoted.
- DDNS plaintext credential tolerance is #4861; DDNS duration overflow is dedup index row 638 (`ps-review-038-A7_go_daemon_host-b1.md`).
- Security-log named `tls-profile` resolution is #3350. F1 is different: a valid `protocol tls` is erased by duplicate-object replacement.
- Unknown security-log transport downgrade is in `codex-review-180`; F1 has the same consequence but a different accepted-input trigger and root mechanism.
- Source-NAT standalone subnet truncation is closed #3049; F3 is the residual range-endpoint mask-erasure path.
- NAT pool overlap is #5144 and range-count overflow is #5194; both guards are present.
- Generic duplicate-block gate #5180 covers only groups, interfaces, and screen IDS blocks. #3562 covers duplicate-root validator traversal; #3842 policies, #4818 zones, #4820 same-block RPM probes, and #4821 SSH known hosts are fixed siblings. None covers F1's protocol/log/service/address-book symbols.

Trace: A hierarchical parser retains repeated same-key blocks as siblings. For `protocols { bgp { group ... neighbor ...; } bgp { export DENY-EXPORT; } }`, `FindChild("bgp")` returns only the first sibling, so the valid second export never reaches `BGP.Export`. `validateRoutingExportReferencesStrict` walks the compiled slice and therefore cannot reject or recover an erased policy. FRR receives a live neighbor with an empty export chain and emits no `route-map ... out`, advertising every otherwise eligible BGP route instead of applying the authored deny/export policy. Separately, two `security log stream audit` blocks, the first with `host` plus `transport { protocol tls; }` and the second with the same host plus severity, produce two fresh objects; the second map assignment removes TLS and runtime defaults to plaintext UDP. `FormatSet` emits both subtrees as set lines, while `SetPath` reuses matching containers, so parse -> compile differs from FormatSet -> set replay -> compile. Fresh `compileFlowMonitoring`/`compileRPM`/`compileIPMonitoring` objects and `compileAddressBook`'s first `global`/fresh map are lower-impact siblings of the same round-trip violation.

Refutation attempt: I checked `validateDuplicateNamedBlockAST`, all security-log AST gates, routing export-reference validation, flat-set `SetPath`, formatter output, and the runtime consumers. The duplicate gate explicitly enumerates only groups/interfaces/screen; log gates validate each individual stream but do not reject duplicate names; routing gates see only already-compiled exports; and flat set merges rather than replacing. Each individual block is schema-valid, so strict compile passes. The issue is not intended last-wins behavior: the dispatcher and existing #4818/#4820/#4821 fixes explicitly state Junos duplicate blocks merge, and formatter replay changes the result.

HPC/invariant check: The traversals are linear and parser depth-bounded; no race, integer overflow, or hot-path allocation is involved. The violated invariants are dual-AST equivalence, duplicate-root author-order merge, strict-gate visibility, and formatter round-trip equivalence. The fail-open route-policy consequence and TLS downgrade occur on the control plane and live Go/FRR consumers, not retired eBPF/DPDK code.

Why it matters: A syntactically valid hierarchical/load-override config can silently remove an outbound BGP filter and leak routes, or silently send an audit stream without the explicitly configured TLS transport. The same text rendered and replayed as set syntax behaves differently, so backups/edits can change enforcement without an operator-visible semantic change.

Fix direction: Normalize repeated same-key containers before compilation, or make each compiler iterate all matching protocol/service/global blocks and find-or-create named objects with Junos merge rules. Merge list fields, preserve scalar last-wins only where defined, and reject ambiguous duplicate terminal/scalar conflicts at strict commit. Add strict and tolerant tests for repeated BGP/OSPF/RIP blocks, same-name syslog streams, flow-monitor/RPM/IP-monitoring blocks, and global address books; compare hierarchical compilation with equivalent flat-set and `FormatSet` replay, and assert FRR route-map/TLS runtime output.

No dedup entry or issue-history item names `compileProtocols` duplicate families, `compileLog` duplicate stream names, or the combined formatter consequence.

The vulnerable lines remain at `compiler_protocols.go:205-207,278-283`, `compiler_security_log.go:38-42,82-96`, and the runtime consumers cited above.

`pkg/flowexport/transport.go:217-226` only repairs nonpositive results:


`pkg/flowexport/netflow.go:604-611` feeds any positive wrapped value directly to a ticker:

```go

	e.sendTemplates()

	// #4423 M10: clamp a non-positive refresh rate so NewTicker never panics.
	templateTicker := time.NewTicker(templateRefreshInterval(e.cfg.TemplateRefreshRate))
	defer templateTicker.Stop()
```

`pkg/flowexport/netflow.go:616-624` sends templates on every delivered tick:

```go
	for {
		select {
		case <-ctx.Done():
			// Flush remaining batches
			e.flushBatches()
			return
		case <-templateTicker.C:
			e.sendTemplates()
		case <-batchTicker.C:
```

Trace: Strict schema accepts `services flow-monitoring version9 template t template-refresh-rate seconds 20211507185753197` because `seconds` has arity only. On linux/amd64, `strconv.Atoi` accepts it. The manager checks the original positive `int`, then `time.Duration(n) * time.Second` wraps modulo 2^64 to exactly `512ns` (`20211507185753197 * 1,000,000,000 mod 2^64 = 512`). The #4423 helper sees a positive duration and returns it unchanged. NetFlow and IPFIX each create that ticker and call `sendTemplates` at the maximum rate their loop and UDP writes can sustain.

Refutation attempt: I checked the schema, compiler, typed field (`int` seconds), both manager resolvers, both exporter `Run` loops, and the #4423 clamp. No `ValidateInteger`, `MaxDurationSeconds` check, checked multiplication, or operational minimum exists on this leaf. Adjacent active/inactive fields are typed, proving schema validation is active rather than globally absent. The exact witness is below `MaxInt64`, positive before and after wrap, and was recomputed on the target `GOARCH=amd64`; neither `Atoi` nor the nonpositive fallback rejects it. Existing tests cover only zero and negative ticker inputs.

HPC/invariant check: This is signed duration multiplication overflow and timer/resource amplification, not a data race. Go's ticker channel coalesces missed ticks, preventing queue growth, but that makes the goroutine a continuous template-send loop rather than bounding work. It consumes daemon CPU and emits UDP templates at send throughput. The same arithmetic is duplicated for v9 and IPFIX.

Why it matters: One strict-accepted config value can turn a 60-second housekeeping timer into a near-busy loop, flooding every configured collector and consuming control-plane CPU. On a firewall daemon, sustained control-plane starvation can interfere with apply, HA, and telemetry processing even though forwarding is in userspace.

Fix direction: Give both `seconds` leaves `ValueInteger` plus `ValidateInteger(1, MaxDurationSeconds)` (or a tighter documented Junos operational maximum). Parse into a width-stable integer and use checked duration conversion in `flowexport` as defense in depth. Clamp/reject sub-operational intervals before ticker creation. Add v9/IPFIX tests for exact maximum, maximum+1, the `512ns` witness, strict rejection, tolerant behavior, and a runtime assertion that no wrapped sub-second ticker is constructed.

Labels: `config`, `flowexport`, `netflow`, `ipfix`, `typed-leaf`, `integer-overflow`, `resource-safety`, `observability`, `vSRX-parity`

Dedup note: Closed #1979 typed active/inactive flow timeouts but omitted template refresh. Closed #4423 handles zero/negative `time.NewTicker` panic only; this witness wraps to positive and bypasses that fix. Dedup searches found no template-refresh `time.Duration` overflow entry.

The untyped leaves remain at `schema_system.go:714-715,733-734`, conversions at `manager.go:298-299,327-328`, and tickers at `netflow.go:609-610` / `ipfix.go:825-826`.

```go
// expandAddressRange expands "low/mask to high/mask" into individual IP strings.
// Both low and high must be /32 CIDRs. Max 256 IPs.
```

Trace: `address 192.0.2.1/24 to 192.0.2.2/24` reaches `expandAddressRange`. `net.ParseCIDR` returns each original host IP separately from its network mask; the helper ignores the masks, compares `.1` to `.2`, and emits two `/32` strings. The source-pool grammar/cardinality gates run later over those rewritten values and pass. Both strict and tolerant compilers therefore accept a malformed range and install a two-host pool rather than rejecting the non-host endpoints. Flat and hierarchical forms share the helper; formatter replay preserves the malformed source text but repeats the same silent canonicalization.

Refutation attempt: I checked whether source-pool prefixes are generally legal, whether an earlier schema validator inspects authored range endpoints, whether the allocator interprets range endpoint masks, and whether the post-compile strict gate can recover them. Standalone source-pool prefixes are intentionally valid after #3049, but this function's own contract specifically requires `/32` for the `low to high` form. `address` remains unmodeled in the schema, and the original masks are irretrievably gone before strict validation. The 256-address cap prevents expansion DoS but does not validate endpoint masks.

HPC/invariant check: The #5194 `uint64` inclusive count and 256 bound are sound, and the `uint32` loop cannot wrap under that bound. No concurrency or allocation-amplification finding remains. The failed invariant is malformed-input fail-closed behavior and validation of authored data before canonicalization.

Why it matters: A typo or imported vSRX range using non-host CIDRs commits cleanly with materially different pool capacity and egress identities. The pool can exhaust ports early or translate through addresses the operator did not intend, while every strict gate reports success.

Fix direction: Parse each endpoint with `netip.ParsePrefix`/`ParseAddr`; accept bare IPv4 or require `Bits()==32` for a CIDR endpoint before extracting its address. Reject any non-host mask in the helper on both paths, retain the 256 cap, and add strict/tolerant tests for `/24`, mixed bare/`/32`, IPv6, reversed, and valid endpoints in flat, hierarchical, and formatter-round-trip forms.

## Finding: High confidence

### F-01

**Title:** Hierarchical duplicate event trigger siblings bypass validation and compilation silently drops every trigger after the first

**Severity:** Medium

**Confidence:** High

**Gate verdict:** MATERIAL

**Evidence:** At the reviewed base, `pkg/config/event_options_within.go:190-199` validates only the first child named `trigger`:

```go
	// trigger — a within clause with no trigger gates nothing; the engine
	// would treat it as an unconditional match (fail-open), so require one.
	trigNode := w.FindChild("trigger")
	if trigNode == nil {
		return emit("event-options policy %q within %d: missing a `trigger on|until "+
			"<count>` (a within clause with no trigger gates nothing)",
			policy, sec)
	}

	specs, unknown := parseEventTriggerSpecs(trigNode)
```

The compiler independently repeats the same first-child selection at `pkg/config/compiler_services.go:1790-1799`:

```go
			case "within":
				w := &EventWithin{}
				if v := nodeVal(child); v != "" {
					if n, err := strconv.Atoi(v); err == nil {
						w.Seconds = n
					}
				}
				if trigNode := child.FindChild("trigger"); trigNode != nil {
					// trigger on N or trigger until N
					for i := 1; i < len(trigNode.Keys)-1; i++ {
```

`pkg/config/ast.go:181-188` explicitly defines `FindChild` as returning the first match. `pkg/config/parser.go:215-229,393-402` appends each hierarchical statement as its own leaf node, so this valid parser shape is reachable:

```text
within 60 {
    trigger on 3;
    trigger until 5;
}
```

**Trace:**

1. The hierarchical parser creates two children under the same `within` node: `Keys=["trigger","on","3"]` and `Keys=["trigger","until","5"]`. It appends rather than coalesces statements.
2. With no groups, `ExpandGroupsWithVars` only checks for stale `apply-groups` references and preserves those siblings. Schema declares `trigger` as an open leaf and has no sibling-cardinality check.
3. `validateEventOptionsWithinAST` reaches the `within`, calls `FindChild("trigger")`, validates `on 3`, and returns success. Strict commit therefore accepts. The tolerant path also sees no defect, so it emits no warning.
4. `compileEventOptions` again calls `FindChild("trigger")`, sets `EventWithin.TriggerOn=3`, and never reads the `until 5` sibling. Reversing the statements retains only `TriggerUntil=5`; a malformed or out-of-range second sibling is likewise never converted or rejected.
5. `pkg/eventengine/engine.go:1323-1393` evaluates only the compiled field. The operator-authored second bound is absent, so automated `then change-configuration` behavior executes under a materially different temporal policy than the committed configuration expresses.

**Refutation attempt:** I checked for later normalization, schema cardinality validation, a second compiler pass, and a runtime backstop. Direct hierarchical siblings survive group expansion; the schema relies on this custom validator; both validator and compiler use the same first-only helper; the runtime receives only typed `EventWithin` fields and cannot recover the discarded AST node. Existing `event_options_within_3751_test.go` covers flat-set commands that merge beneath one trigger node and a single hierarchical leaf `trigger on 3 until 5;`, but not two hierarchical trigger statements. The full Go tests pass because that shape is absent.

**HPC/invariant check:** This is not a hot-path/HPC issue. Parser recursion and numeric ranges are bounded. The violated compiler invariant is: every authored trigger statement in an accepted `within` clause must be validated and represented exactly once, and strict/recovery compilation must not silently select a subset.

**Why it matters:** `event-options` drives autonomous configuration changes. A strict-valid configuration can silently omit a stop or start threshold and run remediation under a different event count than the operator authored. That can produce unintended route/failover/config commits and makes configuration round-trip intent diverge from runtime behavior.

**Fix direction:** Replace first-child reads with one shared normalization helper over `w.FindChildren("trigger")`. Enforce exactly one trigger statement, or aggregate all specs and reject duplicate/contradictory `on`/`until` forms. Have compilation consume the validated normalized result rather than reparsing independently. On tolerant load, warn and compile an invalid duplicate clause to no usable threshold so the engine's existing zero-threshold guard fails closed. Add strict and tolerant tests for two hierarchical siblings in both orders, a malformed/out-of-range second sibling, and a fail-on-revert assertion that no partial trigger reaches `EventWithin`.

**Labels:** `bug`, `config`, `event-options`, `reliability`, `go`, `vsrx-parity`

**Dedup note:** Not a restatement of closed #3751: that issue fixed ignored numeric conversion and combined `on`/`until` specs inside one trigger node; this defect is sibling cardinality plus first-child truncation after that fix. Not the #5250/`ps-review-042` multi-clause latch item, which is runtime state sharing between distinct `within` clauses. Searches of the fresh open issue list and targeted all-state event-options/trigger searches found no issue for this AST shape.

**Verified against origin/master:** Fresh `origin/master` at `ad959117748181dabe46b8ddc2827de670380cea`, fetched `2026-08-02T18:09:13Z`. Still present at `pkg/config/event_options_within.go:190-199`, `pkg/config/compiler_services.go:1790-1799`, and `pkg/config/ast.go:181-188`.

## Findings

### A3-b4-01

Title: Unbounded heartbeat threshold overflows the live peer timeout and defeats the cold-boot liveness guard

Severity: High

Confidence: High

Gate verdict: MATERIAL

Evidence: `pkg/config/schema_chassis.go:90-97` accepts every positive signed 64-bit threshold and documents the decision as safe because the count is not wire encoded:

> 90 `"heartbeat-threshold": {`
> 91 `    desc:          "Missed heartbeats before the peer is declared lost (default 5)",`
> 92 `    args:          1,`
> 93 `    valueType:     ValueInteger,`
> 94 `    valueDesc:     "Missed heartbeats before peer is declared lost (>= 1; xpf default 5, Junos allows 3..8)",`
> 95 `    valueExamples: []string{"3", "5", "8"},`
> 96 `    validator:     ValidateIntegerMin(1),`
> 97 `    children:      nil,`

Trace: On amd64, `ValidateIntegerMin` parses through `math.MaxInt64` (`pkg/config/schema_validators.go:100-120`) and `compileChassis` copies the same value through `strconv.Atoi` into `HeartbeatThreshold` (`pkg/config/compiler_system.go:1823-1827`). `applyConfigLocked` installs it as `m.hbThreshold` (`pkg/cluster/group_state.go:74-80`), and `StartHeartbeat` snapshots it into the receiver (`pkg/cluster/heartbeat_manager.go:56-100`). Both `checkTimeout` and the post-guard freshness recheck calculate `time.Duration(r.threshold) * r.interval` without checked multiplication (`pkg/cluster/heartbeat.go:968-1005,1041-1047`). With the default 100 ms interval, threshold `92233720369` produces `-9223372036809551616ns`. After the 30-second startup grace, every ordinary positive heartbeat age is greater than that negative timeout. `handlePeerTimeout` therefore marks a healthy peer dead, clears peer state, and runs single-node election (`pkg/cluster/heartbeat_manager.go:380-447`); the next heartbeat marks it alive and reruns election (`:314-376`). A symmetric config makes both nodes alternate false loss and recovery, including primary ownership and optional fence activity.

Refutation attempt: The count not being wire encoded does not make the multiplication safe. The interval is individually bounded, but the product is not. The startup grace only delays the first false loss for 30 seconds. The fresh-heartbeat race guard cannot recover because it recomputes the same negative timeout. The transfer-commit suppressor is conditional and temporary; it is not a general liveness guard. The accepted-value test explicitly asserts min-only behavior through 100000 (`pkg/config/schema_validate_chassis_test.go:63-69`) and has no product boundary.

HPC/invariant check: Required invariant: `threshold > 0`, `interval > 0`, and `threshold * interval <= math.MaxInt64 nanoseconds` before constructing a `time.Duration`. At 100 ms the maximum safe threshold is `92233720368`; the first unsafe value is accepted and deterministically wraps negative under Go integer arithmetic. HA failover decisions must never derive from a non-positive configured timeout.

Why it matters: A cleanly committed cluster setting converts fresh heartbeats into repeated peer-loss events after cold boot. That can produce dual-primary churn, RETH/VIP ownership oscillation, GARP churn, and fence attempts against a live peer. This reopens the failure class the cold-boot grace is intended to contain.

Fix direction: Add a cross-field validator that proves the interval/threshold product fits `time.Duration`, and independently use checked or saturating multiplication at every runtime liveness calculation. Reject the unsafe configuration rather than silently clamping operator intent. Add strict-schema boundary tests and a receiver test that advances beyond startup grace while fresh heartbeats continue at the largest accepted product.

Labels: MATERIAL, HA, cold-boot, split-brain, integer-overflow, schema-runtime-contract, userspace-live

Dedup note: No symbol+mechanism+impact match exists in the scratch index or issue history. Closed #1792 involved wall-clock arithmetic at the same timeout expression, not product overflow. Closed #4386 involved the never-seen branch bypassing startup grace. Open #6492 concerns cold-boot fencing gaps. Open #5081 concerns live application of changed timing. None covers an accepted `heartbeat-threshold` overflowing `threshold * interval` into a negative duration.

Verified against origin/master: Yes. `origin/master` is `ad959117748181dabe46b8ddc2827de670380cea`, identical to the detached review SHA, and the schema, compiler, group-state, receiver, timeout, and election lines above are unchanged there.

### A3-b4-02

Title: DDNS TTL schemas admit values that wrap to zero at the RFC2136 uint32 boundary

Severity: Medium

Confidence: High

Gate verdict: MATERIAL

Evidence: Surface A is min-only in `pkg/config/schema_interfaces.go:553-557`, while the live RFC2136 backend narrows the resulting `int` in `pkg/ddns/backend_rfc2136.go:493-497`:

> 553 `    args:          1,`
> 554 `    valueType:     ValueInteger,`
> 555 `    valueDesc:     "Record TTL in seconds (>= 1; default 300 when unset)",`
> 556 `    valueExamples: []string{"300", "3600"},`
> 557 `    validator:     ValidateIntegerMin(1),`
> 493 `// forwardRR builds the A or AAAA RR for a record.`
> 494 `func (u *rfc2136Updater) forwardRR(rec LeaseDNSRecord) (dns.RR, error) {`
> 495 `    name := dns.Fqdn(rec.FQDN)`
> 496 `    ttl := uint32(rec.TTL) //nolint:gosec // TTL is a small positive config value`
> 497 `    if rec.Addr.Is4() {`

Trace: Both operator surfaces use the same unsafe contract: interface Surface A uses `ValidateIntegerMin(1)` (`pkg/config/schema_interfaces.go:551-558`) and DHCP Surface B does too (`pkg/config/schema_system.go:767-774`). Their compilers preserve an amd64 `int` through `strconv.Atoi` (`pkg/config/compiler_interfaces.go:1336-1339`, `pkg/config/compiler_services.go:615-618`). `LeaseDNSRecord.TTL` is also `int` (`pkg/ddns/backend.go:22-29`). The RFC2136 A/AAAA builder narrows it to `uint32` at `backend_rfc2136.go:496`, and the PTR builder repeats the cast at `:517-524`. Thus configured `4294967296` is positive at every default/fallback check but becomes TTL 0 on all emitted RRs. Values `2^32+n` become `n`, so the stored config, owned-record state, and wire records disagree.

Refutation attempt: `buildLeaseRecord` only defaults values `<= 0`; the oversized value remains positive until the final cast. The linter suppression assumes exactly the property the schema fails to establish. Cloudflare and Route53 using an `int` does not protect the RFC2136 backend, which is the live DHCP DDNS backend and an available Surface A provider. Existing DDNS schema tests cover hostname canonicality and source-address parsing, not TTL width.

HPC/invariant check: DNS RR TTL is an unsigned 32-bit wire field. Required invariant: `1 <= TTL <= math.MaxUint32` before any `uint32` conversion. On amd64, `ValidateIntegerMin(1)` accepts `2^32`; Go conversion yields `uint32(2^32) == 0`. No fallback or checked conversion intervenes.

Why it matters: A strict commit can claim a large positive TTL while RFC2136 publishes a zero or unrelated small TTL. Zero-TTL records are not cacheable, increasing authoritative query load and making DDNS behavior and status contradict operator intent for A, AAAA, and PTR records.

Fix direction: Bound both DDNS schema leaves to `[1, math.MaxUint32]` and add a checked conversion in the RFC2136 builder as defense in depth. Preserve the hostname and source-address cases already covered; add max, max+1, and `2^32+n` tests for Surface A, DHCPv4/v6 Surface B, A/AAAA, and PTR construction.

Labels: MATERIAL, DDNS, RFC2136, integer-narrowing, observability, performance, schema-runtime-contract, userspace-live

Dedup note: No scratch-index or issue-history entry matches DDNS TTL narrowing. Open #6555 is transient interface-address withdrawal; #6218's DDNS item is quarantine filename collision; prior `ps-review-038-A7` concerns `ForcedRefreshSeconds` to `time.Duration`. Those differ by symbol, mechanism, and impact.

Verified against origin/master: Yes. `origin/master` is the reviewed SHA; both schema leaves, both compiler assignments, `LeaseDNSRecord.TTL`, and both RFC2136 casts are byte-identical there.

### A3-b4-03

Title: Strict schema validation rejects the compiler-supported Junos hierarchical default-policy form

Severity: Medium

Confidence: High

Gate verdict: MATERIAL

Evidence: `pkg/config/schema_security.go:215-220` declares only a token-valued typed leaf, while `pkg/config/compiler_security_policy.go:9-12` explicitly supports the block spelling:

> 215 `    args:          1,`
> 216 `    valueType:     ValueEnumOf,`
> 217 `    valueDesc:     "No-match default action (permit-all | deny-all | reject-all)",`
> 218 `    valueExamples: []string{"deny-all", "permit-all", "reject-all"},`
> 219 `    validator:     ValidateEnum([]string{"permit-all", "deny-all", "reject-all"}),`
> 220 `    children:      nil,`
> 9 `        policyStr = child.Keys[1]`
> 10 `    } else if len(child.Children) > 0 {`
> 11 `        // Hierarchical form: default-policy { deny-all; }`
> 12 `        policyStr = child.Children[0].Name()`

Trace: The parser represents `default-policy { deny-all; }` as a node with `Keys == ["default-policy"]` and a child named `deny-all`; assigned parser fixtures use this exact vSRX shape (`pkg/config/parser_ast_test.go:74-80`, `pkg/config/parser_stray_brace_4862_test.go:55-61`). `walkSchemaNode` dispatches a typed leaf to `validateTypedLeaf` (`pkg/config/schema_walk.go:328-358`), which takes values only from `node.Keys[1:]` and returns `missing value` when that slice is empty (`:668-676`). The config store invokes `SchemaValidateWithDefinitions` on the expanded AST before compilation for strict commit/check (`pkg/configstore/store.go:585-627`). The compiler's hierarchical branch is therefore unreachable through the strict production path even though direct compiler tests and tolerant loading can use it.

Refutation attempt: Open-world handling does not help because `default-policy` is a known typed leaf, so validation fails before its child can be treated as an unknown extension. Parser acceptance is not commit acceptance. Setting `multi: true` alone would be unsafe because the generic block-list path permits multiple values while the compiler consumes only the first child. The default remains fail-closed when omitted; this finding is vSRX grammar completeness and schema/compiler disagreement, not a default-deny bypass.

HPC/invariant check: For this singleton verdict, the schema and compiler must accept exactly one of three values from either `Keys[1]` or one presence-only child, reject mixed or multiple forms, and compile the same selected value. Current schema accepts only the first representation while the compiler claims both.

Why it matters: A normal Junos/vSRX hierarchical configuration containing an explicit default deny cannot pass strict import, commit-check, or a later strict commit after tolerant boot. The failure occurs on a security posture statement the compiler is already designed to honor, blocking migration and creating two grammar sources of truth.

Fix direction: Add a purpose-built dual-shape tree/tail validator for `default-policy` that accepts exactly one flat token or exactly one child verdict and rejects duplicates, mixed forms, descendants, and unknown values. Keep the compiler and completion behavior aligned. Add config-store strict tests for all three verdicts in both forms and negative multi-child/mixed cases; retain parser-only coverage.

Labels: MATERIAL, security-policy, default-policy, vSRX-completeness, schema-compiler-drift, strict-commit, fail-closed

Dedup note: Closed #3065 added default-deny semantics, `reject-all`, and the missing schema entry; it did not cover rejection of the compiler-supported hierarchical shape after the leaf became typed. Prior `ps-review-042` covers absent-default handling. No index/history record matches this representation mismatch.

Verified against origin/master: Yes. `origin/master` equals the review SHA; the typed schema, walker dispatch, parser fixtures, compiler dual-form branch, and config-store gate all remain present and unchanged.

## Findings - High confidence

### F1

**Title:** Interface-level WireGuard endpoint emission discards strictly accepted per-unit peers and devices

**Severity:** Medium

**Confidence:** High

**Gate verdict:** MATERIAL

**Evidence:** The assigned regression fixture authors a parent WireGuard identity/peer set and two explicit unit peer sets (`pkg/config/tunnel_perunit_deepcopy_test.go:123`):

```go
123	cmds := []string{
124		"set interfaces gr-0/0/0 tunnel mode wireguard",
125		"set interfaces gr-0/0/0 tunnel wireguard listen-port 51820",
126		"set interfaces gr-0/0/0 tunnel wireguard private-key " + priv,
127		"set interfaces gr-0/0/0 tunnel wireguard peer " + peerX + " allowed-ips 10.100.0.0/24",
128		"set interfaces gr-0/0/0 tunnel wireguard peer " + peerY + " allowed-ips 10.100.1.0/24",
129		"set interfaces gr-0/0/0 tunnel wireguard peer " + peerZ + " allowed-ips 10.100.2.0/24",
130		// Per-unit tunnels, each inheriting mode/listen-port/private-key/X/Y/Z
131		// and adding its OWN distinct peer.
132		"set interfaces gr-0/0/0 unit 1 tunnel wireguard peer " + peerA + " allowed-ips 10.200.1.0/24",
```

Strict `CompileConfig` accepts it and materializes both unit tunnels (`pkg/config/tunnel_perunit_deepcopy_test.go:133`):

```go
133		"set interfaces gr-0/0/0 unit 2 tunnel wireguard peer " + peerB + " allowed-ips 10.200.2.0/24",
134	}
135	cfg, err := CompileConfig(buildTree(t, cmds))
136	if err != nil {
137		t.Fatalf("CompileConfig: %v", err)
138	}
139	ifc := cfg.Interfaces.Interfaces["gr-0/0/0"]
140	if ifc == nil {
141		t.Fatal("gr-0/0/0 interface not found")
```

The test then proves the unit-specific typed peer state is present and independent (`pkg/config/tunnel_perunit_deepcopy_test.go:157`):

```go
157	if !hasStr(p1, peerA) {
158		t.Errorf("unit 1 lost its own peer %s: got %v", peerA, p1)
159	}
160	if hasStr(p1, peerB) {
161		t.Errorf("unit 1 was contaminated with unit 2's peer %s: got %v", peerB, p1)
162	}
163	if !hasStr(p2, peerB) {
164		t.Errorf("unit 2 lost its own peer %s: got %v", peerB, p2)
```

The endpoint SSOT nevertheless passes only the parent tunnel under the lowest unit name, then skips all units (`pkg/config/tunnelemit.go:97`):

```go
97				unitNums = append(unitNums, unitNum)
98			}
99			sort.Ints(unitNums)
100			if iface.Tunnel.Mode == "wireguard" {
101				// Interface-level WireGuard is ONE persistent TUN; the
102				// builder emits exactly one endpoint keyed by the lowest
103				// configured unit ref (#1910). Mirror that here.
104				add(fmt.Sprintf("%s.%d", name, unitNums[0]), iface.Tunnel)
105				continue
```

That conflicts with the assigned mapping contract, which treats each explicit unit tunnel as its own device even when a parent tunnel coexists (`pkg/config/types.go:327`):

```go
327			if unit != nil && unit.Tunnel != nil && unit.Tunnel.Name != "" {
328				// Per-unit tunnel: its own Linux device, always.
329				m[ref] = unit.Tunnel.Name
330				continue
331			}
332			if ifaceTunnel {
333				// Interface-level tunnel: unit shares the device.
334				m[ref] = baseName
335			}
```

**Trace:**

1. `compiler_interfaces.go:259-331` clones the parent `TunnelConfig` for each explicit unit, parses the unit WireGuard subtree into that clone, and stores it in `unit.Tunnel`. `compiler_validate_wireguard.go:76-101` validates parent, unit 1, and unit 2 independently and has no mixed parent/unit rejection. The assigned strict test passes.
2. `pkg/daemon/daemon_run_routehelpers.go:94-114` appends the parent tunnel and every unit tunnel to `collectAppliedTunnels`, so routing reconciliation creates the base, `u1`, and `u2` tunnel devices.
3. `Config.TunnelNameMap` maps `.1` to `u1` and `.2` to `u2`; `pkg/dataplane/userspace/interfaces.go:424-433` uses that map for each unit snapshot. Routes and interface state therefore point at the unit devices.
4. `EmitTunnelEndpointNames` sees a parent WireGuard tunnel plus units, emits only `gr-0/0/0.1`, supplies `iface.Tunnel`, and `continue`s before reading either `unit.Tunnel`.
5. `pkg/dataplane/userspace/tunnels.go:135-155,170-171` copies peers only from the supplied tunnel. The sole endpoint attaches to unit 1's Linux interface but contains only parent peers X/Y/Z. Unit 1 peer A and unit 2 peer B are absent; unit 2 and the separately created parent device have no corresponding endpoint.
6. Both HA nodes deterministically build the same broken snapshot. Failover cannot heal it, and traffic resolved to unit-specific routes can blackhole or use the wrong cryptokey-routing peer set.

**HPC/invariant check:** This is cold compile/reconcile work, not a packet-hot-path or lock/cache-line issue. Sorting is bounded by configured interfaces/units. The violated invariant is stronger: every accepted and routed tunnel device must have exactly one endpoint carrying that device's typed state. The commit-time endpoint-ID collision gate reuses this emitter, so it also omits the units and cannot catch the mismatch. No atomic, endianness, or resource-exhaustion defense neutralizes the semantic loss; routing can leave extra TUN devices configured without usable endpoints.

**Why it matters:** A strict candidate commit reports success and preserves per-unit peer data in the public `Config`, while live routing and userspace snapshots disagree about which device and peers exist. An operator can deploy apparently valid unit-specific WireGuard routing and receive a deterministic traffic blackhole on both cluster nodes, with no failover recovery.

**Fix direction:** First choose and enforce one contract. If interface-level WireGuard is one shared TUN, strict schema/compiler gates should reject every explicit unit tunnel below it; tolerant Load/SyncApply should warn and deterministically remove unit tunnels so routing, `TunnelNameMap`, and emitter all reference the parent. If per-unit WireGuard is supported, emit each `unit.Tunnel`, avoid creating an unused parent device, enforce unique/compatible local identities and listen ports, and make the AST collision gate enumerate the same names. Add flat and hierarchical end-to-end tests based on this fixture that assert `TunnelNameMap`, applied tunnel set, emitted endpoint names, endpoint peer sets, both node views, and serialize/parse round trips.

**Labels:** `bug`, `config`, `wireguard`, `userspace-dataplane`, `ha`. Not `vsrx-parity`: this is an internal supported-schema/runtime consistency defect; no vSRX WireGuard unit contract was assumed.

**Dedup note:** Closed #3898 is slice-header aliasing between cloned units; its fix is what makes the independent A/B state visible here. #1910 covers choosing one endpoint for units that do **not** own a tunnel. #5635 fixes per-unit GRE/IPIP emission. Current-open GH#1434 is the umbrella for multiple top-level WireGuard interfaces/engine selection; its issue-history requirements do not describe parent/unit co-residence or `EmitTunnelEndpointNames` discarding an already accepted `unit.Tunnel`. No index/history entry matched this symbol + branch mechanism + typed-state-loss/device-blackhole consequence.

**Verified against origin/master:** Immediately before reporting, `HEAD` and `origin/master` both resolved to `ad959117748181dabe46b8ddc2827de670380cea`. `git diff --exit-code origin/master --` the material files and narrow runtime contracts returned clean. The accepting fixture remains at `origin/master:pkg/config/tunnel_perunit_deepcopy_test.go:123-164`; the dropping branch remains at `origin/master:pkg/config/tunnelemit.go:97-105`; the conflicting map remains at `origin/master:pkg/config/types.go:327-335`; the live creation/snapshot consumers remain at `pkg/daemon/daemon_run_routehelpers.go:94-114`, `pkg/dataplane/userspace/interfaces.go:424-433`, and `pkg/dataplane/userspace/tunnels.go:135-155,170-171`.

### C1 - single cohort issue (5 survivors)

**Title:** Tolerant typed-leaf ingress preserves narrowing/timer hazards, while the strict-gate canary proves only syntactic invocation

**Severity:** Medium for A/B; Low for C/D/E

**Confidence:** High

**Gate verdict:** COHORT

**Evidence:** Store.Load and Store.SyncApply deliberately downgrade typed-leaf failures and compile the unneutralized tree (`pkg/configstore/store.go:543`):

```go
543	// accepted the value when it was committed and still compiles it the
544	// same way today. This is the same doctrine as the #1733/#1798/#1814
545	// lenient compile gates (see freetext.go); the operator's next strict
546	// commit rejects the stale value loudly.
547	if err := s.schemaValidateExpandedTree(tree); err != nil {
548		slog.Warn("typed-leaf schema violation in tolerated config; continuing (a strict commit would reject this)",
549			"err", err, "issue", "#1319")
550	}
```

**A - VRRP advertise interval:** The compiler stores any parseable seconds (`pkg/config/compiler_interfaces.go:776`):

```go
776			case "advertise-interval":
777				if i+1 < len(keys) {
778					i++
779					// #4573: keep the prior value on a bad parse (`_ =`).
780					if n, err := strconv.Atoi(keys[i]); err == nil {
781						vg.AdvertiseInterval = n
782					}
783				}
```

The runtime schedules using the full milliseconds but narrows and masks the advertised wire value (`pkg/vrrp/instance_send.go:59`, with the 12-bit mask at `pkg/vrrp/packet.go:74-75`):

```go
59	// Send IPv4 advertisement if we have any IPv4 VIPs.
60	if len(v4Addrs) > 0 {
61		maxAdvert := uint16(vi.cfg.AdvertiseInterval / 10) // milliseconds → centiseconds
62		pkt := &VRRPPacket{
63			VRID:         uint8(vi.cfg.GroupID),
64			Priority:     uint8(priority),
65			MaxAdvertInt: maxAdvert,
66			IPAddresses:  v4Addrs,
```

The serializer then masks it to the 12-bit VRRPv3 field (`pkg/vrrp/packet.go:72`):

```go
72	buf[3] = uint8(count)
73
74	// MaxAdvertInt: top 4 bits reserved (0), bottom 12 bits = interval
75	binary.BigEndian.PutUint16(buf[4:6], p.MaxAdvertInt&0x0FFF)
76
```

A tolerated 41 seconds schedules sends 41 seconds apart but encodes `4100 & 0x0fff = 4` centiseconds. A peer that trusts the wire field can time the master out between advertisements. The local xpf receive path clamps a learned interval up to its own configured floor (`pkg/vrrp/instance.go:1059-1075`), which refutes the identical-xpf-config case but not a standard peer or rolling configuration with a lower local floor. Current vSRX-specific clamping was not proven, so this is a protocol-interoperability risk, not a claimed vSRX reproduction. Strict schema caps this leaf at 40, so this remains a lenient HA/cold-load survivor, not MATERIAL.

**B - VRRP preempt hold-time:** The assigned test proves only the strict schema range (`pkg/config/vrrp_preempt_holdtime_test.go:108`):

```go
108		{"60", false},
109		{"1", false},
110		{"3600", false},
111		{"0", true},
112		{"3601", true},
113		{"abc", true},
114	}
```

The runtime multiplies the unrestricted compiled `int` after only a pre-multiply positivity check (`pkg/vrrp/instance.go:582`):

```go
582	func (vi *vrrpInstance) preemptHoldDuration() time.Duration {
583		vi.mu.RLock()
584		defer vi.mu.RUnlock()
585		if vi.cfg.PreemptHoldTime <= 0 {
586			return 0
587		}
588		return time.Duration(vi.cfg.PreemptHoldTime) * time.Second
```

A large tolerated positive value can wrap to a non-positive duration; `stepBackup` applies the hold only when `hold > 0`, so a configured delay can become immediate preemption of a live lower-priority master. A negative stale value also becomes immediate. This is cold-load/HA-only because strict candidate commits reject outside 1..3600.

**C - WireGuard persistent keepalive:** Out-of-range parse success is silently converted to the zero/off sentinel (`pkg/config/compiler_interfaces.go:647`):

```go
647		case "persistent-keepalive":
648			if v := nodeVal(prop); v != "" {
649				if n, err := strconv.Atoi(v); err == nil && n >= 0 && n <= 65535 {
650					peer.KeepaliveSecs = uint16(n)
651				}
652			}
```

Zero is live disablement in the userspace engine (`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/wg/timers.rs:317`):

```rust
317        // T8 — persistent keepalive. Pacing anchor is the most recent
318        // authenticated traversal in EITHER direction (wireguard-go
319        // `timersAnyAuthenticatedPacketTraversal`) or the last T8
320        // attempt (skip-pacing), whichever is later.
321        let keepalive_secs = config.persistent_keepalive;
322        if keepalive_secs != 0 {
323            let interval_ns = u64::from(keepalive_secs).saturating_mul(1_000_000_000);
```

Thus a tolerated stale `65536` disables NAT-traversal keepalives after only the generic schema warning. The strict path rejects it; the impact is configuration robustness, so COHORT.

**D - GRE key:** Both interface and unit parsers narrow a successful host-width `int` without a range check; the interface path is (`pkg/config/compiler_interfaces.go:183`):

```go
183			case "key":
184				if len(prop.Keys) >= 2 {
185					if v, err := strconv.Atoi(prop.Keys[1]); err == nil {
186						tc.Key = uint32(v)
187					}
188				}
```

The kernel tunnel omits a zero key (`pkg/routing/tunnel.go:660`):

```go
660			Ttl:       ttl,
661		}
662		if tc.Key > 0 {
663			greLink.IKey = tc.Key
664			greLink.OKey = tc.Key
665		}
666		return greLink
```

On 64-bit builds, tolerated `4294967296` wraps to zero and silently changes keyed GRE to unkeyed GRE; negatives wrap to unrelated high keys. Strict schema enforces 0..2^32-1, keeping this in the tolerant-input cohort.

**E - strict gate wiring canary:** It records any identifier call in any production file, without building a call graph from compile entrypoints (`pkg/config/strict_gate_wiring_canary_test.go:72`):

```go
72			case *ast.FuncDecl:
73				if node.Recv == nil && strings.HasSuffix(node.Name.Name, "Strict") &&
74					isCfgConfigErrorGateSig(node.Type) {
75					defined[node.Name.Name] = fset.Position(node.Name.Pos()).String()
76				}
77			case *ast.CallExpr:
78				if id, ok := node.Fun.(*ast.Ident); ok {
79					called[id.Name] = true
80				}
```

A strict gate called only by an unreachable/dead helper satisfies the canary even though the commit path never executes it. This is a test-coverage limitation, not a live enforcement finding by itself.

**HPC/invariant check:** A-D originate in cold persisted-config/HA-sync compilation. They do not add packet-path allocation or lock contention; B's existing `RLock` is balanced. The defects are integer representation/timer invariants: schema-bounded values must either remain bounded on every ingress or be neutralized before narrowed/wire/runtime use. E is test-only O(package AST nodes), with no runtime cost. No atomic wrapping or endianness issue beyond VRRP's explicit 12-bit big-endian field.

**Why it matters:** A tolerated legacy or peer-synced configuration can boot rather than blackout, but warning-only continuation can alter protocol behavior: VRRP peer timeout/preemption, disabled WireGuard NAT keepalive, or an unkeyed GRE tunnel. The canary can then overstate strict-gate coverage. These are real but low-frequency/tolerant-ingress or test-only mechanisms, so individual issues would overstate materiality.

**Fix direction:** Preserve tolerant availability while neutralizing unsafe leaves. Add universal compiler validators that, in strict mode, return the existing curated error and, in lenient mode, warn and replace with safe deterministic behavior: VRRP default 1 second, disable preemption or cap its hold at 3600, make invalid WireGuard keepalive disablement leaf-specific and loud (or drop the peer), and reject/drop the affected GRE tunnel rather than silently remove its key. Prefer parse-to-wide, validate, then cast. Upgrade the canary to prove each gate is reachable from the exported strict compile entrypoints (or maintain a generated explicit gate registry exercised by a mutation test).

**Labels:** `config`, `ha`, `vrrp`, `wireguard`, `tunnel`, `test-coverage`, `vsrx-parity` (VRRP wire/peer behavior only).

**Dedup note:** A-D aggregate into current-open low-materiality/defense-in-depth/lenient-HA-sync cohort GH#5609. E aggregates into test/observability backlog GH#4422. The already-indexed GRE/IPIP TTL cast was excluded rather than counted as D; D is the distinct `TunnelConfig.Key` `int -> uint32 -> zero means absent` mechanism. Searches for `AdvertiseInterval`, `PreemptHoldTime`, `persistent-keepalive`, `KeepaliveSecs`, GRE key narrowing, and the canary symbols found no more specific open issue in the index/history.

**Verified against origin/master:** COHORT freshness is not an individually-fileable claim, but the setup tip equals the base SHA and every cited mechanism was also present in that tip during the final audit.

## Firewall, HA, DDNS, and observability focus conclusions

- Firewall zones/global/junos-host/default: no new fail-open. Zone IDs quarantine collisions, undefined/cross-zone members warn/drop, duplicate blocks merge, and unsupported policy state uses poison/fail-closed behavior. GH#6515 and the prior mixed-`any` lenient issue were suppressed.
- HA cold boot/sync: availability-motivated schema downgrade is explicit and avoids blackout, but C1 records the leaves whose compiled representation is not neutralized. F1 reproduces identically on both nodes, so deterministic HA does not make it correct.
- DDNS: URL secret/redaction gaps are GH#6703/GH#6609. Malformed configured source binding was checked through current constructors and #4437 tests; no new default-route publication bypass was found. Typed `Secret` scalar fields and WireGuard/VRRP renderers remain redacted.
- Observability: syslog file confinement is fixed and pinned; stream ports remain bounded. Source-unit bounds are GH#6218. Advisory-only TCP leaves are honestly surfaced but unenforced as tracked by GH#6539.
- vSRX completeness: no new zone/default/junos-host parity issue survived. C1-A retains a VRRP peer-wire parity concern only on tolerated out-of-schema input. F1 is not asserted as vSRX parity.

## Findings

### F1

Title: Malformed encrypted-envelope fields bypass decryption and boot as an empty committed configuration

Severity: Medium

Confidence: High

Gate verdict: MATERIAL

Evidence: `pkg/configstore/crypto.go:366-374` treats every typed JSON decode error as legacy plaintext rather than rejecting an envelope-shaped object:

```go
func unmarshalEnvelope(data []byte) (encryptedTreeEnvelope, bool, error) {
	type alias encryptedTreeEnvelope
	var env alias
	if err := json.Unmarshal(data, &env); err != nil {
		// Not JSON, or not the envelope object shape at all — a genuine
		// plaintext (pre-encryption / legacy) config body. Pass through.
		return encryptedTreeEnvelope{}, false, nil
	}
	if env.Format != encryptedTreeFormat {
```

Evidence: `pkg/configstore/crypto.go:380-389` detects reserved fields by decoded non-empty value, not by JSON field presence, so empty or `null` reserved fields also disappear:

```go
		// plaintext. Treating it as plaintext lets json.Unmarshal drop the
		// unknown fields and decode an EMPTY ConfigTree, so Store.Load would
		// boot a committed-empty config (loss of policy) instead of failing
		// closed with ErrConfigDBUnreadable. Only a body with NO format AND no
		// AES-GCM fields is a genuine plaintext body and passes through.
		if env.Format != "" || env.Salt != "" || env.Nonce != "" || env.Data != "" {
			return encryptedTreeEnvelope{}, false, fmt.Errorf(
				"unsupported encrypted config envelope format %q (too-new or corrupted config DB)", env.Format)
		}
		return encryptedTreeEnvelope{}, false, nil
```

Evidence: `pkg/configstore/db.go:373-380` accepts the raw object shape and uses a normal struct decode, which ignores all envelope keys because `ConfigTree` contains only `Children`:

```go
	if err := requireJSONObject(data); err != nil {
		return nil, true, fmt.Errorf("parse %s: %w", path, err)
	}

	tree := &config.ConfigTree{}
	if err := json.Unmarshal(data, tree); err != nil {
		return nil, true, fmt.Errorf("parse %s: %w", path, err)
	}
```

Trace:
1. A current outer config envelope contains a valid JSON object such as `{"format":1,"prf":"sha256","salt":"AAAA","nonce":"AAAA","data":"AAAA"}`. An all-empty or all-`null` reserved-field object is a second trigger.
2. `stripEnvelope` accepts the current outer header and passes the inner object to `unmarshalEnvelope`.
3. The numeric `format` produces `json.UnmarshalTypeError`; line 372 classifies it as plaintext. For `null`/empty values, decoding succeeds but line 385 sees only zero-value strings and line 389 also classifies it as plaintext.
4. AES-GCM key lookup and `Open` are never reached, so ciphertext integrity cannot fail the load.
5. `requireJSONObject` accepts the leading `{`. `json.Unmarshal` into `ConfigTree` ignores `format`/`prf`/`salt`/`nonce`/`data` and returns a zero-child tree without error.
6. `Store.Load` leniently compiles that empty tree and honors the outer `committed=1`, accepting policy-absent state instead of returning `ErrConfigDBUnreadable`.

Refutation attempt: I checked the #4888 unknown-format guard and both assigned #4888 tests; they cover non-empty string discriminators only. I checked `requireJSONObject`; it rejects a top-level `null`, not an object containing null/typed reserved fields. I checked `config.ConfigTree` and found no custom decoder or unknown-field rejection. I also followed `Store.Load`; an empty tree is a valid bootstrap-shaped compile. The semantic checks in `ReadConfirm` do reject an empty confirm record, but active/candidate/rollback tree reads share `readTreeMeta` and do not have an equivalent non-empty semantic gate.

HPC/invariant check: This is off the packet hot path. It violates the fail-closed persistent-state invariant: any object carrying an encryption-envelope field must either authenticate and decrypt or fail; it must never enter the plaintext AST decoder. No integer cast or alignment issue is involved.

Why it matters: A malformed restore, future inner-envelope schema using a non-string discriminator, or deliberate/corrupt root-owned DB can be accepted as a committed empty configuration. Startup proceeds after silently dropping firewall policy and other configured controls rather than stopping on unreadable authoritative state.

Fix direction: Probe the top-level object into `map[string]json.RawMessage` first. If any reserved key (`format`, `prf`, `salt`, `nonce`, `data`) is present, require the complete current envelope, exact string types, supported PRF, and non-empty fields; return an error on every typed decode failure. Pass through as plaintext only when none of those keys is present. Add end-to-end outer-envelope tests for numeric, boolean, `null`, and empty reserved values and require `ErrConfigDBUnreadable`.

Labels: `bug`, `configstore`, `crypto`, `firewall`, `fail-closed`, `persistence`

Dedup note: Closed #4888 fixed a non-empty unknown/missing string `format`; its implementation and tests do not cover decode errors or reserved-field presence hidden by empty/`null` values. Closed #5474 covers a non-object top-level body. Open #5523 C179-053 covers the unauthenticated outer `committed` marker, not this inner typed-object fallback. Exact symbol/mechanism searches in `dedup-index.tsv`, `docs/issues/issue-history.md`, and fresh issues found no match.

Verified against origin/master: Still present at setup/re-fetch tip `ad959117748181dabe46b8ddc2827de670380cea`: `pkg/configstore/crypto.go:366-389`, `pkg/configstore/db.go:373-380`, and `pkg/config/ast.go:203-205` are unchanged.

Gate verdict: MATERIAL
