## Dispositions

### D1

Title: SNMPv3 AES responses can cross a second boundary between encryption and advertised USM time
Severity: Low
Confidence: High
Gate verdict: DUP
Evidence: `pkg/snmp/v3.go:865-869,1141-1144` (9 lines): <code>865 enc, err := encryptAES128(user.privKey, scopedPDU, salt, a.engineBoots, a.engineTime())</code><br><code>866 if err != nil {</code><br><code>867 return nil, nil, err</code><br><code>868 }</code><br><code>869 return enc, salt, nil</code><br><code>1141 // USM security parameters.</code><br><code>1142 usmFields := berEncodeTLV(tagOctetString, a.engineID)</code><br><code>1143 usmFields = append(usmFields, berEncodeIntegerTLV(a.engineBoots)...)</code><br><code>1144 usmFields = append(usmFields, berEncodeIntegerTLV(a.engineTime())...)</code>
Trace: `buildV3Response` encrypts the scoped PDU with authoritative time T, then independently samples the clock for the USM header. If the second advances between calls, the wire advertises T+1. A conformant manager reconstructs the AES-CFB IV from T+1 plus the transmitted salt and cannot decrypt ciphertext generated with T. `v3_priv_iv_test.go` resets `startTime` immediately before a short request and has no injected clock or rollover barrier, so its successful round trip does not refute the boundary. The live daemon sends this result on UDP/161.
Refutation attempt: Serial serving and the short call gap make each individual trigger uncommon, but a scheduler pause or ordinary second tick is sufficient and repeated polling eventually exercises the boundary. HMAC authenticates the internally inconsistent message; it does not repair the receiver's IV. No single captured response timestamp is passed through encryption and header construction.
HPC/invariant check: Capture `(engineBoots, engineTime)` once per response and pass it to encryption and USM encoding. This is O(1), allocation-neutral, and does not add a packet-path lock.
Why it matters: Managers intermittently reject otherwise valid authPriv responses as undecryptable, producing polling timeouts and false device-health alarms.
Fix direction: Add a response-clock seam, force a rollover between the two current call sites, then build both the AES IV and security parameters from one immutable response timestamp.
Labels: `snmpv3`, `aes`, `rfc3826`, `wire-protocol`, `interoperability`, `time`
Dedup note: Exact prior candidate `codex-review-178` A9-b1-09 identifies the same two clock samples and the same missing forced response-clock rollover; its per-file log explicitly states that `v3_priv_iv_test.go` supports that candidate. This is the same root and fix locus.
Verified against origin/master: Present unchanged at local `origin/master` `ad959117748181dabe46b8ddc2827de670380cea`; the assigned-file diff is empty.

### D2

Title: DES privacy salt repeats after 2^32 encryptions in one engine boot
Severity: Low
Confidence: High
Gate verdict: DUP
Evidence: `pkg/snmp/v3.go:843-850` (8 lines): <code>843 // where the monotonic counter re-randomizes its start. Overlay</code><br><code>844 // engineBoots onto the counter's high 32 bits; keep the counter's low 32</code><br><code>845 // bits (salt[4:8]) as the per-message local-integer. That low half still</code><br><code>846 // increments monotonically per PDU and repeats only every 2^32 messages,</code><br><code>847 // so within-boot IV uniqueness is preserved for 2^32 PDUs - this does NOT</code><br><code>848 // reopen #5032 (that defect was birthday-bound random salts; the counter</code><br><code>849 // model is unchanged). The overlaid salt is what we build the IV from AND</code><br><code>850 // what we return as privParams: the wire salt MUST equal the IV salt or</code>
Trace: `nextPrivSalt` allocates a unique 64-bit value, but `encryptPDU` overwrites its high 32 bits with constant `engineBoots` for DES. Encryptions N and N+2^32 in one boots/key domain therefore transmit the same salt and derive the same DES-CBC IV. `TestEncryptPDUDistinctSaltsPerMessage` obtains its user from `newAuthPrivAgent`, whose privacy protocol is AES, and the raw allocator tests observe all 64 bits; none reaches the DES projection or near-wrap state.
Refutation attempt: Normal polling rates make wrap slow and the tests prove atomic uniqueness well below it, but there is no per-key message ceiling, near-wrap rejection, engine rollover, or key rotation. The source comment explicitly acknowledges repetition, so scheduling and random-seed arguments do not restore uniqueness.
HPC/invariant check: Per-key IV uniqueness must hold over the full accepted lifetime. Preserve O(1) allocation by maintaining a DES-specific 32-bit counter with explicit exhaustion and engine/key rollover; do not add per-message randomness or a global contended map.
Why it matters: IV reuse under one DES privacy key reveals repeated first-block relationships and violates the protocol's privacy invariant on a long-lived, heavily polled agent.
Fix direction: Define a hard exhaustion policy before the low 32-bit counter wraps, persist/advance an authoritative domain if required, and add a DES production-path test initialized at `MaxUint32-1`.
Labels: `snmpv3`, `des`, `privacy`, `iv-reuse`, `integer-wrap`, `cryptography`
Dedup note: Exact duplicate of audit-177 `A9-b1-F10`, whose fix direction required fail-closed wrap handling, and archived `codex-review-181` D2. #5032 replaced birthday-bound random salts but only partially fixed this same uniqueness root.
Verified against origin/master: Present unchanged at local `origin/master` `ad959117748181dabe46b8ddc2827de670380cea`; the assigned-file diff is empty.

### F1

Title: Privacy encryption fails closed on an injected salt-seed error
Severity: Medium
Confidence: High
Gate verdict: FIXED
Evidence: `pkg/snmp/v3_rand_failclosed_test.go:118-126` (9 lines): <code>118 // Fail closed: a FRESH agent whose first seed draw fails must drop the</code><br><code>119 // response entirely.</code><br><code>120 fresh, _, _, _ := newAuthPrivAgent(t, 5, 1000)</code><br><code>121 withFailingRand(t, func() {</code><br><code>122 r := fresh.buildV3Response(1, reqFlags, fresh.v3Users["puser"], nil, 1, errNoError, 0, nil)</code><br><code>123 if r != nil {</code><br><code>124 t.Fatalf("authPriv response MUST be dropped when the salt seed fails (fail closed); "+</code><br><code>125 "got %d bytes (plaintext/zero-salt leak)", len(r))</code><br><code>126 }</code>
Trace: The injected `randRead` error makes `nextPrivSalt` return no salt; `encryptPDU` propagates the error; `buildV3Response` returns nil; and `Agent.Serve` writes only non-nil responses. No plaintext, partial ciphertext, or zero-salt packet reaches the socket.
Refutation attempt: Checked partial reads, retry behavior, seed publication order, concurrent first use, plaintext downgrade, and restoration of the package seam. The seed flag is published only after a successful read under the mutex, and race tests pass. The module pins `go 1.24.9`, where real `crypto/rand.Read` is guaranteed to return nil or irrecoverably terminate, so the test's recoverable EAGAIN/FIPS examples are synthetic operator commentary rather than another live weak-IV path.
HPC/invariant check: The one-time seed draw is serialized; steady-state encryption uses one atomic increment and no entropy syscall. Failure stays off the wire without adding per-packet locking or allocation beyond the existing eight-byte salt.
Why it matters: The fixed behavior prevents an entropy-source failure from silently weakening SNMPv3 confidentiality or downgrading an authPriv response.
Fix direction: Retain the fail-closed regression and atomic seed publication. Update comments to distinguish the injectable seam from Go 1.24 production semantics; move the seam onto an agent instance before introducing parallel tests.
Labels: `snmpv3`, `rng`, `privacy`, `fail-closed`, `cryptography`, `fixed`
Dedup note: The prior ignored-`rand.Read` root appears in `dedup-index.tsv` under `claude-review-001` and `ps-review-042`; this base contains the #5453 fail-closed correction and end-to-end regression. Prior `ps-review-037`/`ps-review-040` adjudication also records the Go 1.24 non-error contract.
Verified against origin/master: Fixed behavior and test are present unchanged at local `origin/master` `ad959117748181dabe46b8ddc2827de670380cea`; the assigned-file diff is empty.

### D3

Title: A configured SNMPv3 protocol can derive no key and lose its minimum security level
Severity: Medium
Confidence: High
Gate verdict: DUP
Evidence: `pkg/snmp/v3.go:65-69,272-275` (9 lines): <code>65 if hashFn != nil && cu.AuthPassword != "" {</code><br><code>66 u.authKey = passwordToKey(cu.AuthPassword.Reveal(), a.engineID, hashFn, hashLen)</code><br><code>67 }</code><br><code>68 if hashFn != nil && cu.PrivPassword != "" {</code><br><code>69 u.privKey = passwordToKey(cu.PrivPassword.Reveal(), a.engineID, hashFn, hashLen)</code><br><code>272 if user.authKey != nil && msgFlags&amp;msgFlagAuth == 0 {</code><br><code>273 slog.Debug("SNMPv3: request below user minimum security level (auth required), dropping",</code><br><code>274 "user", userName)</code><br><code>275 return nil</code>
Trace: Runtime users retain configured protocol strings even when an empty password or unusable authentication hash prevents key derivation. The request floor is inferred from non-nil keys rather than configured intent, so a tolerated/programmatic user can name the account with flags zero and avoid the intended auth/privacy floor. `v3_seclevel_test.go` constructs users directly with valid localized keys and therefore proves only the well-formed matrix.
Refutation attempt: Strict normal configuration and valid passwords reduce reachability, and the explicit noAuthPriv guard remains sound. They do not make the runtime object fail closed when live/reconfigured input contains a protocol declaration without derived material. No separate configured-security enum is consulted at admission.
HPC/invariant check: Security intent belongs in the immutable derived user record. Validate it at configuration/reload time and perform constant-time flag checks from an explicit minimum-level enum; no packet-path allocation or additional lock is needed.
Why it matters: An inconsistent user object can turn configured authentication/privacy intent into noAuthNoPriv access, exposing inventory and counters and reopening unauthenticated request work.
Fix direction: Reject any user whose configured protocol cannot derive its required key, and encode/enforce the configured minimum level independently of key presence. Add constructor and live `UpdateConfig` tests for empty, unknown, and privacy-without-auth combinations.
Labels: `snmpv3`, `usm`, `authentication`, `privacy`, `fail-open`, `configuration`
Dedup note: Exact residual of audit-175 `C175-HC-012` / closed #4897 and archived `codex-review-181` D3. That root already specifies protocol-or-key intent and the same admission guard/fix locus.
Verified against origin/master: Present unchanged at local `origin/master` `ad959117748181dabe46b8ddc2827de670380cea`; the assigned-file diff is empty.

### C1

Title: SNMPv3 SET regression checks notWritable status but not complete varbind and response-size contracts
Severity: Low
Confidence: High
Gate verdict: COHORT
Evidence: `pkg/snmp/v3_set_test.go:179-186` (8 lines): <code>179 pkt := buildV3AuthSetPacket(t, authPro, userName, a.engineID, authKey, oidSysContact)</code><br><code>180 resp := a.handlePacket(pkt)</code><br><code>181 if resp == nil {</code><br><code>182 t.Fatal("authenticated v3 SET produced no response (was dropped); want a notWritable response")</code><br><code>183 }</code><br><code>184 if got := decodeV3ResponseErrorStatus(t, resp); got != errNotWritable {</code><br><code>185 t.Errorf("v3 SET error-status = %d, want notWritable (%d)", got, errNotWritable)</code><br><code>186 }</code>
Trace: The fixture always sends one OID with NULL and decodes only `error-status`. Production `decodePDUFields` extracts OIDs while skipping malformed OIDs and never validates or retains value TLVs; the SET branch rebuilds every value as NULL and immediately returns, bypassing the effective manager-size/`tooBig` path. RFC 3416 requires valid ASN.1 throughout and starts SET processing from a response with the request's variable bindings, then applies message-size admission.
Refutation attempt: Every SET is rejected before mutation, `error-index=1` is correct for the first unsupported object, and managers ignore response values when error-status is nonzero. Those facts sharply reduce impact, but they do not establish wire equivalence or manager-size compliance for non-NULL, malformed, or large requests. The residuals share already-owned parser and response-sizing fixes rather than forming a new material root.
HPC/invariant check: Input remains capped at 4096 bytes, so this is bounded control-plane work. A complete single-pass varbind parser should retain validated TLVs without repeated BER scans, and the existing response-size helper should gate the result.
Why it matters: Strict managers can receive a response that does not preserve the request varbinds, and a small advertised `msgMaxSize` can be exceeded, degrading SET diagnostics and interoperability without enabling writes.
Fix direction: Parse every varbind completely and fail closed on malformed syntax; preserve the validated request varbind list for error responses; apply effective-size/`tooBig` handling; extend the test to non-NULL values, malformed value TLVs, and a small `msgMaxSize`.
Labels: `snmpv3`, `set`, `ber`, `wire-protocol`, `message-size`, `test-gap`
Dedup note: The incomplete OID-only decoder is the `codex-review-179` C179-126 malformed-varbind cohort under open GH#5523. Response admission is the already indexed `codex-review-175`/#4918 sizing root. This test gap is a cohort of those roots, not a new finding.
Verified against origin/master: Present unchanged at local `origin/master` `ad959117748181dabe46b8ddc2827de670380cea`; the assigned-file diff is empty.

### C2

Title: Timeliness tests identify report OIDs but not authoritative-engine identity or real USM counter values
Severity: Low
Confidence: High
Gate verdict: COHORT
Evidence: `pkg/snmp/v3_timeliness_test.go:99-106` (8 lines): <code>99 func classifyV3Response(t *testing.T, resp []byte) string {</code><br><code>100 t.Helper()</code><br><code>101 if resp == nil {</code><br><code>102 return "nil"</code><br><code>103 }</code><br><code>104 if bytes.Contains(resp, berEncodeOID(usmStatsNotInTimeWindows)) {</code><br><code>105 return "report"</code><br><code>106 }</code>
Trace: Timeliness fixtures always use the agent's engine ID and classify reports by raw OID presence. Production decodes but discards `reqEngineID`, and both discovery and timeliness reports encode Counter32(0) rather than incremented `usmStatsUnknownEngineIDs`/`usmStatsNotInTimeWindows` values. The core +/-150-second and boots logic is independent and passes.
Refutation attempt: HMAC localization normally prevents a user from authenticating against a different engine's key, and report counters do not decide request admission. A valid local key can still accompany a mismatched authoritative field, while repeated report values remain false security telemetry. These are known low-materiality identity/observability roots; neither invalidates the tested rejection behavior or creates a new root.
HPC/invariant check: Compare the bounded engine ID before timeliness processing and maintain per-agent atomic Counter32 values with defined wrap. Both are O(1), require no per-request allocation, and do not alter socket/goroutine ownership.
Why it matters: Managers cannot trust report values for replay/identity diagnosis, and the agent accepts an internally inconsistent authoritative-engine field, reducing SNMPv3 wire fidelity and operator truth.
Fix direction: Validate the incoming authoritative EngineID against the local engine, increment the correct USM statistic on each report condition, encode its current Counter32 value, and structurally decode OID/value assertions in tests.
Labels: `snmpv3`, `usm`, `timeliness`, `engine-id`, `counters`, `observability`, `test-gap`
Dedup note: Exact known `codex-review-179` C179-125 and C179-128 items in open GH#5523. Closed #2610 owns the underlying timeliness/boots implementation; this base keeps that fix while the identity/counter cohort remains.

## Findings

### A10-M1 - File-backed console load is unbounded before the config ceiling

`pkg/cli/cli_config.go` reads an operator-selected path with `os.ReadFile`, converts the complete byte slice to a string, and only then invokes `configstore`, whose verified 16 MiB ceiling rejects the already-materialized payload. A very large regular file can spike the embedded xpfd heap, while a FIFO or endless special file can block indefinitely or allocate until failure. The safe implementation must bound the read itself and reject unsupported file types. The canonical MATERIAL record is ledger item 101.

### A10-C1 - Mutating CLI grammar has residual ignored operands

The remote DDNS action, embedded `configure`, embedded DHCP renew, and embedded DDNS action accept trailing or unknown operands while executing a valid prefix. Ownership and authorization gates remain intact, so this is low materiality, but automation gets a successful result for a command other than the exact command written. Require exact arity at each mutation boundary. Canonical COHORT records are ledger items 27, 103, 111, and 118.

### Dedup and retirement dispositions

- The local top-20 session implementation is an exact duplicate of `codex-review-179.md` and was not promoted.
- Environment-derived CLI identity is GH#6701, host-inbound union semantics are GH#6515, and the kernel-journal arm gap is GH#6632.
- Raw terminal output, remote pipe buffering, NAT display error suppression, and BGP selector injection map to their indexed issues.
- `xpf_helpers.h`, `xpf_nat.h`, and `xpf_trace.h` have no live retained-shim execution consumer. Their execution-only observations are STALE under PR #1476 retirement policy.

- Title: A10-b1-101 cli_config.go review; Severity: Medium; Confidence: High; Gate verdict: MATERIAL; Evidence: pkg/cli/cli_config.go:140-147 (8-line file-load path calls os.ReadFile on an operator-supplied path before any size or file-type bound); Trace: High/Medium MATERIAL: configure load selects args[1], os.ReadFile materializes the whole regular or special file, string conversion retains it, and only then Store.LoadOverride or LoadMerge reaches MaxConfigSize; Refutation attempt: High/Critical MATERIAL: focused configstore tests confirm the 16 MiB rejection but it runs after allocation, no fstat regular-file gate or LimitReader exists, origin/master is identical, and an intentional dev-zero OOM reproduction was not run because it would be destructive; HPC/invariant check: Bounded control-plane memory and termination must hold before allocation, this invariant is violated inside the embedded xpfd process; Why it matters: A config-capable operator mistake or hostile path such as a huge file, FIFO, or endless device can block the CLI or drive xpfd to OOM before the documented ceiling can reject it; Fix direction: Open the file, reject unsupported file types, enforce MaxConfigSize from fstat when available, read through LimitReader at MaxConfigSize plus one, reject overflow, and add large-file plus blocking-reader seam tests; Labels: A10-b1,MATERIAL,cli,config,resource-exhaustion; Dedup note: No exact match in dedup-index or issue-history after load override, ReadFile, config-size, OOM, special-file, FIFO, and dev-zero searches, GH#6548 is a distinct terminal Ctrl-C partial-paste defect in the same function; Verified against origin/master: yes, origin/master and review HEAD are ad959117748181dabe46b8ddc2827de670380cea.

The requested stale-path rule was applied. The orientation identifies Go plus Rust AF_XDP userspace as live and the legacy eBPF forwarding and DPDK implementations as retired. No BPF header, BPF program, DPDK source, command script, or shell script is in this batch. Legacy eBPF/DPDK implementer comments and non-userspace fallback concerns in the assigned CLI runtime interface are therefore STALE unless a live implementer is proven; none was.

## Triage

| ID | Verdict | Severity | Primary file(s) | Result |

| D5 | DUP | Medium | `pkg/cli/session_filter.go` | Session interface filtering lacks true ingress identity and falls back to zone membership; GH#4983. |
| D6 | DUP | Medium | `pkg/cli/cli_show_routing.go` | Spaces in peer-supplied IS-IS System ID shift columns; GH#6590. |
| D7 | DUP | Medium | `pkg/cli/show_services_ddns.go` (secondary) | Secret-bearing provider/update URLs render cleartext; GH#6703. |

| C2 | COHORT | Low | `pkg/cli/show_services_dhcp.go` | Relay show omits the effective default 100 pps rate and the enforced `trust-option-82` security posture. |
| C3 | COHORT | Low | `pkg/cli/cli_show_security_objects.go` | ALG show labels unimplemented ALGs as enabled instead of unsupported/not available. |
| C4 | COHORT | Low | `pkg/ddns/backend_rfc2136.go` | Config validates TTL >=1 but no uint32 maximum; RFC 2136 narrows `int` to `uint32`. |
| C5 | COHORT | Low | `pkg/ddns/checkip.go` | URL validation checks `parsed.Host`, accepting a port-only authority such as `http://:8080`. |

### Trace

1. The live daemon supplies `cfg.ResolveKernelIfName` on each Surface A reconcile. The manager refreshes that resolver before any provider/check-IP lookup.

```go

	// FAIL CLOSED (#2971, mirroring the DHCP-lease #2650 gate): the ownership
	// state could not be loaded, so we cannot prove which router records this
	// node published. Acting now is unsafe -- a publish could overwrite a
```

2. The assigned cache code resolves the new bind first, but derives its lookup key only from raw configured leaves. On a hit, the new `bindConfig` is discarded.

```go
func bindCacheKey(p *config.DDNSProvider) string {
	if p == nil {
		return ""
	}
	// NUL-separated so distinct field boundaries cannot collide (an interface
	// named "a" + VRF "b" must not key the same as interface "a\x00b").
	return p.SourceAddress + "\x00" + p.DestinationInterface + "\x00" + p.RoutingInstance
}
```

3. The transport constructed on the first miss captures that first resolved `bindConfig` in `DialContext`, and its dialer captures `bindDevice` for `SO_BINDTODEVICE`.

```go
	if d := b.dialer(httpDialTimeout); d != nil {
		// #5327: pin the dial to the configured source-address family via a
		// DialContext wrapper (constrainDialNetwork) so Happy-Eyeballs cannot pick
		// the other family and skip the source bind -- which would egress the update
		// from a kernel-chosen source on the wrong WAN. A device-only bind (no
		// source-address) passes the network through unchanged.
		tr.DialContext = b.boundDialContext(d)
	}
	return &http.Client{
```

4. The called config contract permits the same Junos reference to resolve differently when its reth member, VLAN ID, tunnel mapping, or bridge mapping changes. For example, the unit VLAN ID directly changes the resulting kernel device.

```go

				return unit.Tunnel.Name
			}
			kernelBase := LinuxIfName(c.ResolveReth(base))
			if unit.VlanID > 0 {

```

5. Reap does not repair the stale entry: its live set also uses `bindCacheKey` on raw provider leaves, so the unchanged raw key remains live.

```go
		live := make(map[string]struct{}, len(scopes)+len(catalog)+1)
		live[""] = struct{}{} // unbound default (nil provider / fail-open client)
		for _, sc := range scopes {
			live[bindCacheKey(sc.Provider)] = struct{}{}
		}
		for _, p := range catalog {
			live[bindCacheKey(p)] = struct{}{}
		}
		m.httpClients.reap(live)
```

6. Both recurring HTTP updates and external check-IP probes use this cache. The bug is therefore on the live Surface A path, not an eBPF/DPDK-only path.

### Refutation Attempt

- Raw-leaf invalidation was checked: it works when a source/interface/VRF leaf changes, but that is not the candidate. The same leaf can resolve to a different device.
- Per-pass backend reconstruction was checked: backend objects are rebuilt, but they deliberately reuse this cached `*http.Client` and transport.
- Reap was checked: it preserves the stale entry because its live identity is the same raw key.
- Bind failure handling was checked: malformed source addresses fail closed, but a successful new resolution is computed and then ignored on the cache hit.
- Device validation was checked: an old removed device eventually causes dial errors, which avoids unbound fallback but leaves DDNS broken indefinitely. If the old device remains, traffic can use the wrong WAN.
- A review-only Go overlay test changed resolver output from `ge-0-0-0.50` to `ge-7-0-0.50` while keeping `DestinationInterface="reth0.50"`. It failed because both calls returned the same client.
- Origin/master was checked and is byte-identical to the immutable base for all assigned files.

## Domain Conclusions

- DHCPv4/v6 and relay: live relay anti-spoofing, outstanding-request binding, rate limiting, unknown-server rejection, FORCERENEW refusal, and v4/v6 lease display contracts were followed. No new material protocol defect survived. C1/C2 are display cohorts.
- DDNS ownership: Cloudflare/Route53/RFC2136 exact-value deletes, `PrevAddr` replacement, DHCID ownership, cross-surface co-ownership, durable write-ahead intent, backend fingerprints, and PTR-pending semantics were checked. D1-D3 remain known issues; M1 is independent of record ownership.
- Policy simulator: CLI uses the shared matcher with feed overlay, scheduler state, ICMP fields, source port, strict family, host-inbound interface, content-rejection, and non-first-fragment state. The prior fragment gap is fixed.
- CLI/show and commands: parser widening, RBAC, external command argv, output sanitization, counter-read errors, iterator errors, nil-tolerant paths, deterministic presentation, and effective-vs-configured claims were checked. No new material command-injection or permission bypass survived.
- Concurrency/resources/integer/performance: DDNS provider I/O unlock behavior, cache locking/reaping, monitor goroutine shutdown, response/body caps, pagination, TTL narrowing, session walks, and command count bounds were checked. The race suite passed; M1 is a cache-identity invariant failure, not a data race.
- vSRX completeness: unsupported/inert behavior was checked against show claims. C3 is retained as an observability cohort; no new material enforcement parity defect was found in assigned files.
- Retained BPF/tooling: no BPF headers/tooling are assigned. Non-userspace runtime fallback observations were marked STALE under the campaign rule.

## Material findings

### A10-b3-M1

Title: Cross-surface DDNS co-ownership treats equal RR data at different authorities as one wire resource
Severity: Medium
Confidence: High
Gate verdict: MATERIAL
Evidence: `pkg/ddns/state.go:342` (5 lines) and `pkg/ddns/surface_a.go:1722` (7 lines)

```go
type WireRRClaim struct {
	FQDN        string // canonical form (dnsCanonicalFQDN)
	ForwardType string // "A" | "AAAA"
	Rdata       string // textual published address (the rdata)
}
```

```go
	want := wireRRClaim(fqdn, forwardType, rdata)
	for _, c := range m.leaseCoowners() {
		if c == want {
			return true
		}
	}
	return false
```

Trace: Medium MATERIAL: `daemon_run_bringup.go:96-103` cross-wires the two managers; each advertises only `{canonical FQDN, RR type, rdata}`. A Surface A teardown that matches an unrelated Surface B authority enters `surface_a.go:1538-1563`, re-UPSERTs through A's backend, retains the claim, and can defer forever (`:1597-1611`). The converse lease teardown suppresses its delete at `manager.go:1080-1107`. Equal data in split DNS views, routing instances, or distinct update servers is therefore mistaken for shared ownership.
Refutation attempt: The review checked whether endpoint identity is globally fixed or implicitly shared. It is not: Surface A supports RFC 2136 and HTTP providers, Surface B resolves RFC 2136, both support endpoint/routing identity, and both already compute durable backend fingerprints (`surface_a.go:1779-1813`, `manager.go:1768-1800`). Those fingerprints are omitted from `WireRRClaim`. Surface A's sibling-family guard explicitly requires the same provider because a different provider is a different authority (`surface_a.go:1731-1740`).
HPC/invariant check: The ownership invariant must be keyed by the actual mutable wire resource, including canonical authority/view identity. Atomic snapshot reads and lock ordering remain sound; the defect is semantic key under-specification, not a race.
Why it matters: Removing one binding can preserve or re-publish stale DNS at the wrong authority. After address reuse, clients in that view can be directed to a different host, and ownership can remain stuck until the unrelated lease disappears.
Fix direction: Add a credential-free, normalized authority/view identifier to cross-surface claims and suppress only when both surfaces target the same resource. Define a cross-surface canonical fingerprint because the current `fp1-` and `fpb1-` encodings are not directly comparable. Add same-tuple/different-authority negative tests and same-authority positive tests.
Labels: `ddns`, `ownership`, `split-horizon`, `routing-instance`, `correctness`
Dedup note: No exact `WireRRClaim` authority/view identity owner was found in `dedup-index.tsv` or `docs/issues/issue-history.md`. This is distinct from provider-transition issues `#3735`/`#5814` and the cross-surface claim implementation `#5748`/`#6015`: those preserve endpoint transitions or coordinate deletion, but do not put endpoint identity in cross-surface equality.
Verified against origin/master: Yes; worktree HEAD and `origin/master` were both `ad959117748181dabe46b8ddc2827de670380cea`.

### A10-b3-M2

Title: Malformed or zero-length RFC 3442 option presence falls through to the forbidden Router option
Severity: Medium
Confidence: High
Gate verdict: MATERIAL
Evidence: `pkg/dhcp/dhcpv4.go:410` (9 lines)

```go
	libRoutes := ack.ClasslessStaticRoute() // option 121
	if len(libRoutes) == 0 {
		// Legacy option 249 (Microsoft), identical RFC 3442 encoding.
		if raw := ack.Options.Get(dhcpv4.GenericOptionCode(249)); len(raw) > 0 {
			var r dhcpv4.Routes
			if err := r.FromBytes(raw); err == nil {
				libRoutes = r
			}
		}
```

Trace: Medium MATERIAL: `leaseFromACKv4` calls `classlessStaticRoutes`; the dependency's `ClasslessStaticRoute` returns `nil` both when option 121 is absent and when `Routes.FromBytes` fails (`dhcpv4.go:608-617`). This helper then treats zero decoded routes as `present=false` at `:420-421`; the caller enters `:371-378` and installs option 3. Thus malformed/empty 121, or malformed/empty 249 when 121 is absent, is semantically converted into absence.
Refutation attempt: The dependency was inspected rather than inferred. Its `Options.Has` method (`options.go:73-76`) distinguishes key presence, while `ClasslessStaticRoute` intentionally collapses decode errors to nil. Existing tests cover valid 121, valid 249, and option-3-only ACKs, but no empty or malformed classless option. RFC 3442 requires Router-option suppression when the classless-route option is supplied; see [RFC 3442](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3442).
HPC/invariant check: Presence and decoded cardinality are separate domains. `len(decoded)==0` cannot encode absent, present-empty, and present-malformed without violating the precedence invariant.
Why it matters: A malformed ACK can silently install the option-3 default route that the classless option was meant to supersede, causing wrong-path routing or loss on DHCP uplinks.
Fix direction: Check `ack.Options.Has(OptionClasslessStaticRoute)` and generic 249 presence before decode, preserving 121 precedence over 249. Reject the ACK on malformed data, or at minimum mark the classless option present and suppress option 3 while surfacing the parse failure. Add zero-length, truncated-prefix, truncated-gateway, and 121-malformed-plus-valid-249 tests.
Labels: `dhcpv4`, `rfc3442`, `fail-open`, `routing`, `vsrx-parity`
Dedup note: Issue-history `#4118` owns initial option 121/249 support only. No malformed/presence-collapse owner was found. A prior negative review asserted malformed input still returned `present=true`; direct dependency inspection refutes that assertion.
Verified against origin/master: Yes; worktree HEAD and `origin/master` were both `ad959117748181dabe46b8ddc2827de670380cea`.

### A10-b3-M3

Title: Kea LFC finish file is ignored as a zero-content marker, allowing a trusted-empty destructive lease view
Severity: High
Confidence: High
Gate verdict: MATERIAL
Evidence: `pkg/dhcpserver/lease_lfc.go:24` (9 lines) and `pkg/dhcpserver/ddns_leases.go:178` (8 lines)

```go
//	<f>.2          PREVIOUS -- the COMPACTED result of the last COMPLETED cleanup
//	                          (one row per active lease). Present once any LFC
//	                          has run.
//	<f>.output     kea-lfc's temporary compaction output.
//	<f>.completed  kea-lfc's finish marker.
//	<f>.pid        kea-lfc's pid file.
//
// The .output/.completed/.pid files hold no lease union we must read and are
// ignored.
```

```go
func parseActiveLeases(path string, family int, now time.Time) ([]ddnsLease, error) {
	acc := newDDNSLeaseAccum()
	for _, f := range keaLFCLeaseFilePaths(path) {
		if err := parseActiveLeasesFileInto(f, family, now, acc); err != nil {
			return nil, err
		}
	}
	out := make([]ddnsLease, 0, len(acc.order))
```

Trace: High MATERIAL: Kea moves the current memfile to input and starts a fresh current append log. LFC writes the compacted generation to output, moves it to the finish file, deletes previous and input, then moves finish to previous. During the post-delete/pre-final-rename interval, and after a crash there, `.completed` is the complete baseline while the assigned reader opens only `.2`, `.1`, and current (`lease_lfc.go:69-80`). A header-only current then validates and returns trusted-empty (`ddns_leases.go:193-198`); `keaLeaseParser` feeds that set directly to DDNS, whose pass 1 deletes every owned record absent from desired state (`manager.go:1290-1304`).
Refutation attempt: This was checked against the project-targeted Kea 3.0.x schema and the official [Kea 3.0 LFC documentation](https://kea.readthedocs.io/en/kea-3.0.0/arm/lfc.html). Kea documents `finish` as containing the completed output and retaining it until the other generation files are deleted. The live socket does not mitigate DDNS: display and HA sync can prefer `lease_cmds`, but `keaLeaseParser` calls the memfile parser directly (`ddns.go:45-58`). `lease_source_5938_test.go:172-207` creates an empty `.completed` fixture and therefore pins the incorrect assumption rather than the real state.
HPC/invariant check: LFC files form a generation protocol. Last-row-wins replay is valid only after selecting a complete generation; treating suffixes as an unordered union omits the sole committed baseline during a legal transition.
Why it matters: A routine cleanup or crash can make active leases disappear from the authoritative DDNS input and trigger bulk A/AAAA/PTR withdrawal. Display and memfile fallback can also under-report leases during the same phase.
Fix direction: Implement generation-aware LFC snapshot selection that recognizes `.completed` as the finished compacted generation and retries around unstable rotations. Prefer the live Kea socket for destructive DDNS when available; if generation completeness cannot be proven, return an untrusted error rather than trusted-empty. Add fixtures with populated `.completed`, absent `.1/.2`, and header-only current, including crash points before the final rename.
Labels: `dhcpserver`, `kea`, `lfc`, `ddns`, `data-loss`, `fail-open`
Dedup note: No `.completed`/finish-file ownership defect was found in `dedup-index.tsv` or `docs/issues/issue-history.md`. This is a residual of `#5796/#5938`, whose local invariant describes the finish file incorrectly.
Verified against origin/master: Yes; worktree HEAD and `origin/master` were both `ad959117748181dabe46b8ddc2827de670380cea`.

```go
	if err := cl.ResetFailover(); err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("rolling: reset failover (rejoin election): %w", err)
	}
	logf("rolling: local node rejoined election; cut complete for this node")
	return nil
```

Trace: N/A (DUP): Assigned `cluster_cli.go:580-624` implements fail-closed `LocalRejoinComplete`, but the rolling caller never invokes it after `ResetFailover`.
Refutation attempt: Pre-reset `SyncEstablished` proves peer transport health, not that all local RG weights left ForceSecondary after reset.
HPC/invariant check: Command acceptance is treated as state convergence without a read-after-write fence.
Why it matters: An orchestrator can advance to the peer while this node is still demoted, creating a no-primary interval.
Fix direction: Poll `LocalRejoinComplete` to the rejoin deadline before reporting cut completion or advancing.
Labels: `upgrade`, `ha`, `rejoin`, `readback`
Dedup note: Exact current owner `GH#6557` in `dedup-index.tsv`; the defect is in the narrowly followed caller, while assigned `cluster_cli.go` provides the correct predicate.
Verified against origin/master: Yes; unchanged at `ad959117748181dabe46b8ddc2827de670380cea`.

### A10-b3-N1

Title: DHCP relay L2 length narrowing is unreachable from the live UDPv4 reply path
Severity: Low (candidate severity)
Confidence: High
Gate verdict: NEG
Evidence: `pkg/dhcprelay/l2send_linux.go:164` (8 lines)

```go
func buildL2Reply(dstMAC, srcMAC net.HardwareAddr, srcIP, dstIP net.IP,
	payload []byte) []byte {
	udpLen := udpHeaderLen + len(payload)
	totalLen := ipv4HeaderLen + udpLen
	frame := make([]byte, ethHeaderLen+totalLen)

	// --- Ethernet header (14 bytes) ---
	copy(frame[0:6], dstMAC)
```

Trace: N/A (NEG): The only production caller passes a DHCP packet parsed from a `udp4` datagram and reserialized after removing Option 82. IPv4 UDP payload is bounded at 65,507 bytes, yielding `udpLen<=65,515` and `totalLen<=65,535`; parse requires the End option, and reserialization does not add net payload beyond the input.
Refutation attempt: The earlier review inferred a 65,535-byte payload from buffer size. That is the IP packet bound, not the UDP payload bound. MTU checking further narrows normal execution.
HPC/invariant check: The `uint16` conversions are in-range on the live call domain. The unexported helper itself accepts arbitrary slices, but no retained caller supplies one outside that domain.
Why it matters: Avoids carrying forward an integer-truncation report with no reachable production input.
Fix direction: Optional assertion for defense in depth; no live defect.
Labels: `dhcprelay`, `integer-domain`, `negative`
Dedup note: Refutes prior `ps-review-038-A10_go_services_cli_deploy-b2.md` F-02 / dedup-index row 597 rather than re-reporting it.
Verified against origin/master: Yes; caller and dependency serialization were checked at `ad959117748181dabe46b8ddc2827de670380cea`.

## Material findings

Title: M1 - BootNext can remain armed while all durable software gates classify the node as unarmed
Severity: High
Confidence: High
Gate verdict: MATERIAL
Evidence: pkg/upgrade/kernel_run.go:374 (8 lines)
```go
374 // Positively confirm the firmware accepted the one-shot BEFORE recording the
375 // verified-ARMED journal. If the readback disagrees (firmware silently
376 // dropped / partial-wrote the variable), do NOT advance to ARMED - stay
377 // ARMING and surface the error so no false-ARMED journal is persisted.
378 got, err = sys.GetBootNext()
379 if err != nil {
380     return fmt.Errorf("kernel-upgrade arm: read back BootNext (staying ARMING): %w", err)
381 }
```
Trace: `Arm` durably writes ARMING, `SetBootNext` succeeds, then readback, arm-record creation, or the final ARMED journal write fails. The firmware one-shot may still name the candidate, but `IsArmed` returns false for ARMING (`kernel_run.go:696-701`), `Promote` skips states below ARMED (`kernel_run.go:421-430`), and `xpf-kernel-promote` tests for exact `"state":"ARMED"`. On a later reboot the candidate can therefore boot as an ordinary image, with no promotion gate and no unconditional HA election hold. The shipped fake makes the mismatch concrete: `SetBootNext` stores `f.bootNext` at `kernel_test.go:123-126`; the injected `GetBootNext` error returns without clearing it at `:132-140`; `kernel_arm_two_phase_5847_test.go:48-54` then requires ARMING and `IsArmed == false`.
Refutation attempt: A readback mismatch can mean firmware dropped the write, but a readback error cannot prove that, and failures after a successful readback (`recordPromoteBinary` or `ktransition(ARMED)`) definitely occur after BootNext is set. There is no compensating BootNext clear/readback on any post-write error. Treating ARMING as armed everywhere would recreate the earlier false-armed availability failure when `SetBootNext` really did fail, so the current two-state model cannot represent "possibly armed" safely. Candidate survives.
HPC/invariant check: This is a crash-consistency/publish-order violation: external NVRAM state becomes effective before durable software state can authorize and contain it. It is cold-path work; the fix needs no dataplane allocation or hot-path branch.
Why it matters: A transient efivarfs read or journal/record write failure can turn a deliberately gated kernel trial into an ungated HA-eligible boot. A defective candidate may preempt or forward before verification, defeating the A/B rollback contract.
Fix direction: Persist a distinct fail-closed `ARMED_UNKNOWN`/possibly-armed intent with complete candidate and verifier identity before touching NVRAM. On every post-`SetBootNext` failure, clear BootNext and positively confirm the clear; if that cannot be proved, retain the fail-closed state and election hold. At boot, resolve the state from BootCurrent: gate/promote when the candidate actually booted, or clear it only after known-good is proved. Add crash/error tests after SetBootNext, readback, arm-record write, and ARMED journal fsync.
Labels: upgrade, kernel, UEFI, crash-consistency, HA, fail-open, vSRX-completeness
Dedup note: Searched `KernelStateArming`, `BootNext ARMING`, `recordPromoteBinary`, `unconfirmed BootNext`, `post-write BootNext`, and `5847` in `docs/issues/issue-history.md` and `dedup-index.tsv`; no matching issue/index entry. This is the inverse residual of the source's #5847 false-ARMED fix, not that defect repeated.
Verified against origin/master: Yes - reviewed commit and local `origin/master` are byte-identical at `ad959117748181dabe46b8ddc2827de670380cea`.

Title: M2 - Image-roll recreation erases the drain before the new node's authenticated identity is validated
Severity: High
Confidence: High
Gate verdict: MATERIAL
Evidence: scripts/deploy/xpf-deploy.py:2327 (9 lines)
```python
2327 # it. The recreate wipes /var/lib on the node, so the node's own
2328 # lease is gone afterwards; from here the still-up PEER's lease is
2329 # the sole reservation (renewed every poll tick below), which is
2330 # what actually blocks a successor from acquiring both leases.
2331 _fence_before_mutate(runner, backend, [(node, nid), (peer, nid)],
2332                      holder, lease_ttl, f"image-recreate {node}")
2333 _recreate_node_from_image(runner, backend, node, args)
2334
2335 # 3. poll until the node is back AS THE EXPECTED NODE ON THE NEW
```
Trace: The old daemon's `ForceSecondary` drain is in-memory (`pkg/cluster/failover.go:140-167`). Recreation destroys that process and `/var/lib`; the fresh image has neither the manual-failover state nor the old kernel-upgrade journal that drives `kernelUpgradeHold`. The hook launches and applies day-0, allowing xpfd to join heartbeat/election before the driver first polls `xpf-version` and `/etc/xpf/node-id` at `xpf-deploy.py:2335-2384`. A stale but cluster-authentic image with the expected node ID can complete startup sync and, in supported `preempt` configurations, take primary immediately (`pkg/cluster/election.go:172-182`). The driver notices only afterward and can leave it participating for the entire boot deadline.
Refutation attempt: Non-preempt configurations usually preserve the incumbent, but preempt is a supported contract and can be immediate. Startup sync hold delays preemption until sync readiness; it does not bind the boot to the signed manifest version or orchestrator token. The kernel candidate hold is irrelevant on a fresh image, and the peer-side lease prevents a second orchestrator but does not suppress the new node's local election. Existing identity tests prove eventual rejection, not absence of forwarding before rejection. Candidate survives.
HPC/invariant check: Identity/configuration must be validated before publishing forwarding ownership. This is a cold control-plane sequencing defect; no dataplane cost is needed beyond a generalized startup election hold.
Why it matters: A stale alias, wrong build, or partially restored image can become primary and carry traffic before the orchestrator authenticates what came back, exposing incompatible protocol/dataplane behavior and undermining never-both-down/session-preservation guarantees.
Fix direction: Carry an authenticated image-roll quarantine token in the fresh day-0/config-drive state and set a generalized upgrade election hold before the first election. Release it only through an owner-bound API after exact signed image version, node ID, config generation, and session-sync readiness are confirmed. Add a preempt-enabled end-to-end test proving zero primary/forwarding eligibility before release.
Labels: deploy, image-roll, HA, election, preempt, identity, fail-open, vSRX-completeness
Dedup note: Searched `cmd_image_roll`, `image-roll election`, `recreated node eligible`, `fresh image hold`, `identity before election`, `recreate wipes drain`, and `5075` in issue history and the dedup index; no matching entry. #5075 covers eventual wrong-image acceptance, while this finding is the pre-validation election window that remains after that fix.
Verified against origin/master: Yes - identical base and `origin/master`.

Title: M3 - An indeterminate qcow2 backing-file probe is treated as proof that no dependent overlay exists
Severity: High
Confidence: High
Gate verdict: MATERIAL
Evidence: scripts/deploy/xpf-deploy.py:734 (9 lines)
```python
734 except FileNotFoundError:
735     return None
736 if r.returncode != 0:
737     return None
738 try:
739     info = json.loads(r.stdout)
740 except (ValueError, TypeError):
741     return None
742 bf = info.get("full-backing-filename") or info.get("backing-filename")
```
Trace: `_dependent_overlays` interprets every `None` as "not backed by this golden" and returns an empty set; `_install_libvirt_golden` then overwrites the shared golden. If qemu-img is removed, temporarily broken, denied one sibling, or emits malformed output after overlays were created earlier, every dependency becomes invisible. Focused reproduction with an existing golden and sibling overlay plus `FileNotFoundError("qemu-img")` completed the install and printed `unknown_probe_golden_bytes= NEW-GOLDEN`.
Refutation attempt: The comment claims qemu-img absence means this tool never created an overlay, but absence at replacement time says nothing about its availability during an earlier deploy or about overlays made by another tool. A nonzero probe can likewise be image-specific corruption/permission failure, not "no backing". Existing tests inject only known backing or explicit `None`; none exercise unknown/error. Candidate survives.
HPC/invariant check: The immutable backing store owns every overlay's unresolved blocks. Unknown ownership must fail closed before publishing new bytes. This host-side cold path has no throughput concern.
Why it matters: Replacing bytes beneath one or both HA qcow2 overlays can silently corrupt guest filesystems and both nodes' identity/configuration state in one operation.
Fix direction: Return a tri-state result (`NO_BACKING`, resolved path, `UNKNOWN/error`). Abort replacement on any unknown sibling or unreadable image directory, with the exact qemu-img error. Require a complete successful scan before concluding no dependencies. Add absent-tool, nonzero, malformed JSON, unreadable-directory, and per-file permission tests.

Title: M4 - Golden replacement is an unlocked check-then-in-place-copy and races overlay creation or interruption
Severity: High
Confidence: High
Gate verdict: MATERIAL
Evidence: scripts/deploy/xpf-deploy.py:790 and scripts/deploy/xpf-deploy.py:805 (8 source lines)
```python
790 golden = libvirt_golden_path(image)
791 if os.path.isfile(golden):
792     deps = _dependent_overlays(golden)
793     if deps:
805 print(f"==> installing verified qcow2 -> {golden} (libvirt golden)")
806 try:
807     os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(golden), exist_ok=True)
808     shutil.copyfile(srcq, golden)
```
Trace: No common lock spans `_install_libvirt_golden` and `libvirt_disk`'s `qemu-img create -b <golden>` at `xpf-deploy.py:835-847`. A deploy can create a new dependent after the installer's scan and before `copyfile`; the installer then truncates and rewrites the backing in place. Independently, process death, ENOSPC, or a failed copy leaves the existing golden partially overwritten. A synchronized focused reproduction created an overlay after the scan barrier and observed `race_overlay_created=True`, `race_golden_bytes=NEW-GOLDEN`, with no error.
Refutation attempt: Domain-name preflight does not serialize a concurrent `fetch --install-libvirt`, another VM name, or another tool. Atomic artifact verification protects source bytes but not destination publication. The lease flocks are remote HA-roll locks and do not guard `/var/lib/libvirt/images`. Existing disk tests are serial and assert only the preexisting-dependent case. Candidate survives.
HPC/invariant check: Dependency discovery and backing publication form one ownership transaction. The current check/use split violates that invariant; a host-local lock and atomic rename are cold-path operations.
Why it matters: A normal concurrent deploy/fetch or interrupted copy can corrupt every VM backed by the golden, commonly both HA nodes, or leave future launches on a truncated image.
Fix direction: Use a host-wide/per-golden flock shared by install, overlay create, and relevant destroy operations. Stage verified bytes to a same-filesystem private temporary file, fsync it, acquire the lock, rescan all siblings fail-closed, then atomically rename and fsync the directory. Never copy over the live golden inode in place.
Labels: deploy, libvirt, qcow2, TOCTOU, concurrency, atomicity, data-corruption
Dedup note: Searched `golden TOCTOU`, `golden lock`, `overlay created after scan`, `concurrent golden`, `copyfile golden`, `partial golden`, and `5043`; no matching issue/index entry. This is distinct from both the positive-dependency guard and source artifact verification TOCTOU.
Verified against origin/master: Yes - identical base and `origin/master`.

Title: M5 - Lease renewal stops during the arbitrary destructive hook and other unbounded remote mutations
Severity: High
Confidence: High
Gate verdict: MATERIAL
Evidence: scripts/deploy/xpf-deploy.py:2436 (10 lines)
```python
2436 hook = args.recreate_hook
2437 if not hook:
2438     die(f"image-roll needs --recreate-hook <script> to recreate {node} from "
2439         f"the new image (the backend-specific destroy+launch+day-0 step). "
2440         f"This keeps the never-both-down sequencing here while the recreate "
2441         f"mechanics stay environment-specific.")
2442 env = dict(os.environ, XPF_ROLL_NODE=node, XPF_ROLL_BACKEND=backend)
2443 print(f"   recreating {node} via {hook}...")
2444 r = subprocess.run([hook, node], env=env)
2445 if r.returncode != 0:
```
Trace: The driver renews both leases once immediately before calling the hook (`:2323-2333`), then performs no keepalive until the hook returns. `subprocess.run` has no timeout; the same unbounded wrapper is used for remote drain/arm commands (`:1421-1433`). If the operation exceeds TTL, successor B can reclaim both serialized lease files while predecessor A's hook/remote command is still mutating. A later fence can stop A's next step, but cannot undo the concurrent destructive work already underway. `_renew_lease` also checks holder identity but not whether its own deadline already elapsed, so absent a successor it silently revives an expired lease after the call.
Refutation attempt: `docs/in-place-upgrade.md:1319-1324` documents sizing TTL above one uninterruptible hook and the default 1800 seconds is generous for ordinary VM launch. That is not a fencing guarantee for an arbitrary bare-metal hook, hung hypervisor, package install, or caller-selected positive TTL, and it contradicts the preceding claim that renewal never elapses while the driver is live. Existing tests advance time only in poll loops or inject loss at phase boundaries; none block inside the mutation while a successor reclaims. Candidate survives.
HPC/invariant check: Ownership must remain continuously valid for the complete side effect, not merely at call entry and exit. A background lease heartbeat is cold-path; a server-checked fencing token is needed to contain orphaned remote work.
Why it matters: Two live orchestrators can destroy/relaunch or drain/reboot the same HA pair concurrently, causing no-primary outages, unintended dual mutation, or irrecoverable half-roll state despite the advertised cross-orchestrator mutex.
Fix direction: Maintain an independent heartbeat for the load-bearing peer lease for the entire critical subprocess lifetime, bound local/SSH/incus execution, and pass a monotonically fenced roll token into hooks and remote mutations so the target verifies ownership immediately before each destructive step. On heartbeat uncertainty, terminate/cancel and refuse subsequent mutation. Test a blocked hook past TTL with a real successor acquisition.
Labels: deploy, HA, lease, fencing, concurrency, timeout, availability
Dedup note: Searched `_keepalive_leases`, `_fence_before_mutate`, `lease expire blocking hook`, `renew during recreate`, `hook outlast TTL`, `5816`, and `5545`; no matching issue/index record. #5816's boundary-renewal fix is the predecessor; this finding is the still-uncovered in-call interval.
Verified against origin/master: Yes - identical base and `origin/master`.

Title: M6 - Staged-generation GC discards current-gen resolution errors and proceeds to destructive deletion
Severity: Medium
Confidence: High
Gate verdict: MATERIAL
Evidence: pkg/upgrade/stagedgen/stagedgen.go:320 (7 lines)
```go
320 extraProtected := map[string]bool{}
321 for g := range protected {
322     extraProtected[g] = true
323 }
324 if cur, rerr := c.ResolveCurrent(); rerr == nil && cur != "" {
325     extraProtected[cur] = true
326 }
```
Trace: `ResolveCurrent` deliberately distinguishes absent (`"", nil`) from unsafe, dangling, unreadable, or unstatable current state (`error`) at `stagedgen.go:247-280`. GC drops that error, sorts generations by wall-clock-prefixed name, preserves only the newest two, and removes every older unprotected directory at `:348-369`. A current generation can be older in name after an NTP backward step (explicitly supported by the comments) or an operator rollback. A transient symlink/stat error then removes the active source instead of skipping GC.
Refutation attempt: A normal `Publish` makes the new current and usually places it in the retained name window, but GenID order is explicitly non-monotonic and GC is also called from cut/runtime paths. The existing old-current test covers successful resolution only. Missing current is already a clean no-generation case; returning on non-nil error does not impede first install. Candidate survives.
HPC/invariant check: A collector may delete an object only after positively excluding all live owners. Unknown current ownership is not absence. This is infrequent filesystem work, so failing closed has no dataplane cost.
Why it matters: The running process may continue, hiding the damage until restart or the next cut, when the active staged source has vanished and recovery/rollback loses its durable input.
Fix direction: Resolve and validate current-gen before any deletion; on non-nil error, return it and perform no generation removal. Keep missing-current as the existing nil case. Add tests for an older current with readlink/stat failure and for a backward-clock current outside the retention window.
Labels: upgrade, GC, crash-consistency, filesystem, fail-open, rollback
Dedup note: Searched `stagedgen`, `ResolveCurrent GC`, `current-gen error GC`, `GC delete current`, and `stagedgen fail closed`; no matching issue/index entry.
Verified against origin/master: Yes - identical base and `origin/master`.

Title: M7 - Config-drive secrets are exposed with umask-derived permissions for the duration of ISO construction
Severity: Medium
Confidence: High
Gate verdict: MATERIAL
Evidence: scripts/image/make_config_drive.py:85 (10 lines)
```python
85 argv = [tool, "-quiet", "-V", "xpf-config", "-J", "-r", "-o", out, stage]
86 subprocess.run(argv, check=True)
87 # The finished ISO embeds xpf.conf - the most secret-bearing day-0
88 # artifact. xorriso/genisoimage/mkisofs writes it under the process
89 # umask (~0022 -> 0644, world-readable) and it lingers in CWD until an
90 # explicit destroy, so any co-located UID could `isoinfo -x /xpf.conf`
91 # the secrets out. Restrict it to owner-only immediately after build,
92 # matching the deploy implementation (#4905-C). The owner still reads
93 # it fine when attaching it to the VM.
94 os.chmod(out, 0o600)
```
Trace: Both `make_config_drive.py:80-94` and `xpf-deploy.py:471-483` hand the final predictable path directly to the ISO tool under the caller umask, wait for the child, and chmod only after it exits. During the potentially multi-second build, another local UID can open the 0644 output and retain the descriptor after chmod. The payload includes root password hash, IKE PSK, SNMP community, and DDNS credentials. Focused reproduction recorded `iso_mode_before_builder_return=0o644` and `iso_mode_after_function=0o600`.
Refutation attempt: The source stage is mode 0700/0600 and final tests assert 0600, but neither protects the output while xorriso is writing it. "Immediately after build" still leaves the whole child runtime exposed, and chmod cannot revoke an already-open descriptor. Candidate survives.
HPC/invariant check: Secret artifacts must never be published with broader access, including intermediate creation. This is offline image tooling; private staging and atomic publication have negligible cost.
Why it matters: Any co-located user can race a documented secret-bearing artifact and recover long-lived authentication material despite the final mode appearing correct in audits and tests.
Fix direction: Build to a random path inside a 0700 directory on the destination filesystem (and/or run the child with umask 0077), chmod/fsync there, then atomically replace the requested output and fsync its directory. Add a blocking fake builder test that attempts a second-UID/open-style observation before child return.
Labels: secrets, config-drive, permissions, TOCTOU, deploy, image
Dedup note: Searched `day-0 ISO`, `make_config_drive`, `ISO creation 0644`, `chmod after xorriso`, `secret ISO race`, `4586`, and `4905-C`; no exact issue/index entry. #4586/#4905-C fixed persistent final mode; this finding is the distinct creation-time exposure left by that implementation.
Verified against origin/master: Yes - identical base and `origin/master`.
